title: Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage
summary: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
story: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
NEW YORK -- Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage, according to court records.
The case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in Brooklyn, New York, and is listed as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant.
Attorneys for Qualley and Antonoff did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The couple separated in July.

Qualley, 32, is an actor known for films including “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer who has worked with artists including Taylor Swift, Lana Del Rey and Sabrina Carpenter. He is also a member of the band Bleachers.
The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023.

title: Judge orders 3 taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads to be pulled
summary: A judge has ordered the federal government to pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads from television, social media and elsewhere that she says appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes
story: A judge has ordered the federal government to pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads from television, social media and elsewhere that she says appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes

NEW YORK -- The federal government must pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads that appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes, including one touting the president’s claim that every American will get $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress in the upcoming election, a judge ruled Friday.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, in ordering the government to take down the advertisements entitled “$5,000 to Americans,” “Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips,” and “Cost of Socialism."

She said they must be taken off official government websites, including social media sites such as YouTube, Instagram and the like. She also ordered the cancellation of any slots, placements, reservations, or arrangements for the airing or distribution of the ads through authorized third parties, including by Trump’s flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc.
Responding to the ruling, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: "This Biden-appointed activist judge issued a lawless order to stop the administration from sharing patriotic videos.”

Rochon ruled during a hearing in which she considered expanding a temporary restraining order she issued two weeks ago, when she banned a series of ads that glorify President Donald Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs, according to the plaintiffs.

After Rochon issued the order, she noted that she was doing so on a Friday afternoon and that the government would have no excuse to delay taking them down immediately. Rochon was nominated to the court by then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
A government lawyer acknowledged that he would be able to immediately notify relevant individuals responsible for taking down the ads.

“Everyone is here. Everyone can hear my order. No one is at the theater,” the judge quipped in a reference to excuses offered by government lawyers when her recent order, which was issued during a weekend, wasn't immediately obeyed.

The plaintiffs sought the removal of at least 13 ads, but Rochon only ordered that the three be pulled, at least for now. She said there are instances in which the president's office is entitled to inform the public of its policies, justify its policies and respond to attacks on its policies.
Rochon said the plaintiffs were seeking to restrict the office in ways that were “broad and far reaching” and she found herself siding with the government on many of the ads.

But she added that irreparable harm could result to the plaintiffs if she didn't ban the ads while the court case proceeds, though she noted that she could reverse herself and restore the ads or ban additional ads after hearing more evidence in the coming weeks.

“This court can neither postpone an election nor turn back the clock,” Rochon said after concluding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims regarding the ads and would suffer harm if they were not taken down.

“This temporary restraining order will stop the administration’s wanton disregard for the law while the court hears the full case,” said Bradley Girard, a lawyer with Democracy Forward. “Congress has made clear that partisan ads cannot be funded with taxpayer dollars, and we are proud to work with this coalition to earn today’s result.”

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
summary: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her
story: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her

MIAMI BEACH, Fla. -- Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.

The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.

Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations. Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.

According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on Aug. 28. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later — after Ross left — to collect her belongings.

Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin'.”

The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin'” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.

Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: King Charles III arrives in Guyana as part of official 9-day Caribbean trip
summary: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era
story: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era

GEORGETOWN, Guyana -- GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AP) — King Charles III arrived Thursday in Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era.
Charles landed in the South American country following an invitation from Guyanese President Irfaan Ali, who has publicly requested an apology as some Caribbean leaders press for slavery reparations.
Charles, who is on a nine-day official trip in the Caribbean, descended from the plane in a tan suit and greeted Ali, who was wearing an all-ivory Jodhpuri suit.

Guyana is a diverse country of some 840,000 people that recently became one of the world’s largest offshore oil producers after massive oil deposits were discovered off its coast more than a decade ago.
About 36% of Guyana’s population is Black while 50% is East Indian, descended from indentured servants from India brought to the South American country after slavery was abolished.
Charles last visited Guyana in 2000 as a prince.
He is scheduled to meet with Ali, business owners and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos” during his two-day stay in Guyana.

Hilary Beckles, head of the Caribbean Reparations Commission, said at a recent press conference that the region has never been better prepared to confront Britain and the monarchy about its links to slavery.
“The region is mobilized, the governments are mobilized," he said.
The commission was established by regional governments to make Britain and other former European slave-trading nations pay reparations for their role.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
The British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.

Charles was previously in the Bahamas and is scheduled to arrive Friday in Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

title: Elke Sommer, German-born star of ‘A Shot in the Dark’ and ‘The Prize,’ dies at 85
summary: Elke Sommer, the German actor known for her roles in 1960s Hollywood comedies and espionage films, has died at 85
story: Elke Sommer, the German actor known for her roles in 1960s Hollywood comedies and espionage films, has died at 85
Elke Sommer, the striking blonde bombshell of German descent who was a mainstay of 1960s Hollywood comedies and espionage movies including “The Prize” and “A Shot in the Dark,” has died. She was 85.

Sommer died at home in Bel Air, in Los Angeles, on Wednesday, her stepson Sebastian Walther told the German outlet Bild. The Los Angeles Police Department told The Associated Press that it responded to the death of an 85-year-old woman on Sommer’s block Wednesday night.

With big almond eyes and golden locks, often styled high in a beehive, Sommer worked with some of the biggest stars of the time, including Paul Newman in “The Prize,” Peter Sellers in the Pink Panther film “A Shot in the Dark,” James Garner and Dick Van Dyke in “The Art of Love,” Bob Hope in “Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number!” and Dean Martin and Sharon Tate in “The Wrecking Crew.”

Sommer was born Elke Schletz in Berlin in the midst of the World War II, on Nov. 5, 1940, though the family had to evacuate to the south in 1942. Her father, who died when she was 14, was a Protestant pastor.

She’d intended to study languages, but during a trip to Italy with her mother, Renata, in 1958, she caught the eye of someone in the Italian film industry who invited her to appear in her first film: “The Friend of the Jaguar.” Actor and filmmaker Vittorio De Sica noticed her too, and soon she was working nonstop throughout Europe, in Italy, Spain and England, with the newly adopted surname Sommer.

Her big Hollywood break came from producer Pandro S. Berman, who had seen her in a German drama that screened for the Golden Globes, and offered her a role in “The Prize” where she played chaperone and love interest to Newman’s Nobel Prize-winning character. In the trade publication Variety’s review, they wrote that Sommer, “hasn’t a very scintillating role, but has the looks to make that a secondary issue.” And it would win her the Golden Globe for most promising newcomer.

In Blake Edwards’ Pink Panther sequel “A Shot in the Dark,” she played Maria Gambrelli, a maid framed for murder, who also sparks the romantic interest of Sellers’ Inspector Clouseau. She also posed for Playboy Magazine around that time, in photographs shot by her first husband Joe Hyams. They married in November 1964 and divorced in 1981.
In 1993 she married German hotelier Wolf Walther, who died in July at age 77.

Sommer didn’t take the sex symbol designation too seriously, saying that it was essentially meaningless. She told Film Talk in a 2014 interview that some of her favorite actors, like Rita Hayworth and Ava Gardner, were also considered sex symbols. Besides, she said, she was always just acting the part.

“My whole life, I have been directed, I have been produced, I spoke the lines written for the character,” she said in the interview. “I was always playing, and the only thing I could bring was my energy. So what is it, this sex appeal? Why was I voted in this list of most sexy women? It’s not because of my looks or anything; it’s because of the energy.”

title: Hometown of ‘Addams Family’ creator becomes ghoulish Halloween destination
summary: The New Jersey town that helped birth “The Addams Family” is embracing its ghoulish legacy
story: The New Jersey town that helped birth “The Addams Family” is embracing its ghoulish legacy
WESTFIELD, N.J. -- Before there was “The Addams Family,” there was Westfield.

Cartoonist Charles Addams, who created the eccentric, fictional family, drew inspiration for his signature macabre style from the elegant Victorian homes, historic cemetery and other landmarks of his New Jersey hometown.
Today the affluent community, about 25 miles (40 kilometers) southwest of Manhattan, has embraced its ghoulish legacy, honoring its darkly humorous native son each October with AddamsFest.
Downtown storefront windows have been transformed into temporary canvases for seasonal scenes depicting Gomez, Morticia, Wednesday, Pugsley and the rest of the family.
Throughout the month, there are Addams-themed events, including an art exhibit, a music and beer festival, a masquerade ball and a competition among homeowners for spookiest front lawn display.

“Everyone really gets into it,” said resident Kelly Heuschkel, whose young daughter is dressing up, appropriately, as Wednesday Addams this Halloween. “I think people decorate more for Halloween here than they do for Christmas.”
Joy Fox was among the visitors surprised that such a seemingly picturesque town could have inspired something so morbid.
“It looks like a very nice suburb,” the Cleveland, Ohio, resident remarked as she passed by Addams’ childhood home one recent afternoon. “I grew up watching the ‘Addams Family.’”
The monthlong festival, which is completing its ninth year, was launched when the town’s former mayor sought something uniquely Westfield for the town to celebrate.
Dawn Mackey, a former town councilor who helped found AddamsFest, admits that there was some initial skepticism when the idea of leaning into Addams’ lore was first floated.
“A lot of people didn’t even know he was from here,” she said.

But Mackey said she knew organizers had struck a chord when a visiting family once rattled off their three-stop Halloween itinerary to her: Salem, Massachusetts; Sleepy Hollow, New York, and Westfield.
“I felt like that was the moment,” she said.
Mackey said it was pure “serendipity” that the festival launched in 2018, the year before “The Addams Family” animated movie was released, followed by its sequel in 2021.
The hit Netflix series “ Wednesday,” focusing on the family’s dour, fiercely independent daughter, also helped introduce a new legion of fans to the frightful family.
Beyond the festival events, visitors can take in some of the town’s sights by foot. A self-guided heritage trail covers landmarks that informed Addams’ art.
At Addams' colonial-style childhood home, a historic marker says his grandmother lived in the attic and is believed to be the inspiration for the fictional Grandmama Addams.

Nearby, along the street a young Addams likely walked to school, is a Victorian-era house that helped inspire the fictional family's imposing, gothic abode. A miniature version of the family’s fictional mansion sits in the middle of a pond in the town center.
Farther along, there’s an old cemetery next to a white steeple church filled with tombstones dating to colonial times that officials say a young Addams frequented.
A historic movie theater with an old-time marquee hosts an art exhibit showcasing a selection of Addams' work on loan from his family foundation, alongside related pieces from local artists.
An entire section of a barn wall has also been cut out and preserved in order to display a life-size skeleton drawing made by a young Addams.

“The entire barn was graffitied except for this piece,” Mackey explained. “It was as if decade after decade, teenagers who hung out in this barn still had a reverence, even though they didn’t know who drew this.”
Mackey says Addams was ahead of his time, drawing strong female lead characters and quirky families that resonate generations later.

Addams spent most of his career as a cartoonist for The New Yorker magazine, which published many of his Addams family cartoons, including his very first, in 1938. He died in New York in 1988 at the age of 76.

At the Addams art exhibit, Mackey highlighted one piece depicting Wednesday and Pugsley waiting beside the fireplace for the arrival of Santa on Christmas. But instead of leaving out milk and cookies, the mischievous siblings are lighting a roaring fire to torch St. Nick as he comes down the chimney.

“Every wholesome town has secrets and a dark side. I think he saw that,” Mackey said of Addams. “To take the darkest parts of people and put a spin on it, that makes it funny instead of terrifying, and that’s what he did best.”

title: South Carolina police close investigation into Hayden Panettiere's death after coroner's ruling
summary: Police in South Carolina say they have closed their investigation into the overdose death of actor Hayden Panettiere following a coroner’s findings that it was accidental
story: Police in South Carolina say they have closed their investigation into the overdose death of actor Hayden Panettiere following a coroner’s findings that it was accidental
Police in South Carolina have closed their investigation into the overdose death of actor Hayden Panettiere following a coroner's finding that it was accidental.
The decision was based on the medical examiner's determination as well as the findings of the investigation, Greenville police said Wednesday in a statement.
Panettiere, who starred in the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead in an apartment in Greenville on Aug. 16 at age 36 after paramedics found her unresponsive.

A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press last month said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, and she had been in rehab just weeks before. Her on-and-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.

It remains unclear whether federal authorities may still be examining the case separately. In a petition to a California court last month, Panettiere's ex-fiance, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, said some of her property had been taken by federal law enforcement agents investigating her death and by an unnamed nonrelative looking to sell it.

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment Wednesday, and Greenville police Sgt. Diana Munoz said she could not comment on whether any other agencies were investigating.
The California court granted Klitschko legal status this month to protect Panettiere’s property for their 11-year-old daughter, who is her sole heir.

In “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” a memoir that was published in May, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter’s birth in 2014. The girl went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2.
Panettiere’s father told investigators that at the time of her death, she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later.

title: Movie Review: In the family drama ‘Gentle Monster,’ the evil is coming from inside the house
summary: Léa Seydoux plays a mother in crisis in “Gentle Monster.”
story: Léa Seydoux plays a mother in crisis in “Gentle Monster.”

“Gentle Monster” lets you fall a little bit in love with Lucy, Philip and their young son Johnny, before blowing everything up. This is a film about moral and societal evils and the webs we might spin to give a loved one the benefit of the doubt. Filmmaker Marie Kreutzer is not interested in letting the audience off the hook with a villain that looks like a villain.

Instead, Philip (Laurence Rupp) seems to be a loving father to Johnny (Malo Blanchet) and partner to Lucy ( Léa Seydoux ), a popular avant garde musician who plays experimental covers of well-known songs. Philip is a filmmaker who has had to work in television to pay the family bills. And we meet them in a moment of transition — Lucy has been practicing at the piano, a slowed down, melancholy version of Charles & Eddie’s “Would I Lie To You” when Philip comes home sobbing. He is in the midst of some kind of breakdown.

We next see them relocating to a peaceful home in the German countryside, where they make love on a mattress on the floor, build a trampoline for Johnny and talk about getting rid of their cellphones altogether. It is a quiet, peaceful and bohemian life and there is evident love and joy in this family. And then, one day, several police cars descend on the house with a warrant to confiscate Philip’s computer and hard drives. He’s ashen but does not seem to protest. This is a man who knows why the police are there. Lucy does not.

But we’ll all learn together when she heads to the police station and looks for department K17. In the elevator she pushes the button for the second floor. K17, we discover, deals in sexualized violence against children and child sexual abuse images. She’s barely had time to register the words when the elevator door cruelly opens and she wanders into the office in a daze.
Philip has left and she gazes out through a window to see him in the parking lot, with his lawyer, lighting a cigarette. But he quit smoking, she says.

An officer, a young woman, Elsa Kuhn (Jella Haase), informs Lucy that Philip is active in online forums, and there’s an investigation into whether he may have produced content himself. This is about 20 minutes into a nearly two-hour film in which we and Lucy process this information.

Lucy leaves their countryside home with Johnny immediately, going straight to her mother’s house ( Catherine Deneuve plays mom), but avoids telling her, or anyone else, the specifics of this sudden separation. She is, you suspect, holding out hope that it’s all a big misunderstanding, that there is some explanation and that she’d rather not risk having their friends and family know anything. It’s also certainly a bit of denial, and she’s eager to grasp at threads that might make it a little less bad in her mind. But really, how much solace is there in believing that Philip might have done it for money instead of pleasure? And then there is the looming question of whether Johnny might also be a victim.

Seydoux is movingly understated in this difficult film and role, with the camera often lingering on her face in harsh close-up. There are no obvious Oscar reels here, monologues or breakdowns. Instead, she masterfully draws you in and keeps your attention in a slow-burn film where not all that much happens.

We also get a bit of a glimpse into Elsa’s home life, where her senile father seems to be developing a habit of harassing his female caretakers. Elsa, for whom the issue is so black and white in her job, offers a nurse on her way out the door more money to stay and look the other way.

Kreutzer, the Austrian writer-director, was inspired to start working on this idea by distressing reports of a pedophile network in Germany. Then she too found herself uncomfortably close to the situation. A principal actor in her excellent Empress Elisabeth film “Corsage,”Florian Teichtmeister, was charged with possessing and producing child sex abuse images and would be found guilty.

Some have criticized “Gentle Monster” for not digging deeper, for not offering any resolution, for positing the uncomfortable idea that we’re the ones who are enabling the villains and maybe even suggesting that no men are to be trusted.

I don’t think Kreutzer is saying that all men are secret pedophiles or sex pests, even if you might walk out of “Gentle Monster” with that gnawing feeling. Lines blur when loved ones are involved, and mothers will always want to protect their sons.

There’s always that neighbor who will say things like “he was always nice to me” or “he was the last guy I’d suspect would do this.” “Gentle Monster” is a film that wants you to question your own complicity, to remove the blinders that obscure and excuse and to just look a little more closely at our world. Similar to Lucy's songs, it's a deconstructed social horror in a minor, haunting key.

“Gentle Monster,” a Netflix release in theaters Friday and streaming Nov. 18, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “graphic nudity, some language and sexuality.” Running time: 114 minutes. Three stars out of four.

title: Bill Raftery might have 'a little kiss' for the pope's ring at college hoops season opener in Rome
summary: Bill Raftery is gearing up for his first college basketball broadcast of the season, and it’s a special one
story: Bill Raftery is gearing up for his first college basketball broadcast of the season, and it’s a special one
ROME -- Hold the onions. Don't mention the lingerie. But maybe “a little kiss” of the pope's ring.
Bill Raftery is considering dialing back some of his famous catchphrases for his first broadcasting assignment of the college basketball season.
That’s because Pope Leo XIV could be listening.
Raftery will be the Fox analyst when Leo’s alma mater, Villanova, meets fellow Catholic university Notre Dame in Rome on Sunday. The Eternal City Tip-Off was created to honor the first American pope.

Raftery is known for phrases like “onions!” for clutch baskets and “lingerie on the deck” for when a defender figuratively gets faked out of their shorts by an opponent. And, of course: “With a little kiss” for old-school bank shots off the glass.

“I’ve got to refrain from some probably in deference to the pope,” Raftery told The Associated Press in a phone interview before flying to Rome. “But something might pop out that might cost me a day in the confessional booth.”
Because, as Raftery explained, “anything I’ve ever done has been spontaneous.”
More than halfway through his fifth decade as a college basketball commentator, Raftery is relishing his first trip to Rome since his 1969 honeymoon.

The event — it’s a doubleheader between the Villanova and Notre Dame men’s and women’s teams, though Raftery will call only the men’s game — includes a private audience with the pope on Saturday for the four teams and their fans.

“It’s a business trip, but this one’s got side doors to go out and see some incredible sights,” Raftery said, adding that between his wife, Joan, four children and multiple grandchildren, “over 10 of us will be there.”

Raftery wishes one more person could experience the trip, too: Rollie Massimino, the coach who guided Villanova to the 1985 NCAA title in one of the greatest upsets in the history of college basketball. Massimino died in 2017.
“I would love to see Rollie (meet) the pope. He would be advising him on church matters, business matters, basketball,” Raftery said. “And food, too.”

After coaching Seton Hall for 11 seasons, Raftery started commentating on games in the 1980s. Along with Dick Vitale, he was a pioneer in bringing catchphrases into the expanding college game, becoming a beloved fixture of the game.

“Part of what you’re doing, not that you think of it as entertainment, but it’s to make the audience enjoy what they’re watching,” Raftery said. “I can’t express deep enough to just be a small part of a lot of kids’ lives and a lot of great institutions. It’s like you got on the bandwagon and you never got off. Everything I did or said, was to be said succinctly and with meaning — to get in and out of the play-by-play man’s way.”

Despite his longevity and dedicated fan following, Raftery wasn’t elevated to CBS’ lead Final Four analyst until 2015 when he replaced Greg Anthony, who was arrested on a charge of soliciting a prostitute.
Raftery is in his mid-80s but keeps his exact age a mystery: He says he was born in April 1941, but that he's 86.

One of the hallmarks of Raftery’s career has been his dedication to the Big East. He was there in 1985 when three Big East teams reached the Final Four and Massimino’s Villanova upset Georgetown for the title.
“I was at the game and sat with Mike Tranghese, eventually the Big East commissioner. Dave (Gavitt) was the commissioner then,” Raftery said. “It was like a signature event for all of us.”

Raftery left ESPN in 2013 when the Big East’s media rights switched to Fox. Now Fox has multiple conferences and he calls games across the country with play-by-play partner Gus Johnson, who has plenty of fans of his own for his unabashed approach to calling games.

“The biggest thing, no matter what game you do, it’s a really important game for a lot of people. Whether it’s the schools, the towns, the communities,” Raftery said. “I’ve never really delineated what the league is when I’m going in, as much as trying to do as much good for these kids and these programs that their performance will allow.”
Raftery finishes each season with CBS at the Final Four.
So what does Raftery make of the current college landscape, which is dominated by roster chaos thanks to the transfer portal; name, image and likeness payments and conference realignment?

“I don’t know of anybody who likes it, but if you’re in it, you’ve got to play by the rules,” he said. “A lot of coaches have left. Some can afford to leave. … My only concern is these kids that don’t make it to the level that they’re all playing for. And are they sure they have a degree? Are they sure that they have a major that will help them contribute in life, raise a family?”
Those concerns fade away when game times come around, though.
“The greatest thing for anybody that does what we do is between 7 and 9 (p.m.), nobody cares about the rules, the eligibility,” Raftery said. “They just want to watch the game.”

Raftery is a basketball lifer: He starred in high school and college (for La Salle) before being drafted by the New York Knicks but never played in the NBA. He grew up in Kearny, New Jersey, which is known as “Soccer Town USA” and still enjoys watching that sport, too.

His late brother, Francis Raftery, was a state champion soccer coach at St. Cecilia High School in Kearny and also a teacher, principal and superintendent. His late sister was a nun: Sister Francis (Rita) Raftery served 16 years as president of what is now Saint Elizabeth University.
Raftery’s mother kept a strict Catholic household.
“We had to say the rosary every night,” Raftery said, recounting how he and his brother would groan about it. “My mom went every morning to church. She sort of set the standards for everybody.
So might Raftery be considering retirement as he prepares to call his first game in Rome?
“What a way to go out, right?” he said, but then added that he has no health issues and prefers to wait until his employers decide that he’s done.

“I’m just as enthusiastic as I was when I started," he said. "I enjoy what I’m doing. It keeps you young, interested, and you feel like you can still contribute. Hopefully, I’ll be able to do that until the bell rings."
