Puente acknowledged that the German-made LZB system regularly goes offline due to many factors, including damage to infrastructure from vandalism, maintenance work and bad weather. He said it has gone offline 170 times this year, but that is “normal” within the average of recent years.
The minister added that Spain is ahead of most other European countries in replacing it with a new system demanded by the European Union.
Investigators from a special committee for rail accidents removed the trains’ black boxes late Thursday and gave them to the Civil Guard for inspection. A judge is also investigating the crash.

Seventy families have presented missing persons reports to police for unaccounted-for passengers. Only five bodies have been identified so far. Thirty-nine people remain hospitalized on Friday from the over 200 who were injured.
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain.

title: Kim attends a North Korean drone exhibition and calls for boosting the technology
summary: North Korea says leader Kim Jong Un attended a drone-only exhibition and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology
story: North Korea says leader Kim Jong Un attended a drone-only exhibition and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended a drone-only exhibition, apparently the first of its kind in the North, and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology, state media reported Friday, as his military escalates threats against South Korea and the U.S.

Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to beef up both conventional and nuclear capabilities. Experts say his troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine likely gained valuable expertise on drone warfare from Russian forces and their own battlefield experiences.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of uncrewed aeronautical technology.

In a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to seize “the absolute superiority in the drone technology” and announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.

South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it appeared to be North Korea's first exhibition exclusively dedicated to drone technology. South Korean media reported the exhibition displayed more than 30 kinds of drones including stealth drones and first-person-view attack drones.

To mark the event, KCNA said North Korea conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from the 600 mm-caliber ultraprecision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him. South Korea's spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim's heir.

South Korea's military earlier said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off the North's east coast on Thursday. They were North Korea's first ballistic weapons firings in 17 days.

Tensions between the two Koreas are running high since last month's land mine blasts at their border that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

North Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday slammed an ongoing U.S.-South Korea combined aerial exercise as “provocative” and warned it was increasing the danger of an armed conflict. South Korea's military earlier said the two-week biannual Freedom Flag drill was to run until Nov. 6 and was meant to improve combined operational capabilities. It said aerial assets like fighter jets, helicopters and drones would be mobilized.

North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.

On Saturday, Kim made a surprise visit to a Chinese border town via a newly opened bridge and vowed to develop bilateral ties. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea's economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by supplying thousands of troops and ammunitions likely in return for economic and military assistance.

Meanwhile, Switzerland’s Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday to see the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang and meet North Korean officials. He is travel on to South Korea on Friday.

title: Court orders Erin Patterson never to be released from prison for mushroom poisonings
summary: An Australian appeals court has ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the “shocking criminality” involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband’s relatives with death cap mushrooms
story: An Australian appeals court has ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the “shocking criminality” involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband’s relatives with death cap mushrooms

MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian appeals court on Friday ordered triple-murderer Erin Patterson to never be released from prison because of the “shocking criminality” involved in poisoning four of her estranged husband’s relatives with death cap mushrooms.

The three judges of the Victoria state Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson's appeal of her convictions and upheld prosecutors' challenge to the leniency of her 33-year nonparole sentence, meaning she will spend the rest of her life behind bars. Beforehand, she would have been 82 years old when she could be considered for release.
“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of all three judges.
“In all the circumstances after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period,” McLeish added.

Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be imprisoned for life without possibility of parole. The first is meatworker Katherine Knight, who was sentenced in New South Wales state in 2001 for the murder a year earlier of her partner John Price, whom she'd stabbed at least 37 times.
Patterson's convictions stemmed from a family meal she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023.
She can apply to Australia's High Court to overturn the verdicts on her sentence and her convictions. The High Court is her last appeal option.
Patterson insisted she added death cap mushrooms to the beef Wellington pastry dishes accidentally.
She was sentenced last year to three life sentences for murder and 25 years for attempted murder.

The deaths of Patterson’s parents-in-law Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, within days of having lunch immediately attracted an extraordinary level of global media attention.
The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations.
Emmy-nominated actor Melanie Lynskey announced this week she will star as Erin Patterson in a six-episode series for the subscription video-on-demand streaming service Paramount+.
Lynskey is also executive producer of the series that dramatizes the 97 days from the fatal lunch until Patterson's arrest.
Heather’s husband Ian Wilkinson survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital. Erin Patterson was convicted of his attempted murder.
Prosecutors argued at an appeal hearing in August that she should never become eligible for parole.
They argued the minimum period behind bars did not reflect the “calculated criminality” of the case.
McLeish said Patterson's intent to murder all four was sustained for almost three weeks from when she invited them to lunch.
Her crimes involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including falsely claiming a cancer diagnosis to explain the absences of her two children from the lunch, the judge said.
The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Erin Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice about what to tell the children about her diagnosis.
McLeish noted Erin Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from.
“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust,” McLeish said.
Patterson opted not to attend court and watched the verdicts by video link from prison.

Because of her notoriety, Patterson is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne’s Dame Phyllis Frost Centre women’s prison. The unit is for prisoners assessed as being at high risk from other inmates.
In sentencing her in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Bale said there was a “substantial chance” that Patterson could be held in “solitary confinement for years to come.”
Patterson’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was invited to the lunch but declined the day before.
After her conviction, pretrial evidence was released that detailed the husband's suspicion that Erin Patterson had previously attempted to kill him.
Simon Patterson testified at a pretrial hearing that he had declined the lunch invitation out of fear.

title: King Charles III arrives in Guyana as part of official nine-day Caribbean trip
summary: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era
story: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era

GEORGETOWN, Guyana -- GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AP) — King Charles III arrived Thursday in Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era.
Charles landed in the South American country following an invitation from Guyanese President Irfaan Ali, who has publicly requested an apology as some Caribbean leaders press for slavery reparations.
Charles, who is on a nine-day official trip in the Caribbean, descended from the plane in a tan suit and greeted Ali, who was wearing an all-ivory Jodhpuri suit.

Guyana is a diverse country of some 840,000 people that recently became one of the world’s largest offshore oil producers after massive oil deposits were discovered off its coast more than a decade ago.
About 36% of Guyana’s population is Black while 50% is East Indian, descended from indentured servants from India brought to the South American country after slavery was abolished.
Charles last visited Guyana in 2000 as a prince.
He is scheduled to meet with Ali, business owners and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos” during his two-day stay in Guyana.

Hilary Beckles, head of the Caribbean Reparations Commission, said at a recent press conference that the region has never been better prepared to confront Britain and the monarchy about its links to slavery.
“The region is mobilized, the governments are mobilized," he said.
The commission was established by regional governments to make Britain and other former European slave-trading nations pay reparations for their role.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
The British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.

Charles was previously in the Bahamas and is scheduled to arrive Friday in Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

title: A helicopter with the EU force in Bosnia crashes, reportedly killing 3 and injuring 12
summary: A Italian helicopter of the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia has crashed in the country’s north
story: A Italian helicopter of the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia has crashed in the country’s north

SARAJEVO, Bosnia-Herzegovina -- A helicopter with the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia crashed Thursday in the country's north and "a number” of personnel died or were injured in the accident, according to a statement from the force.

Officials told local media in Bosnia that three people died and 12 were injured in the crash of the Italian CH-47 Chinook in an area around the town of Brcko. The EU force, or EUFOR, said an investigation was underway and more information will follow later.
The Klix news portal carried photos of the wreckage showing a largely destroyed helicopter on a lawn.
The Brcko district mayor, Sinisa Milic, also told the Bosnian Serb RTRS television that three people died and 12 received medical care, including one person in critical condition.
EUFOR said earlier in a separate statement that “no civilian infrastructure, property, or vehicles were damaged, and there were no injuries to civilians.”

EUFOR's 1,200-soldier mission took over from NATO in 2004 to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of a peace agreement that ended the 1992–95 war. It operates under a U.N. Security Council mandate.

title: Polish opposition leader floats EU exit talks to force reforms
summary: Poland's main opposition leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, suggests that countries led by nationalist parties could negotiate leaving the European Union
story: Poland's main opposition leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, suggests that countries led by nationalist parties could negotiate leaving the European Union

WARSAW, Poland -- A year before Poland’s general election, the country's main opposition leader suggested that countries led by nationalist parties could open negotiations to leave the European Union to pressure it to return powers to member states.

“The European Union must be changed. This is my deep conviction, shared by my party and, I believe, very many Poles,” Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice, said Wednesday at an economic forum in southern Poland.

He said EU institutions like the European Commission, the EU's executive body, have too much influence, but that upcoming elections in France and Spain, which could bring far-right politicians to power, could open the way for discussions about change.
He offered several ideas for change, including having national parliamentarians monitor how often EU bodies break EU law.

But as a last resort, he suggested that countries seeking reform could conclude a new treaty that would take effect at a later date while simultaneously opening EU withdrawal negotiations. He presented that as a way to pressure other countries and EU bodies to accept changes.
His remarks sparked criticism from senior government figures in Poland.
“Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the conditions of leaving the European Union," the pro-European prime minister, Donald Tusk, wrote on X.
Kaczyński accused Tusk of misrepresenting his intentions. “We want the union to benefit not the elites, but the ordinary citizens,” Kaczyński shot back on X.
Poland, a key country on NATO’s eastern flank and one of the EU’s fastest-growing economies, has gained strategic importance in recent years, partly through its crucial role in supporting Ukraine.
Kaczyński’s party led Poland between 2015 and 2023, leading to major conflicts with EU institutions over the rule of law and human rights.
One year ahead of general elections, polls indicate that Kaczyński could bring his party back to power if he allies with smaller far-right groups that have been on the rise in Poland in recent years.

Kaczyński said the EU reform he is advocating was focused on “improving citizens' living conditions, lowering energy prices, strengthening security, pursuing a responsible migration policy and an ambitious economic and agricultural policy without unnecessary bureaucracy.”
Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said Kaczyński's remarks should help Polish voters understand the consequences of choosing the far-right.
“I thank Jarosław Kaczyński for his honesty,” Sikorski said.

title: Families hold out hope for loved ones missing after deadly Spain train crash
summary: Families are desperately searching for missing loved ones after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
story: Families are desperately searching for missing loved ones after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain

TOLEDO, Spain -- Families desperately searched for missing loved ones Thursday, more than 24 hours after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing at least 69 and injuring dozens of others.

“I have my father, and I don’t know where he is. I hope to find him, oh my Lord," said César Vicente, an actor who traveled 495 kilometers (307 miles) from his native Seville to Toledo in search of his father. He spent the night with many other families at a religious center converted into a base for those affected by the disaster.

Vicente was with his mother and his aunt, all of whom were looking for César Vicente, who was sitting in seat 13A on the RENFE train that struck another operated by the private company Iryo, which had stopped on the tracks. The family was among those who braved the cold to take a short walk on a chilly morning.
“I don’t want this to happen to anyone. This is unbearable,” he added. “This is hell.”

Online, relatives and friends flooded social media with desperate appeals for information on the whereabouts of their loved ones, posting photos or describing the clothes they were wearing when they boarded the trains bound for Seville and details about their physical appearance or the seat in which they were traveling.

In a post Wednesday on Instagram, Alejandra Marroquín told her followers that her sister Adriana, who was wearing dark blue clothes, was traveling in car 8 of the RENFE train and that they had been unable to contact her.
“We’re still praying, we don’t know anything,” Marroquín said in a post Thursday morning, as search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims.

“The entire government is working to respond to the victims’ families, shed light on the tragedy, and strengthen security so that this never happens again,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told reporters on Thursday morning.
This was the second high-speed rail disaster this year. In January, 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.

The high-speed rail network has been considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
Life in Urda, a small town of about 2,500 people south of Madrid, was turned upside down early Wednesday.

Residents rushed to help in any way they could: from assisting the injured to preparing sandwiches for the unharmed passengers, many of whom they even carried from the tracks to a nearby sports pavilion in their cars.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.

“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said.
With 180 people injured, including 110 taken to hospitals, authorities issued a call for blood donations.
The response was immediate: in Castilla-La Mancha alone, the region where the collision occurred, more than 2,000 people volunteered in the aftermath.

“I want to express my personal and very sincere gratitude to everyone who has stepped up, starting with the all-time record number of donations,” said the region’s president, Emiliano García-Page, who also thanked the 1,300 emergency service personnel who were mobilized.
Medrano reported from Madrid.

title: Haiti announces new election dates as 2,000 Salvadoran troops help fight gangs
summary: Haiti’s government has announced new election dates as police and soldiers, backed by over 2,000 troops from El Salvador, fight gangs
story: Haiti’s government has announced new election dates as police and soldiers, backed by over 2,000 troops from El Salvador, fight gangs
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Haiti’s government has announced new election dates as police and soldiers backed by the recent arrival of more than 2,000 troops from El Salvador fight gangs.
The Provisional Electoral Council said late Wednesday that the first round of general elections will be held next July 18 and the second round on Oct. 4.
Haiti has not held elections in more than a decade and is run by an unelected prime minister. The presidency has been vacant since President Jovenel Moïse was killed in 2021.
The council said it expects to publish the final candidate list, including those running for the presidency or the Senate, by mid-January, with May 20 marking the end of voter registration.

The first round of elections was initially scheduled for Dec. 13, but was delayed by gang violence in Haiti’s central region and in Port-au-Prince. Four aviation technicians from El Salvador working with a U.N.-backed gang suppression force went missing on Oct. 18 in the capital after coming under attack.
In response, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti to help rescue the four technicians, who the Haitian government says were abducted.

El Salvador’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement late Wednesday that Bukele had spoken with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé about the security operation to rescue the technicians.
Meanwhile, Haiti’s government issued a statement saying the two leaders are reinforcing cooperation within the framework of the U.N.-backed gang suppression force.
Experts have questioned exactly what role the Salvadoran troops are playing in Haiti.

Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said their rules of engagement, chain of command, objectives and duration “remain opaque.” He questioned what kind of coordination they might have with the gang suppression force, Haitian police and Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.

“Are we witnessing yet another model of deployment, parallel to the multilateral framework? The role of the United States, which supported and facilitated this deployment, also deserves scrutiny,” he said.
Le Cour said the number of Salvadoran troops in Haiti will surpass that of personnel in the gang suppression force, raising questions about the future of the U.N.-backed force.
“What does that mean for its authority, its coherence and its future?”
He added: “the most basic question remains unanswered: why were the Salvadoran technicians in a gang-controlled neighborhood in the first place?”
Le Cour and others also raised concerns about the safety of Haitian civilians caught in a gun battle between Haitian gangs and the international forces.

On Wednesday, Doctors Without Borders issued a statement calling on “the authorities and all parties involved to spare civilians and ensure access to health care facilities for all the wounded and sick, without distinction.”

The aid agency said it treated 30 patients injured by gunfire or drone explosions from Oct. 18-26, and that it took some of the wounded several hours to reach hospitals run by Doctors Without Borders.

“Roads and bridges are blocked, and any travel is extremely risky,” said Davina Hayles, Doctors Without Borders head of mission in Haiti. “In a capital city where the health care system has collapsed and many facilities are closed, it is essential to ensure there is access to functioning health care facilities like ours.”

More than 5,700 people have been killed or wounded in Haiti from January to mid-September, according to the U.N. Those recently killed include two Haitians who worked for the Norwegian Refugee Council.

“We call on all parties concerned, including Haitian authorities as well as the international community, to do everything in their power to protect civilians, uphold international law, and prevent further violence,” the council said in a statement Thursday. “Neither the Haitian society nor the outside world can tolerate that civilians, including aid workers, are killed with impunity.”

title: A rock formation collapse in Turkey's touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 2
summary: Parts of a large volcanic rock formation have crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia, killing at least two people and injuring five others
story: Parts of a large volcanic rock formation have crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia, killing at least two people and injuring five others

ANKARA, Turkey -- Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least two people and injuring five others, officials said.
A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams.
Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site.
He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris.
There was no immediate information on the nationalities of the dead.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident, in which five people were also injured.
HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation.

Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations.
The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.

title: China elevates a military general to Politburo, seeks to strengthen party discipline
summary: China's top leaders have elevated the only remaining general of the body that oversees the country's military to its Politburo, the Communist Party's top governing body
story: China's top leaders have elevated the only remaining general of the body that oversees the country's military to its Politburo, the Communist Party's top governing body
BANGKOK -- China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.

During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party’s leader.

The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China’s top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission’s only member besides Xi himself.

The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were “increasingly arduous,” such as “uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests.”
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.

The party should “with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people,” according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency. “The Party must remain unswerving in its commitment to a rigorous tone, improve the system for full and rigorous self-governance.”

Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials going for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
This version corrects the spelling of the general's name.

title: French prosecutor seeks pretrial detention for suspect in shooting near Paris
summary: France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor has asked for a 39-year-old suspect to be held in pretrial detention over a suspected racist attack in the Paris suburbs
story: France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor has asked for a 39-year-old suspect to be held in pretrial detention over a suspected racist attack in the Paris suburbs

PARIS -- France’s national counterterrorism prosecutor asked Thursday that a 39-year-old suspect be held in pretrial detention over a shooting in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded seven others, saying he targeted people he believed to be Muslim or from Africa.

The suspect, a 39-year-old French national identified by authorities as Kevin T., was arrested less than 20 minutes after the shooting began Friday in Trappes and neighboring La Verrière, a suburban area west of Paris. His last name has not been made public.
An 11-year-old girl was among the injured when a gunman fired from his vehicle at several locations along a 12-kilometer (7.5-mile) route.

The suspect “now acknowledged that the acts were premeditated,” national counterterrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen said. The suspect admitted to “specifically targeting” people he believed to be Muslim or from sub-Saharan Africa or North Africa based on their appearance, Christen said.
Christen added that the suspect said he chose the suburb of Trappes because it is “a haven for Islamists.”
He denied any terrorist intent and said “he had no regrets,” Christen added.

A judicial investigation has been opened into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the crimes were committed because of the victims’ actual or perceived race, ethnicity, nationality or religion.

Authorities identified the man killed as Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old Black French national. Four other people were seriously wounded, including one who remained Thursday in life-threatening condition. Three others suffered lighter injuries. Authorities have not disclosed details about the identities of those injured.

Christen said the suspect has a history of psychological and psychiatric problems and of drug addiction. Toxicology tests revealed the presence of cannabis and cocaine in his blood, as well as drugs prescribed by a doctor.
A search of his car uncovered a Sten-type submachine gun and investigators found his apartment had been booby-trapped with three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer.

Investigations have shown he bought several firearm parts last month, Christen said. Two days before the shooting, he deleted all his social media accounts, sold his laptop computer and concealed his phone, but police managed to find it.

Investigators also found Adolf Hitler’s manifesto “Mein Kampf” as well as stickers stored in a drawer with inscriptions including “Long live France," “Proud to be French,” and “RN,” the French acronym for far-right party National Rally.
The suspect told investigators he had himself designed and ordered the stickers. The suspect said he was neither a member nor a supporter of any political party, Christen said.

title: South African police seek court ban on anti-immigration marches
summary: South African police have approached the courts to stop planned marches by anti-illegal immigration groups in Durban
story: South African police have approached the courts to stop planned marches by anti-illegal immigration groups in Durban

JOHANNESBURG -- South African police have asked the courts to halt planned marches by anti-illegal immigration groups in the coastal city of Durban following alleged threats of violence and plans to burn down a refugee reception office in the city.
The application to block the marches follows recent violence at some of the demonstrations, which reportedly left a foreign national dead last week.
The KwaZulu-Natal High Court on Wednesday granted an interim order against the demonstrators, but will consider Friday whether to make the order permanent.
Some African countries have repatriated their citizens following the violence. In some cases, protesters have set unofficial deadlines for foreigners who had entered illegally to leave.
Earlier this month, at least 24 cars were torched and shops looted as protests over a court ruling easing access to asylum turned violent.
March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma criticized the government and police action, saying it was an attempt to suppress demonstrations.
The government has deployed over 500 soldiers to KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the city of Durban.
President Cyril Ramaphosa also spoke out against violence at the protests, vowing that the police would clamp down on people breaking the law.

“There are those who are exploiting public sentiment around illegal migration to stir up communities and to provide cover for criminality," Ramaphosa told a meeting of businesspeople in KwaZulu-Natal on Wednesday.
With South Africans set to vote in local elections next week, the issue of illegal immigration has featured prominently in the campaign.

title: European Central Bank head resigns, allowing EU leaders to choose successor before French election
summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before her term ends
story: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before her term ends

FRANKFURT, Germany -- European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months before the end of her term, a move that opens the way for European leaders to choose a successor ahead of France's presidential election next year.
Lagarde, 70, will leave Feb. 7, the ECB said Thursday. Her eight-year term was to end Oct. 31, 2027.

The resignation opens the way for complex political horse trading over her successor and replacements for two other top officials who are leaving next year. The ECB president leads the bank's governing council, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro currency, affecting borrowing costs for everything from house purchases to new factories and serving as the European Union's chief crisis fighter in times of economic and financial turbulence.

“It has been a great pride and a huge privilege to serve this institution,” Lagarde said in a video message posted on X. “I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future.”

Asked about her reasons at a news conference following the bank's decision to leave rates unchanged, she said that she wanted to be freed from the obligation of political neutrality that comes with being ECB head.

“I want to, have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” she said. “I don’t think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality at the present time." She didn't elaborate.

The announcement was expected following speculation that Lagarde would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose a successor while pro-EU French President Emmanuel Macron is still in office. That would guard against the possibility that right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen might win the election and influence the choice.
“That she leaves early is no surprise and does not change the outlook for ECB policies,” said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Berenberg bank.
European Council President Antonio Costa said that the selection process “will be initiated today and will proceed without delay.”

The term of another top ECB official — chief economist Philip Lane — is to end May 31, while another member of the ECB's executive board, Isabel Schnabel, is resigning Jan. 3 to move to the International Monetary Fund. European leaders are expected to work out a package deal to apportion the three vacancies among member countries in a complex round of political bargaining.
EU leaders would likely seek to reach agreement on all three posts before a summit meeting on Dec. 17-18, Schmieding said.

He said that leading candidates for Lagarde's job appeared to be former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. The BIS is an international organization of central banks.

“The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April-May 2027,” Schmieding wrote in an email. “Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Elysee Palace.”

Lagarde, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, was appointed in 2019 to succeed Mario Draghi. A key decision during her tenure came in 2020, when the bank deployed 1.35 trillion euros ($1.5 trillion) in emergency stimulus in the form of bond purchases to keep the COVID-19 pandemic from drying up credit for the economy.

The bank's ability to act swiftly — in contrast to the often drawn-out negotiations among the 27 European Union national governments — has given it a leading role in combating Europe-wide crises such as the pandemic and the peak period of the eurozone's debt crisis in 2010-2012. Most notably, Draghi's promise in 2012 to “do whatever it takes to preserve the euro” calmed bond market turmoil that raised fears the eurozone would break up.

Lagarde’s announcement overshadowed the bank’s decision Thursday to leave its interest rate benchmark unchanged at 2.5% despite annual inflation of 3.8% fed by high oil prices caused by the US-Iran war. High rates restrain inflation, which is above the bank’s target of 2%. However, rising bond market rates are already tightening credit independent of the ECB, in effect doing the central bank’s job for it, analysts say.
This story has been corrected to show Christine Lagarde succeeded Mario Draghi in 2019, not 2011.

title: Europe's economy brushes off energy shock from Iran war, shows moderate growth in Q3
summary: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before
story: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before

FRANKFURT, Germany -- Europe's economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the U.S.-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before.

The figure released Friday for the 21 European Union member countries that use the euro currency was better than the 0.2% expected by market analysts. Compared to the same quarter a year ago, the economy of the 21 countries using the euro grew by 1.3% in the July-September period, according to EU statistics agency Eurostat.
The continued growth shows that “households and businesses have not pared back their spending due to the Iran war,” said Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics.
“All in all, the eurozone economy remains resilient amid geopolitical turmoil and a worsening inflationary environment,” wrote Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics.

That is despite “worrying signs” that higher oil prices are spreading to other sectors. Those so-called second-round effects — where high oil prices start to influence wages and prices throughout the economy — would support higher interest rates from the European Central Bank.

Inflation of 3.8% remains above the 2% target set out by the ECB, which left rates unchanged at its policy meeting Thursday. That means the ECB may raise rates at its next meeting in December to cool inflation, imposing higher borrowing costs on the economy even as growth remains modest and unevenly distributed among member countries.

Germany, the largest of the euro economies, saw growth of 0.2% despite headwinds from high energy prices and low river levels that disrupted commerce. France, however, shrank by 0.1% as a political deadlock over how to address an outsized budget deficit continues to weigh on business confidence. Stronger performers were Spain, the Netherlands and Estonia with 0.6%

The eurozone growth figure was distorted by an increase of 5.5% in Ireland, where figures are volatile because it is host to multinational tech and pharmaceutical companies whose global activities can influence the figures. Excluding Ireland, growth was 0.2%.

title: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
summary: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
story: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
BARCELONA, Spain -- Was Spain's second major train collision this year caused by human error or failures in its once touted high-speed rail network?
It depends on whom you ask.
Spain’s transport minister was quick to lay most of the blame a traffic controller’s poor judgment for Wednesday's collision in Toledo province, which killed 69 people.

But railway unions are pushing back. They point instead to what they describe as deteriorated working conditions — fewer traffic controllers with more work than ever — that have made it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of 45 million passengers annually.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly crash, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged to get to the bottom of it.

“This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened,” Spain’s King Felipe VI said on Thursday after visiting injured passengers in a Toledo hospital. “We will have to take measures so this never happens again.”

The chain of events that ended in disaster started at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, when the communication system key to the functioning of the line’s security system went down. The system, called LZB, monitors the position of trains and can even trigger the automatic braking of a train to prevent a collision.

That malfunction meant that human controllers based at a control post in Madrid took over full responsibility for monitoring the positions and safety of the trains on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) between Madrid and Seville. At that time authorities believe there were six trains on the affected stretch of track.

At 8:36, a controller told one train, belonging to the state-owned RENFE company, that it could start running again at normal speed. The other train, operated by privately owned IRYO, located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) down the line, also tried to restart, but the engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and informed the controller.
At 8:53 the collision occurred, derailing carriages and shredding parts of the trains to bits.

It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, over two hours further south, one train jumped the track and hit another train going the other direction, killing 46 people.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente, who is under pressure to resign, called the controller's decision to let one train restart at full speed while the other remained still “inexplicable” and “erroneous.”
Puente said that the RENFE train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a stop signal active on that line.

“An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision,” Puente told reporters. The decision “was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Unions, however, argue that the context matters.

Raquel Ayllón, spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that the workload is regularly too much for the current staff to safely handle. She said that traffic controllers have been asking for more personnel for years, while the safety systems keep failing.

“We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” she said. “Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”

Spain's union for train engineers, SEMAF, said that this was not the first time the three-decade-old LZB security system, which is still in use on the Madrid-Seville line while being phased out, has gone offline and left human operators to fend for themselves.

“The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago,” said Diego Martín, spokesperson of the SEMAF union of Spain’s train engineers. “It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past.”
Train workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand the government fulfill its commitments to improve safety conditions after the January crash.
Representatives from several unions also criticized what they called the “irresponsible” leak of audio clips of conversations between the control room and the train engineers to Spanish media.
Spain’s railways only serviced state-owned trains until it opened its high-speed rail to private operators in 2021.
Both of this year’s collisions involved a train operated by RENFE and one operated by IRYO.

Rail traffic increased after the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for instance, the average number of daily trips increased from 56 to 89 between 2019 and 2024, according to the SCF union.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on railways.

“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

title: The sell-off for tech stocks drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
summary: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
story: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
NEW YORK -- A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 dropped 2.3% and was heading toward its worst day since June and a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 3.5%, as of 3:05 p.m. Eastern time, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 723 points, or 1.4%.

The U.S. stock market remains only 3.4% below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers' 401(k) accounts, but it's become increasingly shaky just days before Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States. Worries about AI in general have already become a bipartisan concern for voters, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market's performance as a measure of his own success.

Intel's stock led the way lower and is flirting with the worst day in its history, which goes back to 1972, after tumbling 30.7%. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon  sank 1.9% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.

A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12% to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.
A drop of 4.9% for the stock price of Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.

Coinbase Global fell 13.6% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 8.3%. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.
Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.
ExxonMobil climbed 1.8%, and Chevron added 1.7% after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.
Mondelez International rose 4% after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.
Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.9% after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 4.98% late Thursday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month.

Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4% to $113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.
South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5% as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5%.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1% after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: DEA approvals could bring big tax benefits for medical marijuana businesses
summary: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses
story: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana dispensaries, a bureaucratic maneuver under President Donald Trump's historic rescheduling of the drug that could pave the way for the businesses to receive tax benefits long denied the industry.

The agency issued the registrations Friday to more than 900 state-licensed dispensaries in Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia, the Justice Department said in a news release. The department did not immediately identify the approved businesses.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement that the regulated distribution of cannabis for medical use from those shops “will help ensure broader access to chronic pain treatment and the safety of the American people.”

In April, Blanche signed an order shifting the classification of state-licensed medical marijuana from Schedule I — reserved for drugs without medical use and with high potential for abuse, like heroin — to the less strictly regulated Schedule III.

The decision largely legitimized medical marijuana programs in the 40 states that have adopted them, and it set up an expedited system for state-licensed medical marijuana producers, manufacturers and distributors to register with the DEA. Businesses must undergo a pre-registration investigation and have security, recordkeeping, inventory controls and other safeguards governing the handling of controlled substances.

Registering with the agency is also expected to ensure immense tax benefits. Historically, state-licensed cannabis businesses haven't been able to deduct normal business expenses — like advertising, rent or labor costs associated with sales — on their federal taxes because they were dealing with a federally illegal, Schedule I drug. Many in the industry have found that financially crippling.
Nearly 7,000 other cannabis dispensaries, manufacturers and distributors across the country have similarly applied for registration, according to a list published by the DEA on Friday.

Steph Sherer, the founder of the medical cannabis organization Americans for Safe Access, noted that the registrations were issued just days before the 30th anniversary of California becoming the first state to legalize the medical use of marijuana.

“For the first time, the federal government is recognizing and registering the medical cannabis dispensaries that patients fought to establish," Sherer said in a written statement. "This is a tremendous victory for patient access and an opportunity to build on 30 years of progress.”

But questions abound. The way state-licensed medical marijuana businesses are regulated is vastly different from how most companies dealing with Schedule III drugs are overseen, and it remains unclear exactly what requirements the DEA may seek to impose on medical cannabis.

For example, some cannabis industry attorneys have noted, state regulators have often sought to mitigate the effects of the drug war by allowing people with some criminal history to run licensed marijuana businesses. It isn't certain whether the DEA will adopt that approach with the businesses it registers.

Furthermore, many states have merged their recreational and medical marijuana industries. While the Trump administration has sought to reschedule marijuana more broadly, it remains unclear how the DEA will treat businesses that handle both adult-use and medical cannabis.

Two dozen states plus Washington, D.C., have authorized adult recreational use of marijuana, 40 have medical marijuana systems, and eight others allow low-THC cannabis or CBD oil for medical use. Only Idaho and Kansas ban marijuana outright.

“It's obviously a positive step to see the program taking shape,” said Chris Lindsey, vice president of policy and state advocacy at the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp. “What everybody's watching for is, what can we expect to see now that we have companies that are going to be operating in this class? What are they going to have to start to do?”
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz in New York contributed.

title: ExxonMobil and Chevron top Q3 estimates on higher prices and strong output
summary: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
story: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production.

Besides the disruption caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine that have driven up the cost of fuel, Exxon is also seeing strong production in its fields in Guyana and the Permian Basin in the Southwest. Chevron said its results include one month of production in Venezuela where it’s making a big investment.
Utilization at Exxon's U.S. Gulf Coast refineries was at 100%, and U.S. Gulf Coast diesel production was at the second-highest on record.
The price of diesel, currently about $6.32 per gallon, is up 71% since last year, according to AAA. Regular gasoline is up about 38% in the past year as well.

Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chairman and CEO, noted that investments such as the expansion of its Beaumont refinery in Texas have contributed to an increase in its distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019.
For the third quarter, net income more than doubled to $3.72 per share. On an adjusted basis, profit totaled $4.23 per share, easily topping the average analyst estimate of $4.12 per share.
Revenue during the three months ended in September rose 33% to $113.16 billion, also beating estimates.
The Spring, Texas-based company also raised its quarterly dividend to $1.07 and set a $20 billion stock buyback plan.
Houston-based Chevron said Friday it earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, during the third quarter, as revenue surged 36% to $67.8 billion. Its results handily topped estimates.
Crude utilization at Chevron's U.S. refineries totaled 98%. The company said it set production records at its Eastern Mediterranean and Australian assets.

Chevron, the second-largest U.S. oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. Last month it announced it will invest $7 billion over the next five years in Venezuela. It said Friday that following an accounting-related change during the quarter, it’s now including those results.
Overall capital expenditures during the quarter were lower compared with a year ago because it spent less in the Permian Basin.

Mike Wirth, Chevron’s chairman and CEO, said that the company signed agreements to reduce Bakken midstream costs by about 50%, strengthening the asset’s competitiveness. Chevron increased its holdings in the Bakken fields in North Dakota and Montana following its $53 billion acquisition of Hess Corp. last year.
In premarket trading, Exxon shares rose 1.9%. The stock is up 64% in the past 12 months. Chevron shares rose 1.1%.

title: Dockworkers stage international strikes to denounce arms shipments
summary: Dockworkers across Europe and beyond are staging strikes as part of an international campaign against arms shipments and to demand better working conditions
story: Dockworkers across Europe and beyond are staging strikes as part of an international campaign against arms shipments and to demand better working conditions
PARIS -- Dockworkers in Europe and beyond were staging strikes on Friday as part of an international campaign against arms shipments and to demand better working conditions, unions said.
Unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco issued a joint call to demand an end to the wars in the Middle East, including the war in Gaza, and “an end to the militarization of ports.”
“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”
Organizers say more than 100 ports across multiple countries joined the protest movement that could affect port operations in parts of Europe, the Mediterranean region and North America.

In Greece, the ENEDEP dockworkers’ union has called for a strike at Piraeus, the country's largest port, as part of the international day of action. In addition, ships remained docked at several ports, disrupting ferry services, because of a separate seafarers' strike demanding better pay, working conditions and improved safety measures.
In Istanbul, Turkey, protesters gathered outside Haydarpasa port beneath a banner reading: “No to war, no to armament!”

Italy’s Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) said port demonstrations were planned in key ports, including Genoa, Trieste and Gioia Tauro, coinciding with a nationwide general strike called by major unions to protest rising living costs, low wages and military spending.

France's CGT ports and docks federation has called a one-day strike in major ports including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen to reject “the militarization of port facilities” under European policies and denounce the French government’s budget proposals, which the union says threaten social protections.
The scale of the disruption remained unclear. Organizers say participation will range from full-day strikes to shorter walkouts and demonstrations.

Supply chain management company C.H. Robinson issued an advisory to its clients that “operational disruptions and shipment delays may occur at participating ports, with the duration and severity expected to vary by port, terminal, and level of local participation.”
Experts said they expect the impact on the global supply chain to be limited.

Marcus Baker, global head of marine, cargo and logistics for insurance broker and risk adviser Marsh, said a 24-hour strike is unlikely to cause a material disruption to global trade flows, although it could affect perishable goods and time-sensitive shipments.

But it “adds another layer of complexity to supply chains already under pressure from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, climate-related events, including El Niño, restrictions affecting the Rhine and the Panama Canal, and shifting tariff regimes,” he said.

Judah Levine, head of research for online shipping marketplace Freightos, said at ports such as Genoa, where vessels are already waiting one to two days for a slot, the strike could exacerbate congestion.

Ed Anderson, a professor of supply chain and operations management for the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas, said the protest movement was not expected to cause outright shortages. “Just one day is not that much in terms of disruption,” he said.
Associated Press journalist Mae Anderson in New York contributed.

title: Volkswagen posts $6.5 billion quarterly loss amid China slump, Porsche writedown
summary: Volkswagen has posted a $6.5 billion after-tax loss for the July-September quarter
story: Volkswagen has posted a $6.5 billion after-tax loss for the July-September quarter

FRANKFURT, Germany -- FRANKFURT, Germany (AP) — Automaker Volkswagen posted a 5.8 billion euro ($6.5 billion) after-tax loss for the July-September quarter as large one-time charges piled on top of weak demand in China, U.S. tariffs and lower profits from electric vehicles.

The results announced Thursday underline the challenges facing the company as it seeks to cut costs through a restructuring that could mean the loss of up to 100,000 jobs and the closure of four German plants.
Chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a statement that the company's results so far this year mean that “we cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively.”

Sales revenue decreased 6.3% to 80.3 billion euros from the year-earlier quarter. Earnings also suffered from a 6.4 billion euro reduction to account for the fallen value of Volkswagen's stake in luxury carmaker Porsche.

China was once a key profit center for Volkswagen, but now the company faces declining demand for cars there on top of fierce price competition from local carmakers. U.S. tariffs, or import taxes, imposed by President Donald Trump have also weighed on profits, as has the increasing share of electric vehicles, which earn less per vehicle than internal combustion models.

title: CNN, MSNOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent
summary: Three news outlets are telling a federal court that the White House is defying a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump
story: Three news outlets are telling a federal court that the White House is defying a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump

Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press “pool.”

CNN, MSNOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president.

Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in “the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press,” Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets' attorney, said in a statement.
The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent.

At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is “viewpoint discrimination” forbidden by the First Amendment’s free-speech protections.

Trump insists that he doesn’t have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning.

“Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable," the outlets wrote in their filing, "and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government.”
The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him.

In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.

Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.
“Simply put,” Kelly wrote in the opinion, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.

title: Hong Kong's housing minister resigns after fire investigation finds inadequate oversight
summary: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight
story: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight

HONG KONG -- Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out last November engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.

Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were then undergoing building maintenance work.

At the opening of the news conference, Lee and seven other top officials bowed in apology. Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho “should bear political responsibility," although no personal wrongdoing was found. He said Ho had resigned Wednesday.

An independent committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit failed in its duties supervising the maintenance work. Lee said the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labor Department had shortcomings in supervision over fire hazards of the apartment complex.
He said a three-month investigation will be conducted into the four government agencies to determine whether staff were derelict in their duties.
Officials also proposed a series of measures, including criminalizing bid rigging.

The committee's report said evidence pointed to a lighted cigarette being the cause of the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House. The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, including on the scaffolding, while a few cigarette butts and some partially burnt materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, among other factors, the report said.

A majority of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns. The replacement of some staircase windows with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience allowed smoke to infiltrate residents’ escape routes. Opaque foam boards that covered the apartments’ windows blocked residents’ views, delaying evacuation. The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll.

The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Company, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor on the project, had cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.

It said the evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber-stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee. The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.

“However ... deception succeeded because the regulators’ own practices enabled it,” the report said. “In each case, the regulator’s reliance on the good faith of the regulated parties left obvious fire hazards uninvestigated.”

The committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit and the Buildings Department, as the two agencies primarily responsible for supervising the execution of the maintenance work at Wang Fuk Court, had failed in their supervisory duties in ensuring the safety of such work.

Among the shortcomings were the lack of proper investigations into the use of the foam boards and the fire-retardant quality of the scaffolding nets despite multiple complaints. The Independent Checking Unit should be criticized for adopting the practice of giving prenotification to consultants and contractors about site inspections, it added.

The committee's work is separate from criminal investigations in which seven people and two companies, Will Power and Prestige, were charged with offenses including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud over the fire.

Authorities alleged that the two companies and some defendants conspired together to defraud the apartment owners by concealing previous litigation records of the company later awarded the renovation project, a contract worth more than 300 million Hong Kong dollars (over $38 million).

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure
summary: Get ready to fall back
story: Get ready to fall back

WASHINGTON -- The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.

As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.

Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.

Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT."
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”

An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year."

The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump's pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.

Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.

In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.

An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.

“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.

“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”
Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed to this report.

title: Airbnb pledges $500M to nonprofit, scaling emergency stays and raising questions over housing relief
summary: Airbnb is dedicating more than $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years
story: Airbnb is dedicating more than $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Airbnb plans to dedicate $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years to increase temporary housing support for medical travelers and disaster survivors.
