The short-term rental platform will fund the expansion by donating 10 cents from every booking and make up any shortfall, according to Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky. Airbnb.org, the independent nonprofit whose operating costs are already covered by the company, aims to scale up to eventually provide 1 million nights of free housing each year.

The pledge, announced Wednesday, arrives at an uncertain time for corporate philanthropy overall. Most companies reduced their giving over the past five years, according to a recent survey by Chief Executives for Corporate Purpose. Tax law changes have prompted businesses to reconsider their charitable strategies.

Airbnb.org's new funding model has resurfaced questions about the charitable endeavors of a corporation criticized by some affordable housing advocates for worsening the supply of lower-cost, residential housing. The affordable housing crisis — which critics say is exacerbated by Airbnb — means less housing is available for people displaced by disasters.

Should a for-profit enterprise use its philanthropy to offset less desirable business impacts? Leading artificial intelligence companies, currently sketching out plans to share some of their wealth, say yes.

For Chesky, the answer is emphatically “no.” He denied Airbnb is “the contributor of the reason cities are expensive” but acknowledged that some hosts take a small fraction of their area's housing off the market. This week's commitment is about doing the “right thing” with the company's “natural superpower,” he said.

“I don’t like this idea that somehow you create a nonprofit to make up for or apologize for your core business," Chesky told The Associated Press. "Our core business, independently, is gonna affect a lot more lives than this organization. And our core business needs to be responsible. And if we’re doing something that’s not responsible, we need to correct it.”

Many governments, including the country of Spain and the city of New York, have recently moved to curb short-term rentals. The company could use its growing philanthropic footprint to further ingrain its product into communities and legitimize the presence of short-term rentals as its model is contested, according to Ka­ro­lina Mikoła­jew­ska-Za­jąc, a postdoctoral fellow at Copenhagen Business School who researches the societal impacts of digital platforms. She cautioned the humanitarian sector against growing too dependent on commercial platforms.
Murray Cox, the founder of the data activist project Inside Airbnb, noted one “crisis” missing from the nonprofit's list of emergency housing interventions.

“There’s also the housing crisis that’s occurring around the world,” Cox said. “And, although they’re not causing the housing crisis, they’re contributing to it by taking millions of housing units -- residential houses -- off the housing market.”
Airbnb.org is squarely focused on short-term emergency housing.

Launched formally in 2020 as the San Francisco-based company went public, the nonprofit uses company-donated credits to book stays on its platform for those experiencing crises. Since then, the nonprofit reports having provided 1.6 million nights of free, temporary housing in nearly 140 countries. Fees are dropped and hosts are compensated. The nonprofit also provides credits for other relief organizations to book stays.

Beneficiaries include people recovering from natural disasters, families traveling for medical care and survivors escaping domestic violence. When Washington state wildfires forced tens of thousands of evacuations in August, Airbnb.org said it provided more than 1,400 nights of free housing in the disaster's early days.

Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org, compares the nonprofit to “the ambulance that'll get you to the hospital.” Short-term housing is a “great product-market fit," he said, because they're able to “house a lot of people very quickly with an enormous amount of flexibility to meet their particular needs.”
He emphasized that the new funding mechanism will provide a “lot more money” that the nonprofit can depend on each year. “It’s not just shuffling the deck chairs around,” he said.

The $500 million five-year injection would more than double the total contributions reported by Airbnb.org between 2021 and 2025. The company would have to register 5 billion bookings over the next five years to reach that figure through the sliver of each booking donated to the nonprofit.
Chesky emphasized that the commitment will be completed regardless of business outcomes.
“We felt like this is a responsible number where it’s sufficiently big to make a difference in the world," Chesky said. “But it’s also a number shareholders can be comfortable with.”

Short-term assistance from nonprofits such as Airbnb.org and government entities such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency are “key for preventing that initial displacement,” according to Noah Patton, the director of disaster recovery at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. That's especially so as an AP analysis showed President Donald Trump takes longer to approve disaster aid and denies a greater percentage of requests than his predecessors.
But Patton said there's a need for more lasting solutions so “folks have homes to return back to."
“It's a Band-Aid if you don't also focus on the long-term aspect of this,” he said.
Airbnb.org will also expand its medical stays program to 20 countries by the end of the year.

The nonprofit partners with medical relief organizations to provide housing for families traveling to get treatment. Airbnbs, according to Gorder, allow families to bring additional relatives and pets that some alternatives don't allow. Amenities such as kitchens, sometimes not available in hotels or hospital lodgings, give the option to cook patients' favorite foods.
“And then they just have a quiet place at the end of the day,” Gorder said. “So, it's a lot more than four walls and a roof.”

In Mexico, where the program was piloted last fall, Airbnb.org says it has housed medical travelers for nearly 1,500 nights. Its first partner, Vuela Fundación, supports children diagnosed with cancer. Many of the Mexico City-based organization's clients travel from poor rural towns and lack access to the country's social security system.

Diego Parada Herrera, the co-founder and CEO, said it's not uncommon to see families camping in tents or sleeping in parked cars outside of hospitals because they couldn't afford to stay anywhere else.
“The need was there. And we were conscious of it,” he said. “But we didn't know how to address it.”

Airbnb.org now provides his organization with credits that case managers use to complete bookings for families in need. Some hosts offer discounted rates, he said. Vuela Fundación stocks fridges with ready-to-cook food packages.

The challenge, he's found, is that many families aren't technologically savvy. Some aren't familiar with Airbnb's business model and struggle to grasp that they'll be staying in someone else's home. His nonprofit created instructional videos and shows them how to use the platform.
Chesky said the company will likely “keep going” based on how this expansion goes.
“Whatever people think of us, we’re doing this for decades,” he said. “It’s up to them to judge us and our motivations. And it’s up to us to have a commitment that’s a decade-long commitment.”

title: Average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
WASHINGTON -- The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month.
The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell to 7.24% from 7.32% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.17%.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also fell this week. That average rate dipped to 6.60% from 6.68% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.41%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.
The yield was at 4.98% at midday on the bond market Thursday. It surged to more than 5.30% earlier this month and remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

title: Starbucks reports lower than expected revenue on softer international demand
summary: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
story: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened.

The Seattle coffee giant said global same-store sales rose 7.2% for the July-September period, which was higher than the 6% increase Wall Street was expecting, according to analysts polled by FactSet.

That was largely due to strong demand in the U.S., where same-store sales jumped 7.7%. International same-store sales rose less than 1%, and Starbucks noted a 2.8% decline in international store traffic.
Net revenue fell 4% for the quarter to $9.14 billion. That was lower than the $9.2 billion analysts were forecasting.

title: Tech sector rally continues with Fed expected to leave benchmark interest rate alone
summary: Tech stocks have surged this week ahead of a meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve with markets anticipating no change to the benchmark U.S. interest rate, at least not yet
story: Tech stocks have surged this week ahead of a meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve with markets anticipating no change to the benchmark U.S. interest rate, at least not yet
HONG KONG -- Tech stocks have surged this week ahead of Wednesday's meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve with markets anticipating no change to the benchmark U.S. interest rate, at least not yet.

The rapid-growth tech sector is fueled by easy access to credit and hyperscalers like Microsoft and Alphabet will post quarterly earnings reports after the bell. Amazon and Intel release earnings Thursday.

The tech rally continued before the opening bell Wednesday as futures for the Nasdaq, already up 2% this week, rose 0.4%. Futures for the S&P 500 edged up 0.1%, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 144 points, or 0.3%.

The Fed is in a bind, however, with higher energy prices from the conflict in the Middle East intensifying inflation. Benchmark U.S. crude rose more than 2% early Wednesday after an attack on a major Saudi Arabian refinery by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, is also up almost 2% to $111.38 a barrel.

Alphabet is up almost 2% early and Microsoft is essentially flat. Memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 11.4% to its highest level in two weeks after it reported a record-high operating profit of 83.3 trillion won ($62.8 billion) for the last quarter, up nearly sevenfold from a year earlier and beating market estimates.

In other early trading, the cryptocurrency platform Robinhood is down sharply after its quarterly profit fell short of expectations. Stellantis rose 6% after the automaker stood by its guidance for the year despite heavy costs related to its turnaround bid.
In Europe, Germany’s DAX edged up less than 0.1% to 25,598.39, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 0.1% to 7,876.05. Britain’s FTSE 100 fell 0.3% to 10,656.49.
In Asia, South Korea’s Kospi surged 6.6% to close at 6,012.44.
The Bank of Japan begins a two-day policy meeting on Thursday, with markets expecting its benchmark interest rate to be unchanged.

Treasury yields are relatively steady before the Federal Reserve announces its decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury, an important indicator on inflation for the Fed, edged up 0.25% to 5.0% early Wednesday.
The U.S. dollar slid to 157.92 Japanese yen from 157.95 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1128, up from $1.1126.

title: Samsung keeps shattering profit records as AI boom lifts chip demand
summary: Samsung Electronics has reported a record operating profit of $80.5 billion, driven by high demand for computer memory chips used in AI systems
story: Samsung Electronics has reported a record operating profit of $80.5 billion, driven by high demand for computer memory chips used in AI systems

SEOUL, South Korea -- SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — Samsung Electronics said Thursday that its operating profit for the last quarter reached a record 107.4 trillion won ($80.5 billion), fueled by surging demands for its computer memory chips used in artificial intelligence systems.
Revenue for the July-September period rose to an all-time high at 195.3 trillion won ($146 billion), marking the company’s fourth straight quarter of record profit and revenue.

Samsung’s regulatory filing came a day after domestic rival SK Hynix also reported record third-quarter profit, as the two South Korean semiconductor giants, which together control about two-thirds of the global memory market, face seemingly insatiable demand for their chips amid the global AI boom.

Samsung said in a statement that it expects the demand for its AI-related chips to accelerate through 2027, outpacing supply as clients race to expand AI infrastructure. The company said it will focus on supplying advanced memory chips and storage products used in AI servers, including high-bandwidth memory chips, server DRAMs and solid-state drives.

South Korean tech companies are making major investments in semiconductor manufacturing facilities and data centers as the country expands its AI ambitions. Samsung and SK Hynix in June announced plans to invest a combined 800 trillion won ($599 billion) in a new chipmaking hub in the country’s southwest to capitalize on AI-driven demand.

But some analysts question whether the spending will ultimately pay off, and South Korea’s central bank has warned that the country’s trade-dependent economy is becoming too reliant on chips, which it said could deepen the damage of any AI-related downturn.

title: Netanyahu’s party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his party have amplified claims that the country's election was “stolen” by Arab-led parties
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his party have amplified claims that the country's election was “stolen” by Arab-led parties

JERUSALEM -- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.

The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.

Results released by election officials early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.

Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.

Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!” it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was “aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government.”
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”

As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. “They are doing this because they lost,” he said.

Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: “I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel.”
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.

By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.

The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”

The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.

On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of “attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular.”
“Netanyahu is working to steal the election,” the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.

The head of the Arab-led Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.

President Isaac Herzog called it a “sensitive moment” and called for a full investigation. He warned that “we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”

The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.

If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.

Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate.

There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.

If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.

New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
Saeed reported from Abu Snan, Israel. Associated Press reporters across Israel contributed to this report.
This version has corrected that the final results were released early Friday, not Thursday, local time.

title: Frances Tiafoe supports young tennis players' careers while still building his own
summary: Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone
story: Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone
Frances Tiafoe may still be waiting for his first Grand Slam championship, but the up-and-coming American tennis star has already celebrated a meaningful career milestone.

His Frances Tiafoe Fund, which supports tennis programs for young people in underresourced communities, recently passed $1 million in funds raised, only three years after its launch. It’s unusual for athletes to start nonprofits early in their careers, but the 28-year-old says he didn’t want to wait to start giving back because his impact would be greater now.

“I think young players will know me more now,” Tiafoe told The Associated Press. “While I’m at my ‘peak’ and doing things on a high level, I wanted to inspire, to give back. I wanted to be a man of the people because I was given so much.”

Tiafoe, who made his third trip in the past five years to the U.S. Open semifinals this summer, first started playing tennis when he was 4 years old at the Junior Tennis Champions Center in College Park, Maryland. His father was the center’s head of maintenance after immigrating from Sierra Leone in 1996.
“I’m just a kid who got a chance,” said Tiafoe, adding that the support he received from his team at an early age was critical to his success.

“It helped me believe it before I actually did it,” he said. “You’ve got to have a big support system. You’ve got to have people who believe in the vision before you do, who see you in a bigger place than you do so that they continue to push you. They hold you to a certain standard so you’re able to go to work every day with an approach in hand.”

Ginny Ehrlich, CEO of the USTA Foundation, the United States Tennis Association’s charitable arm which administers Tiafoe's fund, said Tiafoe is not just “one of the few players” who started a fund while still an active player, but is also hands-on in where and how its donations are made.
“He is so passionate about wanting to give back,” she said, adding he wants young people who are growing up in situations similar to his to “have that same access and opportunity.”

The Tiafoe Fund provides college scholarships, as well as smaller grants to help individual players get ready for playing collegiate tennis, Ehrlich said. The fund also supports young players so they can pay for travel, equipment and training they would otherwise not be able to afford. And Tiafoe also supports programs at some tennis centers, including the Maryland center where he got his start.

“It’s so electric to have someone who walks the talk, right?” Ehrlich said. “It’s priceless, really, in terms of his impact. I don’t mean impact in dollars, I mean impact on inspiring the next generation to achieve whatever their dreams are.”

Tiafoe said he is proud to be able to help in these ways, especially in a time where scholarships for tennis players are harder to come by as athletic departments prioritize money-generating sports like football and basketball.
“College is becoming the Wild, Wild West for sure,” he said. “But I think they’re still stages for guys to give back and help.”
Jade Flores, a freshman at Allegheny College, received a scholarship from the Tiafoe Fund and also got the chance to practice with Tiafoe during this year’s U.S. Open.
“I was a bit nervous to meet him at first – it’s Frances Tiafoe,” Flores said after the session. “But he makes you feel like he’s known you forever.”
Tiafoe said he wants to keep expanding the Tiafoe Fund as much as he can.

“Let’s just keep pushing and see where it goes,” he said. “There’s always gonna be another kid to help. There’s always going to be another club to bless. There’s gonna be a kid to take to college. So I don’t want to put the caps on it.”

title: UK Treasury chief faces headwinds as he delivers first budget under new PM Burnham
summary: British Treasury chief John Healey faces a fine balancing act when he delivers his first budget statement, with the economic backdrop made more difficult as a result of the turmoil caused by the Iran war
story: British Treasury chief John Healey faces a fine balancing act when he delivers his first budget statement, with the economic backdrop made more difficult as a result of the turmoil caused by the Iran war

LONDON -- British Treasury chief John Healey faces a fine balancing act when he delivers his first budget statement Wednesday, with the economic backdrop made more difficult as a result of the turmoil caused by the Iran war.

Healey, who was appointed Chancellor of the Exchequer in July when Andy Burnham became prime minister, takes center stage when he stands up in the House of Commons in what is arguably Parliament's key set-piece of the calendar.

Even though the British economy has been more resilient than anticipated this year and has grown strongly, the problem is that the money just isn’t there for Healey to enact many of the Labour government's ambitions on restoring the health of the country's public services.
The U.K.’s economy has been hit — like others — by the inflation generated by the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.

Inflation in the U.K. has risen to a near one-year high of 3.5% as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, and is expected to go higher in coming months. As a result, the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates soon, which will further raise the costs to the government of servicing the debt.

As a result, Healey’s budget is expected to be relatively low-key, especially at a time when bond markets are fretting over debt levels around the world. France has been in the spotlight recently following a wave of protests that have exposed the parlous state of its finances.

Matthew Amis, an investment director at Aberdeen Investments, said a “dull budget” could well be rewarded in the financial markets by lower government borrowing costs, which could in the longer run free up extra resources to plow into schools, hospitals and the military, for example.
“The one note of caution is that international investors are very quick to punish countries with a weak fiscal story. Just ask France,” he said.

In his few comments ahead of the budget, Healey has said he will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. These could include measures to cushion the blow from higher energy prices.
Burnham has also made pledges about reducing, and even eradicating, homelessness, improving care for the elderly and meeting NATO targets on defense spending.

One source of revenue is expected to come from the banks, which have benefited from higher interest rates. A higher surcharge on their profits is anticipated. Another revenue source may come from higher taxes on the gambling sector.

The main problem facing Healey is the same as that which confronted his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was Chancellor after Labour returned to power in a landslide election victory — the country's debt mountain.

Even though the trajectory of the public finances was recently given a nod of approval from the International Monetary Fund, the U.K.’s debt has passed 3 trillion pounds ($4 trillion) for the first time ever, requiring 8% of government spending to service it.

There will be particular interest on what Healey says on defense, as he quit as defense secretary earlier this year in protest at the lack of money being provided, a move that heaped pressure on Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.
Paying for those measures would require him to find the money from somewhere else — tax rises or spending cuts — if he is to fend off nervous bond market investors.

title: Wendy's, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
summary: Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
story: Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Wendy’s shares jumped 15% at the opening bell Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores.

Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private.
Wendy's, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, declined to comment Wednesday. At the end of last year, Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries.

Wendy's, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where's the beef?” ad campaign.

But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy's fell behind. Wendy's share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

In recent years, inflation has also hurt Wendy's and other U.S. fast-food chains, who have seen traffic from lower-income consumers fall as they raised prices to combat rising labor, food and packaging costs.

Wendy's has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations this year.

Then, last month, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.”

“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture," Peltz wrote. "The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category."
Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%.

Peltz considered a take-private bid for Wendy's in 2022 but told the company in January 2023 that he had decided against it, citing its improved business momentum, according to TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles.
Charles said an independent special committee is expected to evaluate the proposal and both parties have entered into a confidentiality arrangement.

“In our view, a take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category,” Charles wrote Wednesday in a note to investors.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect the company to post earnings of 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million, according to FactSet.
Shares rose 88 cents to $7.01 Wednesday. They have fallen 26% since the start of this year.

title: Putin woos African leaders at a Moscow summit aimed at expanding Russia-Africa ties
summary: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit, part of his efforts to bolster Moscow’s clout across the continent
story: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit, part of his efforts to bolster Moscow’s clout across the continent
MOSCOW -- Russian President Vladimir Putin courted dozens of African leaders at a Russia-Africa summit that wraps up Thursday as he seeks to bolster Moscow's clout across the continent.
Speaking during a meeting in the Kremlin on the second day of the summit, Putin said that “Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership.”

“We are natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order, free from diktat and double standards and based on respect for the norms of international law and the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter,” Putin said.
He mentioned Moscow's support for the African nations' anti-colonial fight during Soviet times.

“Russia has always been and remains committed to seeing African nations defend their sovereignty, achieve steady growth, and strengthen their economies and social sectors,” the Russian leader said. “We stand ready to continue working together with you across all these areas to achieve these goals."

The summit marks a persistent effort by the Kremlin to expand ties with a continent of nearly 1.6 billion people that is increasingly assertive on the global stage. Africa’s 54 nations make up the largest voting bloc at the United Nations.
Moscow first hosted the Russia-Africa summit in 2019, and then again in 2023. This week’s summit drew nearly 50 African nations, about 20 of which were represented by their leaders.

Putin noted that Russia's trade with African countries topped $27 billion last year and vowed to expand it. He noted that Russian companies have pursued major investment projects in Africa in such spheres as energy, mining, industrial cooperation and logistics.
“Our business community approaches cooperation with African partners with honesty, respect, and integrity, conducting business on an equal footing,” Putin said.

“Rather than siphoning off profits in the manner of the colonial practices by former imperial powers, they reinvest their earnings into the development of your national economies, they readily share advanced technologies and expertise, broadly engage local subcontractors, and help create new production facilities and jobs," he said.

Putin emphasized Russia's role as a major supplier of grain and other agricultural products to African markets, casting it as a “concrete and tangible contribution to ensuring food security across the entire African continent.”

He said that Russia delivered over 18 million metric tons of grain to Africa last year, and another 13 million metric tons in the first nine months of this year. Russian exports of mineral fertilizers reached approximately 1.5 million metric tons last year, and have already exceeded 2.2 million metric tons so far this year.
Putin also mentioned Russia's assistance in the spheres of healthcare and education, noting that nearly 40,000 students from African nations are currently studying at Russian universities.

He specifically underlined Moscow's efforts to help African states in “maintaining internal stability and security, and in strengthening their defense and law enforcement capabilities,” adding that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African countries.

As Russia competes with the United States, Europe and China for greater influence across Africa, it also has relied on its military contractors to strengthen its sway on many fronts, from the economy to security and politics.

title: Drones strike a container ship off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast and its crew members are rescued
summary: Three maritime drones have struck a container ship in the Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast, according to the country's defense minister
story: Three maritime drones have struck a container ship in the Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast, according to the country's defense minister

SOFIA, Bulgaria -- Three maritime drones struck a container ship sailing in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday, the country’s defense minister said, the latest in a string of such incidents on NATO’s eastern flank.

The attack on the Liberian-flagged container ship, the Contship Jet, occurred a little before 1 p.m. local time about 21 nautical miles southeast of the coastal town of Shabla, near Cape Kaliakra in northeastern Bulgaria, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters.

The crew evacuated the vessel and were eventually taken on board rescue vessels of the Bulgarian Navy and border police, according to the state news agency BTA. The rescued sailors — 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians — were being transported to the port city of Varna for medical checks.
The ship was en route from Israel’s port of Haifa to Constanța in Romania. It was not immediately clear what the 421 containers on board were carrying.
The incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, for trilateral talks focused on security in the Black Sea region.

In a statement after the talks, the three NATO countries strongly condemned the drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and called for an “immediate cessation of attacks that threaten commercial ships, maritime infrastructure and the safety of maritime activities.” They also agreed on stronger intelligence sharing, early warning capabilities and coordination in the Black Sea.

A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, leading some members of the alliance to wonder if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

Russia has not taken responsibility for the attacks, but suspicion has fallen on Moscow. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament earlier this month that “the logic points in that direction … The problem is that we cannot prove it.”

On Oct. 15, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that NATO had “strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities” in the face of increasingly frequent strikes on commercial vessels.
The attacks in Bulgaria and Romania’s exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing.

Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports.

In early October, two commercial ships were attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, and a week later, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank after being struck about 17 nautical miles east of Shabla while the Malta-flagged Chelsea 3 was damaged in a separate attack about 17 nautical miles east of Byala, according to reports at the time.
On Oct. 23, a foreign-flagged cargo ship capsized and sank in the Black Sea following a suspected drone strike about 13 nautical miles off the Romanian port city of Constanta.

title: As war strains Kremlin finances, Putin searches for new revenue streams
summary: With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine intensifying the strain on state finances, President Vladimir Putin is reaching for cash to fund his government and the war, squeezing tax revenue from an economy that’s increasingly skewed toward the military — while ...
story: With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine intensifying the strain on state finances, President Vladimir Putin is reaching for cash to fund his government and the war, squeezing tax revenue from an economy that’s increasingly skewed toward the military — while ...

With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine intensifying the strain on state finances, President Vladimir Putin is reaching for cash to fund his government and the war, squeezing tax revenue from an economy that’s increasingly skewed toward the military — while civilian needs take a back seat.
The country's 2027-2029 state budget, which will be taken up Thursday in the rubber-stamp parliament, is accompanied by a string of tax hikes announced after the September parliamentary elections.

While last year the Kremlin went for a broad tax increase, raising value-added taxes at the cash register and making more small businesses pay VAT, this cash grab hits a narrower segment: mining companies and better-off citizens with investment income, property sales and bank accounts.

The budget deficit this year has swelled beyond forecast s due to lavish military spending and tepid economic growth amid sanctions, high interest rates for non-military companies, labor shortages and Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and export terminals.

The deficit hit 5.8 trillion rubles ($72 billion) through August, almost 50% higher than last year's figure and above the already revised target of 4.8 trillion rubles, according to the Kyiv School of Economics.

The government proposes a 20%-30% windfall profits tax on mining companies that have benefited from prices that have risen since last year. That will hit companies producing iron ore, nickel and gold. Another measure imposes higher rates of 13% to 22% on income from interest, dividends and proceeds from selling property. Such income is currently taxed at 13% for amounts under 2.4 million rubles ($29,800) and 15% above that.

Other proposals to take effect Jan. 1 include a 100-ruble per parcel charge and 22% VAT on formerly tax-free foreign goods worth less than 200 euros that are bought online. There's also a 35% tax on dividends paid into restricted accounts for foreign investors from “unfriendly countries."

People asked about taxes and finances on the street in Moscow responded with a mix of complaints and resignation. "They need money for state coffers, they need to collect more from people, from ordinary people,” said Denis Bystrov, 39.

“What can you do?” said Nelly Godunova, 92. “I've got four university degrees, they were all free, you know? True, I've given plenty to this country. But no matter... If you earned something, you've got to give back.”

“Everyone knows perfectly well that the money's going for the military operation, right?” said Sergei Sukachev, who gave his age as “almost 70.” “I've suffered a little as a businessman, to be honest, but I clearly understand, it's best to hang on and to get our way.”

Russia has enough financing available to cover the deficit in 2027 and probably 2028, says Chris Weafer, CEO of consultancy Macro-Advisory Ltd. “But that is at the expense of raising taxes, of increasing costs for households as well as business,” he said.

“And it means that there is much less money available for normal economic development or infrastructure. Basically, the budget is now moving to a phase where it is primarily funding the military and the military operation.”

“So the economy is now becoming very skewed,” he said. "While there’s still modest positive growth, it is coming from the state spending into these ... state-linked industries, whereas the rest of the economy is struggling badly or even failing.”

A subsidiary of German retailer Metro was seized under a law permitting the temporary administration of firms from “unfriendly countries” and tapped for a billion-ruble ($12 million) contribution to the war effort.
Metro AG headquarters in Germany said it had no role in the donation, which “does not reflect our position or the way we run our business.”

Metro Russia, no longer under the control of headquarters, said the contribution to the “National Front - Everything for Victory” fund would buy vehicles, communications devices and anti-drone equipment for soldiers in what Russia calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Weafer said Russia may be seizing control of foreign companies in anticipation of a deal to secure Russian assets frozen abroad. But the forced donation also raises the risk that the Finance Ministry may see foreign companies as sources of windfall revenue.

Russia's economic numbers don't look that bad — on the surface. The government predicts growth this year of 0.6% of GDP, not great but not a recession either. Unemployment is at a record low, and the government carries very little debt. Earnings from oil exports have held up thanks to higher global prices caused by the war in Iran. The revised deficit for this year will come in around 3% of GDP, according to Finance Minister Anton Siluanov. That is more than the 1.6% achieved last year, but smaller than in many other countries. For instance, the US booked 5.8% of GDP last year. Russia is roughly equal to the EU average of 3.1%.

But that isn't the whole story. Due to sanctions that forbid banks and investors from dealing with Russia, the Kremlin can’t tap international bond markets. And Russia's domestic financial resources have already been extensively drawn down.

One way is to borrow from Russian banks through bond sales. But that came under stress this summer when banks balked at the low interest rate. Sales resumed after the government offered better terms. The government has already tapped the banking system by having banks fund the war with loans to defense companies, shifting the true costs of the war off the federal budget and onto the balance sheets of banks and state-controlled companies, according to the Kyiv School of Economics.

Another pot is the National Wealth Fund, a reserve built up from oil and gas export earnings. But the fund's liquid assets available for spending, such as Chinese currency and gold, have dwindled to 1.7% of GDP.
The Kyiv School of Economics says that Russia's finances are stable -- for the moment.
But “the room for maneuver is limited: an adverse shock such as a drop in global energy prices or an erosion of confidence in the financial system could quickly destabilize the fragile equilibrium.”

title: Amazon's 3Q results miss analysts' estimates, but posts solid sales gains in cloud computing unit
summary: Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations
story: Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations

NEW YORK -- Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current fourth quarter that encompasses the critical holiday shopping period after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts' expectations.

The Seattle-based company, however, posted strong growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its cloud computing unit called AWS rose 39.3% during the latest quarter ended Sept. 30, higher than the 37% clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said.
Still, shares were down more than 6% in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.

Analysts will be looking for any comments from Amazon executives on the earnings call Thursday about the holiday shopping season. The tech giant said earlier this month that it would hire 300,000 U.S. seasonal workers for the shopping period. That’s up from 250,000 last year.
Investors also have been closely watching Amazon’s quarterly earnings to see if the company’s big spending on artificial intelligence is starting to pay off.

CEO and President Andy Jassy disclosed to investors in July that it now expects capital spending, mostly in artificial intelligence, to total $220 billion. That number includes outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That’s up from the $200 billion investment plan that was announced in February and well above the $128 billion in capital spending for all of last year. Jassy had cited the higher cost of memory chips as the main reason for the increase.
Jassy told investors this past summer that even at the $220 billion level, Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all of the demand it has this year.

The latest earnings report from Alphabet late Wednesday raised alarm bells when it reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The company behind Google and YouTube also said it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cash flow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51 billion. Its stock plummeted Thursday.
Such worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a big push to build data centers and fill them with AI chips.
Amazon reported net income of $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, in the three-month period. That compares with $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, in the year-ago period.
Sales rose to $201.94 billion, compared with the same year-ago period's $180.17 billion.
Analysts were expecting $1.97 per share on sales of $202.2 billion, according to FactSet.

For the fourth quarter, Amazon said it expects net sales to be between $240 billion and $247 billion, which translates to a 12% to 16% increase compared with the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $244.16 billion.

title: US unemployment claims slide to 194,000, the lowest since mid-July
summary: The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security
story: The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security
WASHINGTON -- The number of Americans applying for unemployment claims dipped last week to 194,000 — the lowest since mid-July — as layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security.

The Labor Department reported Thursday that initial jobless claims were down last week from a revised 195,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which strips out week-to-week volatility, fell to 196,750.

Applications for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have remained at historically low levels, never topping 230,000 in a single week. They've come in at or below 200,000 for seven straight weeks.

So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have been adding an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. That is an improvement on a lackluster 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Consumer spending has remained resilient and a surge in investment in artificial intelligence has lifted economic growth.

The Labor Department will release hiring numbers for October next Friday Nov. 6. They are expected to show that the economy added 55,000 jobs this month, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet.

title: US cruise ship suspends global voyage due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
summary: A U.S. cruise ship on a three-year voyage has suspended its journey in Cambodia due to high fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark
story: A U.S. cruise ship on a three-year voyage has suspended its journey in Cambodia due to high fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark

SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia -- A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.

The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.

Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.

“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.

Passengers however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.

Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.

Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.

“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.

Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over.”

Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.

The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.

Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.

Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.

In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.

After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
Associated Press writers Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Cleveland plays Milwaukee for conference showdown
summary: The Bucks will take on conference opponent Cleveland
story: The Bucks will take on conference opponent Cleveland
Cleveland Cavaliers (3-2, sixth in the Eastern Conference) vs. Milwaukee Bucks (1-4, 13th in the Eastern Conference)
Milwaukee; Saturday, 8 p.m. EDT
BOTTOM LINE: Milwaukee plays Cleveland in a matchup of Eastern Conference teams.
Milwaukee went 32-50 overall and 21-31 in Eastern Conference games a season ago. The Bucks averaged 25.8 assists per game on 40.8 made field goals last season.
Cleveland went 52-30 overall, 11-5 in Central Division action and 25-16 on the road a season ago. The Cavaliers averaged 28.3 assists per game on 43.3 made field goals last season.

title: JuJu Watkins returns from an ACL tear as USC eyes its first title since 1984
summary: JuJu Watkins is returning to college basketball after missing last season due to an ACL tear
story: JuJu Watkins is returning to college basketball after missing last season due to an ACL tear
LOS ANGELES -- The bun is back. Along with the smile and that silky jump shot. JuJu Watkins is returning to college basketball after missing last season while rehabbing an ACL tear.

The star guard who averaged 25.6 points in her first two seasons for Southern California is surrounded by a talent-laden supporting cast as the third-ranked Trojans bid for their first national championship since 1984.
“It's on my mind every day,” Watkins said. “So much anticipation has gone into this year. I want it really badly, but also in a healthy way. I just want to have fun and really enjoy this year.”
Watkins has already envisioned seeing her first basket go in.
“I've had dreams about that every night. I might shed a tear, honestly, I can’t lie,” she said. “That’ll be a really amazing feeling for me.”
Watkins scored 18 points while playing 22 minutes in USC's exhibition win over California recently.

She joins Big Ten Freshman of the Year Jazzy Davidson, who averaged 17.9 points last season, in the backcourt for the first time. The duo began developing their chemistry while Watkins was sidelined from the injury she sustained in the second round of the 2025 NCAA Tournament. She could be spotted encouraging Davidson on the sideline during games.

“She saw me being hard on myself and I think she saw a little bit of her in me,” Davidson said, "and so she kind of knew what it was like going through that. Being able to build the friendship that we were able to build, it’s a huge blessing.”

Davidson led the Trojans in points, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks per game last season, when they finished 18-14 overall, 9-9 in the Big Ten and lost in the second round of the NCAA Tournament.

USC's stockpile of talent includes guard Saniyah Hall, who had 23 points, six rebounds and five steals in the Trojans' exhibition, as well as forward Sara Okeke, one of three five-star recruits to join the roster.
"They have proven that they’re going to be really impactful players at a high level,” coach Lindsay Gottlieb said.
The expectations on Watson are huge, as always. She was named the Big Ten Preseason Player of the Year.

“I’m just trying to be myself and peak at the right time,” she said. “I'm definitely a smarter player coming back. I know more about the different reads and was able to study a lot and assert myself in different situations when I wasn't playing.”
Last season, Watkins would set up chairs in the locker room for the team talk on the road. It was one of the small ways she found to be useful without being on the court.

“I was able to take on a leadership role for sure and I can’t say I really owned that role prior to that,” she said. “Being able to do that and also see the game from a different perspective and seeing how can I help my team really helped grow my IQ and leadership skills.”

The Trojans open the season on Monday in Las Vegas against UNLV in the Hall of Fame Series. Their early games include a visit to top-ranked South Carolina on Nov. 15, and facing No. 13 Notre Dame and No. 4 Duke in the Players Era Showcase in Las Vegas in mid-December.

“We’re going to get hit in the mouth,” associate head coach Beth Burns said. “The good thing is when you get hit in the mouth you either cower or you bite back, and we got a lot of people who want to bite.”
That includes Watkins.
“Everybody wants to know the secret, why is JuJu JuJu? The secret is there ain’t no secret, it’s work and focus,” Burns said. “Her choice is to be elite in every facet in her life.”

Last year, Watkins' favorite class was Pete Carroll's “The Game is Life” offered through USC's Marshall School of Business. The former Trojans football coach emphasized his mindset of always competing and it made an impression on her.
"Coming back, I haven’t lost my confidence, I haven’t lost my attention to detail,” Watkins said. “Everything is the same. It’s just I’ve been out for a minute.”
And now she's back, with a will to win that's as strong as ever.

title: Brewers fans flood Milwaukee streets for a long-awaited World Series victory parade
summary: Tens of thousands of exuberant Brewers fans flooded the streets, watched from parking garages and cheered from office building windows in downtown Milwaukee to celebrate the franchise’s first World Series title
story: Tens of thousands of exuberant Brewers fans flooded the streets, watched from parking garages and cheered from office building windows in downtown Milwaukee to celebrate the franchise’s first World Series title

MILWAUKEE -- Tens of thousands of exuberant Brewers fans flooded the streets, watched from parking garages and cheered from office building windows in downtown Milwaukee on Friday to celebrate the franchise's first World Series title.

The small-market Brewers gave their long-suffering fans the championship they had been waiting for with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, clinching the Series in five games. It was their first time playing in the Fall Classic in 44 years.
“Unbelievable,” said parade attendee Mark Diedrich, a 76-year-old who has been an on-and-off partial season ticket holder since the 1980s. “You just never thought it would happen. But it did.”

Players on buses chugged cans of Miller Lite beer, walked the parade route high-fiving fans and hoisted the Commissioner's Trophy as the cheers echoed through the streets. Every level of the Brewers franchise was represented in the parade, from owner Mark Attanasio to manager Pat Murphy, grounds crew members and behind-the-scenes staff.
The Johnsonville sausages, fan favorites that race during every home game, were also walking the parade route.

Brewers players, coaches and staffers waved to fans from the top of buses, some of them bearing the message, “Won. Our Way,” to update their postseason slogan of “Win Our Way.” Several players, such as outfielder Sal Frelick and second baseman Brice Turang, removed their shirts in a nod to this seasons’ MLB-wide “Tarps Off” craze as they exhorted the crowd.
Players took turns holding the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft, with many of them getting off their buses and greeting fans.

Hall of Famers Rollie Fingers, Robin Yount, Paul Molitor and other members of the 1982 Brewers team that made Milwaukee's last World Series appearance, also rode along the parade route. Current and former players posed for pictures, signed autographs and reveled in the moment.

Members of the 1982 team had traveled a similar route in the parade that year after losing the World Series in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals. Many fans at Friday's parade weren't even born the last time Milwaukee celebrated the Brewers.

Milwaukee Public Schools canceled classes on Friday, allowing fans to enjoy the parade that ran past a mural of beloved Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker and was to conclude with a fan fest at Henry Maier Festival Park, not far from the shores of Lake Michigan.
Milwaukee city officials were expecting about 400,000 people to attend the parade and celebration.

Kasey Diedrich, a son of Mark Diedrich, said he attended his first Brewers game as a 4-year-old in 1983, the year after that World Series appearance. Little did he know at the time how long he would have to wait for the Brewers to make it back.
“I don’t think we still think it happened," Diedrich said. “It seems like a dream.”
Mark Diedrich said he owns the seats from the old Milwaukee County Stadium where he and one of his sons were sitting when Hall of Famer Yount got his 3,000th hit in 1992.

“We could tell you stories for days of all the games we went to,” Mark Diedrich said. “I remember going to opening day with these guys and there was ice on the steps of County Stadium. We’re sitting down to get ready for the game and a guy’s spreading salt to melt the ice on the steps.”
The Diedriches were one of many families who had multiple generations representing them at the parade.
Craig Muehl, a 42-year-old from the Milwaukee suburb of Brookfield, said he inherited his Brewers fandom from his father. Muehl woke up early to attend the parade with his young son and daughter.

“It all started, just like many families around here, sitting outside in the summer and fall,” Muehl said. “My dad had the Brewers game on the radio everywhere we went. Some families have music on the radio. We had the Brewers games all summer long.
The celebration actually started well before Friday.

Several Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, went to Lambeau Field for Thursday night's Green Bay Packers game. They received a huge ovation, especially when pitcher Brandon Woodruff emerged from the tunnel in the second quarter holding the Commissioner's Trophy.

A few players attempted a “Lambeau leap” into the crowd, with Frelick having the most success. Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”
A large police presence was on hand for the parade to handle the big crowds and heavy traffic.
The franchise originated as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 before moving to Milwaukee and becoming the Brewers the following year.
Milwaukee has celebrated a World Series title once before. The Milwaukee Braves won the 1957 World Series over the New York Yankees before moving to Atlanta in 1966.
Scott Bauer contributed to this story.

title: Tayven Jackson, Jahiem White propel North Texas to 48-41 victory over Florida Atlantic
summary: Tayven Jackson passed for 404 yards and four touchdowns, Jahiem White rushed for 193 yards and two scores and North Texas held off Florida Atlantic 48-41
story: Tayven Jackson passed for 404 yards and four touchdowns, Jahiem White rushed for 193 yards and two scores and North Texas held off Florida Atlantic 48-41
DENTON, Texas -- Tayven Jackson passed for 404 yards and four touchdowns, Jahiem White rushed for 193 yards and two scores and North Texas held off Florida Atlantic 48-41 on Thursday night.
Jackson completed 33 of 46 passes as North Texas (6-2, 4-0 American Conference) extended its win streak to five. White did his damage on 26 carries.

Caden Veltkamp finished with a season-high 452 yards and five touchdowns — matching his career high — on 37-for-56 passing for Florida Atlantic (5-3, 2-2). Easton Messer totaled a school-record 16 receptions for 189 yards and three scores.
Veltkamp's 18-yard touchdown pass to Branden Hoch helped the Owls lead 10-3 after one quarter.
Jackson connected with Baron Tipton for an 8-yard touchdown to tie it 10-all early in the second quarter, but Veltkamp and Messer teamed up for a 27-yard score and a 17-10 lead on the ensuing drive.
Jackson answered with a 3-yard scoring toss to Kyle Koch to tie it, and White scored on a 59-yard first-down run after a three-and-out by the Owls for a 24-17 advantage.
Veltkamp connected with Messer for a 12-yard score with 39 seconds left to tie it 24-all at halftime.
Jackson threw a 4-yard touchdown pass to Justin Stevenson following an Owls' turnover to up the lead to 34-24.
Veltkamp answered with 22-yard touchdown pass to Kaden Shields-Dutton, but White ran 20 yards to the 1 before scoring two plays later and North Texas took a 41-31 lead into the fourth quarter.
Veltkamp fired a 34-yard scoring strike to Messer to cut it to 41-38 with 8:26 remaining, but Jackson came back with a 2-yard scoring toss to Koch to push the lead back to 10.
It was the first FBS game this season with two 400-yard passers as the teams combined for 1,167 yards of offense.
Florida Atlantic: Hosts UTSA on Nov. 5.
North Texas: Hosts Rice on Nov. 7.

title: Russia is back in the ice hockey world championships after sports court ruling
summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russia teams must be allowed to play International Ice Hockey Federation events such as the world championships
story: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russia teams must be allowed to play International Ice Hockey Federation events such as the world championships
LAUSANNE, Switzerland -- Russia teams must be allowed to play International Ice Hockey Federation events such as the world championships, the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Friday.
CAS overturned IIHF decisions which excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season including the men’s and women’s world championships.
In a brief statement, CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support the IIHF’s security concerns.

CAS said its ruling did not address issues such as whether Russia should be required to play without national symbols as a team of neutral athletes, as in some other Olympic sports, or other “organizational consequences.”

The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling and said it “maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions."
“While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov wrote on the Telegram social media app that CAS “recognized the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified.”
The IIHF has barred Russian teams from its world championships since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia also missed the Olympic hockey tournaments this year.
The ruling is an immediate challenge for new IIHF President Franz Reindl, whose home country of Germany hosts the men's world championship next year.

title: The 4th edition of the NBA Cup opens on Friday, with all 30 teams in mix to chase a trophy
summary: This season’s NBA Cup tournament begins Friday, kicking off the start of the fourth in-season competition that features some wild court designs and gives all 30 teams the chance to compete for a trophy
story: This season’s NBA Cup tournament begins Friday, kicking off the start of the fourth in-season competition that features some wild court designs and gives all 30 teams the chance to compete for a trophy
This season's NBA Cup tournament begins Friday, kicking off the start of the fourth in-season competition that features some wild court designs and gives all 30 teams the chance to vie for a trophy.

It also offers a payday: Each player on the NBA Cup championship-winning team will collect $604,985, with $241,994 going to those on the runner-up squad, $120,997 to the players on the clubs that fall in the semifinals and $60,499 to those whose teams lose in the quarterfinals.

The format has teams split up into six groups, with five teams apiece. Those five teams play one game against each of their group opponents; the winner of each group goes to the quarterfinals, and one wild-card team from each conference will get a quarterfinal spot as well.

Quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at higher seeds, followed by a Dec. 11 championship game at Hinkle Fieldhouse on the campus of Butler University in Indianapolis. The NBA moved the title game out of Las Vegas for the first time, deciding instead to seek iconic college arenas for the matchup.
Every NBA Cup game, except the final, counts in the regular season standings. The final is a standalone event, with no impact on standings or league statistics.
Last season's Cup event was a preview of the NBA Finals. New York beat San Antonio in the Cup final, and the Knicks went on to beat the Spurs in the title series as well.
The Los Angeles Lakers won the first tournament, with Milwaukee winning in 2024 and the Knicks prevailing in 2025.
And the tournament's calling card has become the specially painted courts used only in Cup play. They're designed to stand out compared to the “regular” designs teams use for most other games.
A breakdown of the groups and the schedule, along with other things to know:
Teams — Detroit, Brooklyn, Orlando, Toronto, Milwaukee

Schedule — Detroit at Brooklyn, Friday; Orlando at Toronto, Friday; Toronto at Milwaukee. Nov. 6; Milwaukee at Orlando, Nov. 13; Orlando at Brooklyn, Nov. 20; Toronto at Detroit, Nov. 20; Detroit at Orlando, Nov. 24; Brooklyn at Milwaukee, Nov. 25; Milwaukee at Detroit, Nov. 27; Brooklyn at Toronto, Nov. 27.
Teams — New York, Philadelphia, Indiana, Miami, Cleveland
