Teams — Charlotte, Washington, Chicago, Boston, Atlanta

Schedule — Charlotte at Washington, Friday; Chicago at Boston, Friday; Washington at Atlanta, Nov. 6; Boston at Charlotte, Nov. 6; Atlanta at Chicago, Nov. 13; Charlotte at Atlanta, Nov. 20; Washington at Chicago, Nov. 20; Boston at Washington, Nov. 24; Chicago at Charlotte, Nov. 25; Atlanta at Boston, Nov. 27.
Teams — Houston, Dallas, Denver, Phoenix, Utah

Schedule — Houston at Dallas, Friday; Denver at Phoenix, Friday; Utah at Dallas, Nov. 6; Utah at Houston, Nov. 13; Phoenix at Utah, Nov. 20; Houston at Denver, Nov. 20; Dallas at Denver, Nov. 24; Phoenix at Houston, Nov. 25; Dallas at Phoenix, Nov. 27; Denver at Utah, Nov. 27.
Teams — Los Angeles Clippers, Minnesota, Oklahoma City, Memphis, New Orleans

Schedule — LA Clippers at Minnesota, Friday; Oklahoma City at Memphis, Nov. 6; Minnesota at New Orleans, Nov. 6; Memphis at New Orleans, Nov. 13; Oklahoma City at LA Clippers, Nov. 13; New Orleans at Oklahoma City, Nov. 20; Minnesota at Oklahoma City, Nov. 25; LA Clippers at Memphis, Nov. 25; Memphis at Minnesota, Nov. 27; New Orleans at LA Clippers, Nov. 27.
Teams — Los Angeles Lakers, Golden State, Portland, San Antonio, Sacramento

Schedule — LA Lakers at Golden State, Friday; Portland at LA Lakers, Nov. 6; San Antonio at Sacramento, Nov. 6; Golden State at San Antonio, Nov. 13; Portland at Sacramento, Nov. 13; Sacramento at LA Lakers, Nov. 20; Sacramento at Golden State, Nov. 25; San Antonio at Portland, Nov. 25; LA Lakers at San Antonio, Nov. 27; Golden State at Portland, Nov. 27.
Quarterfinal games will be Dec. 4 and Dec. 5. Semifinal games will be played on Dec. 8 and/or Dec. 9. The championship game is Dec. 11 at Indianapolis.
While mathematically possible that a 2-2 team could advance, history says that won't happen.
Of the 24 quarterfinalists in the first three years, 10 had 4-0 records in group play, and the other 14 all went 3-1.

Oklahoma City's Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is the all-time leader in Cup points with 502 (including a championship game that doesn't officially count in any league totals). New York's Jalen Brunson has scored 457 points in Cup games and Miami's Giannis Antetokounmpo has 453.

And here's a reason to pick Detroit to win the Cup this season: Taurean Prince plays for the Pistons now. He has appeared in 14 Cup games with the Lakers and Milwaukee — and his teams went 14-0 in those games.
Every NBA team started the season with 80 games on its schedule. The 81st and 82nd game on each regular season slate hinges on the group play standings.

For the teams that make the quarterfinals, that'll be their 81st game. For the teams that make the semifinals, that'll be their 82nd game. (That's why the title game doesn't count in the standings; it would be an 83rd game for the two finalists.)

Teams that lose in the quarterfinals will play another team that fell in that same round to fill out those schedules. And the 22 teams that don't make the quarterfinals will have their two remaining games scheduled against other non-qualifiers, those games to be played in early December.

title: Packers' Watson goes to hospital with chest injury in 2nd quarter. Then he returns to the game.
summary: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Christian Watson hurt his chest bad enough to get sent to the hospital Thursday night
story: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Christian Watson hurt his chest bad enough to get sent to the hospital Thursday night
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- Green Bay Packers wide receiver Christian Watson hurt his chest bad enough to get sent to the hospital Thursday night.

Hours later, he was back on the field — broken rib and all — helping his team finish off a 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers. It was the type of stunning transformation seen more often in professional wrestling than in actual non-scripted sports.

“I used to watch WWE as a kid,” Watson said after the game. “I felt like I was watching ‘WWE Smackdown vs. Raw’ or something, seeing the cameras on me when I was coming out of the ambulance. That was a little crazy.”
Watson's teammates offered stunned reactions after the game as they tried in vain to remember any other instances of a player returning to a game after getting sent to the hospital.
“That's some crazy (stuff), right there,” safety Javon Bullard said.

Watson's injury occurred in the second quarter as he made a 53-yard catch, with Carolina Panthers cornerback Will Lee also getting hurt on the play while making a diving stop. Lee was carted into the locker room with a hamstring injury and didn't return to the game.

“I couldn’t breathe on the field,” Watson said. “I got the wind knocked out of me. I got back to the sideline and I was kind of spitting up some blood or something like that. So the doctor said I had to go get a CT (scan)."

Watson said the CT scan showed no signs of internal bleeding, but he did break a rib on the play. Watson said he probably spent between 45 minutes and an hour at the hospital before getting transported back to Lambeau Field.
He put some padding on the broken rib and got himself ready to play again.
“I think it shows resiliency, I think it shows toughness and I think it just shows the love that he has for this team,” safety Xavier McKinney said.

Watson already had six catches for 100 yards at the time of his injury as he continued his breakthrough season. Watson has 42 catches for 708 yards — both career highs — through the Packers' first eight games.
No wonder Watson got a huge ovation when he sprinted out of the tunnel and back on the field in the third quarter. His teammates also gave him a hero's welcome.
“I was getting dap-ups like I was getting resurrected or something,” Watson said. “It was crazy. Guys were definitely shocked.”

Watson's return helped the Packers thwart Carolina's comeback attempt, as he finished with eight catches for 113 yards. After Carolina cut a 27-10 deficit to 27-19, Watson had a 7-yard reception on a third-and-2 play with about 2 1/2 minutes left to help the Packers essentially seal the victory.

He never thought about remaining out of the game once the CT scan came back clean. After all the time Watson has missed with a variety of injuries including a torn anterior cruciate ligament, he wants to make the most of every opportunity.
“This means everything to me, to be out there on the football field,” he said.

story: Elena Rybakina, the world’s No. 1 player and top-seed in the Pan Pacific Open, withdrew from her quarterfinal match, handing the win to Leylah Fernandez of Canada

Rybakina said she could not play because of an undisclosed injury. She stood on the tennis court in Tokyo and delivered the news to fans and ended by saying “I hope to see you all next year.”

title: As NFL trade deadline nears, several teams are clear sellers and others have 2 weeks to decide
summary: Jeffery Simmons, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have already been traded
story: Jeffery Simmons, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have already been traded
Jeffery Simmons, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have already been traded. More players will be on the move soon.

With the NFL trade deadline approaching on Nov. 10, several teams still have to determine whether they will be buyers or sellers. The Titans and Colts already made their intentions clear. And, they may not be done yet.

Tennessee got first-round picks in 2027 and in 2028 along with a 2027 fourth from Chicago for All-Pro defensive tackle Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Running back Tony Pollard, safety Amani Hooker and edge rusher Jermain Johnson could be next to go.

Indianapolis acquired a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick from San Francisco for eight-time Pro Bowl guard Nelson. The Colts sent Buckner to San Francisco for a 2027 fourth. Jonathan Taylor could land them a haul. Wide receiver Josh Downs will bring interest.
Here’s a look at where some teams stand and players who might be available:

The underachieving Chargers (0-6) are the NFL’s only winless team. They need to be sellers, looking to add draft picks. Veteran edge rusher Khalil Mack is still productive, though only a situational player at this point of his career. Veteran cornerback Donte Jackson has value. Wide receiver Quentin Johnston is young enough to be part of a rebuild if the Chargers keep him. Trading franchise quarterback Justin Herbert would be a massive and highly unlikely blockbuster. He has a full no-trade clause and would generate dead cap hits of $31.6 million this year and $50.4 million in 2027. That won't stop folks from speculating.

The Dolphins (1-5) are heading nowhere and need to add young talent. Defensive tackle Zach Sieler, right tackle Austin Jackson and edge Josh Uche can help them add some picks. Linebacker Jordyn Brooks is coming off an All-Pro season and could be a core player for the future if he stays.

The Cardinals (2-5) have edge rusher Josh Sweat and safety Budda Baker to place on the open market. Both players are talented and would get a nice haul. Arizona already traded wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Texans. There’s a possibility QB Jacoby Brissett could be available, opening a path for rookie Carson Beck to play. Backup QB Gardner Minshew is expendable.

After making blockbuster trades last year, sending Sauce Gardner to Indianapolis and Quennen Williams to Dallas, the Jets (2-5) have three first-round picks in 2027. They seem to be in constant rebuild mode so more picks are always beneficial. Wideout Garrett Wilson and running back Breece Hall would land the best return. Teams will be interested in pass rusher Will McDonald, a former first-round pick. Could the Jets pry Herbert from the Chargers for a package that includes those first-round picks? Doubtful.

After going to the NFC championship game following the 2024 season, the Commanders (1-4-1) have gone backward. They could deal defensive tackle Daron Payne, wideout Stefon Diggs, edge rushers K’Lavon Chaisson and Dorance Armstrong Jr. Washington could be one of those teams that sells and buys, looking to add young talent with upside. A receiver like Jacksonville’s Brian Thomas Jr. fits that caetgory.

Despite a 2-5 record, the Buccaneers are still in the race in a wide-open and weak NFC South where every team has a losing record. A win over Atlanta (3-4) on Sunday puts Tampa Bay just a half-game behind Carolina (3-4) for first place. A loss won’t knock them out but the Bucs face Chicago on the road next week. If they fall to 2-7, general manager Jason Licht could stock up on draft picks. Veteran receiver Chris Godwin Jr., edge rusher Yaya Diaby, defensive tackle A’Shawn Robinson, running back Kenneth Gainwell and safety Antoine Winfield Jr. are among the players who could be available. Defensive tackle Vita Vea has value but carries a 2027 dead cap hit of $19.7 million if he’s traded.

They’re in a similar position to the Buccaneers. The Eagles (2-5) are in a winnable division despite five straight losses. They’ve been decimated by injuries and won’t have quarterback Jalen Hurts the rest of the season. If they find a way to beat the Commanders and Giants (4-2-1) in the next two games, Philadelphia would be right back in the race for the NFC East. Otherwise, GM Howie Roseman could start unloading talent. He already sent Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens to Baltimore a few weeks ago. Roseman has more of a sell/buy philosphy so he'll be looking to add also.

When he’s healthy, Saquon Barkley is still productive and could be the missing piece for several contending teams like the Seahawks, Vikings, Packers and Bengals. He’s under contract through the 2028 season with just $2.5 million guaranteed next year so that’s an attractive for potential suitors. Linebacker Zach Baun, cornerback Riq Woolen, guard Landon Dickerson and tight end Dallas Goedert also could be moved for the right price.

title: From 2,000 runners to 60,000: The 5-borough New York City Marathon at 50
summary: Fifty years ago, the New York City Marathon ran through all five boroughs of the city for the first time
story: Fifty years ago, the New York City Marathon ran through all five boroughs of the city for the first time
NEW YORK -- Fifty years ago, the New York City Marathon ran through all five boroughs of the city for the first time.
There were just over 2,000 competitors in that seventh running of the race, including only 88 women. Now about 60,000 runners will step up to the starting line Sunday with nearly half of them women.
Bill Rodgers, a year after winning the Boston Marathon for the first time, won in the debut of the five-borough course and is the only man to win the event four times, from 1976-79.

“I remember everything distinctly, it was so intense,” Rodgers recalled Thursday. “The first time being on the Verrazzano Bridge (at the start), we were nervous. It was so different as we were used to running in Central Park.”

The race was moved out of Central Park in celebration of the U.S. Bicentennial and to help uplift the city, which was struggling. It ended up turning into one of the marquee events in New York and marathoning for the past 50 years.
“The sport really evolved that day,” Rodgers said. “Some ways it's the same, but the competitive side is more and more global then it was during those days.”

There will be runners from more than 140 countries competing Sunday, including defending champion Benson Kipruto of Kenya. He won in thrilling fashion last year, edging Alexander Mutiso by three-hundredths of a second.
Kipruto said he has watched the finish of last year's race many times and each one he marvels at the ending.
“One of my friends ask me, is it real? It looks like a movie and you're the main actor,” Kipruto said. “I was just laughing, so it was really amazing last year.”

Two-time champion Hellen Obiri, who is also Kenyan, returns to defend her title a year after she broke the women's course record in 2 hours, 19 minutes, 51 seconds. That was nearly three minutes faster then the previous best set in 2003 by Margaret Okayo.
“Last year we weren't expecting to run fast," Obiri said. ”First and foremost on Sunday the goal is to win."
The New York City Marathon began in 1970 and the first six years were run inside Central Park doing loops. Obiri said she couldn’t imagine doing that now.
“The fans are great all across New York City and that would be lost,” said Obiri, who ran the race for the first time in 2022 and won it in 2023.
New Yorker Dana Smolin is running the race for the fourth time and agreed with Obiri's thoughts on what makes the race so special.

“There are so many people out there cheering,” she said. “I grew up watching the race and always wanted to run it. I love running through all five boroughs and this year is extra special because it's the 50th anniversary of the five-borough race. Now, when I see kids cheering, I hope I inspire them just like it inspired me.”

For the first time in 15 years there will be a minor change in the course. The runners will take a slightly different route in Mile 20 when the race is in the Bronx. The move was made to reduce the number of turns in the borough from seven to five and will also ease some of the street closures in the area.
Two-time defending wheelchair champion Susannah Scaroni will look for her third straight title nearly three months after giving birth to her first child.
The fact she's competing left fellow wheelchair racer Tatyana McFadden in awe.

“It's crazy,” said McFadden, who is looking for her sixth New York Marathon title and 25th overall. “I’m excited for her. I think it’s wonderful to see, you know, women, and mothers coming back and racing. We need more support around that and more encouragement.”

title: Packers' Jacobs says TD celebration that drew criticism was modeled after a gospel song
summary: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night
story: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night

GREEN BAY, Wis. -- Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night.

This was Jacobs’ second game of the season after coming off the commissioner’s exempt list. He was placed on that list after charges were filed against him in August stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend during which she said he threw her to the ground.
Jacobs pleaded no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property.

Jacobs had just scored on a 1-yard run in the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers when he put his hands behind his back for a moment while accepting congratulations from teammates. The video garnered plenty of attention on social media as some who watched on television believed Jacobs was simulating getting handcuffed.
Jacobs said he instead was modeling his celebration after a gospel song called “Break Every Chain.”
“The guys did it with me,” Jacobs said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.”

Jacobs said he had spoken with Savion Williams and other receivers before making his season debut, and they came up with the idea that he would do a celebration thanking God after his first touchdown of the season. That celebration happened Sunday, as he went to his knees and raised his arms aloft after scoring in a 20-17 loss at Detroit.

They also had planned this “Break Every Chain” celebration after his second touchdown of the season. When Jacobs was asked about putting his hands behind his back as part of the celebration, he noted that the telecast only showed a brief portion of what he did.
“It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. Like I said, it is what it is.”

Jacobs hadn’t been able to play or practice while he was on the commissioner’s exempt list. He was removed from that list last week, enabling him to play again even though the NFLs investigation of him remains ongoing.

title: Kentucky appeals judge denies NCAA bid to block 30 athletes from playing as hoops season draws near
summary: A Kentucky Court of Appeals judge has denied the NCAA's request for emergency relief, allowing 30 college athletes to remain eligible as the basketball season is about to begin
story: A Kentucky Court of Appeals judge has denied the NCAA's request for emergency relief, allowing 30 college athletes to remain eligible as the basketball season is about to begin

The NCAA was denied emergency relief by a Kentucky Court of Appeals judge Friday, leaving eligible a host of college athletes as the basketball season is about to begin until a panel of three judges can consider the governing body's request for relief.

The 30 athletes involved, including Missouri basketball player Mark Mitchell and LSU's Skyy Clark, received a temporary injunction Oct. 16 to compete while the NCAA appealed a ruling that allowed members of the 2022 high school graduating class to play a final season in their respective sports under the NCA's new five-for-five model.

Kentucky judge Sara Walter Combs wrote in her decision that the NCAA failed to prove that the injunction created “imminent, ruinous and incalculable injury," and that it serves no purpose “to flip-flop repeatedly as our courts work through the underlying issues.”

Along with allowing the basketball players involved in the case to begin their seasons next week, the ruling allows football players Alex Afari Jr. of Kentucky, Texas Tech quarterback Thomas Castellanos and Louisville football players Jabari Mack and Kalib Perry — all of whom are also involved in the litigation — to continue to compete while the case plays out.

Multiple lawsuits filed in several states have focused on the NCAA's new eligibility model due to be implemented next fall. It allows athletes five years of eligibility beginning when an athlete turns 19 or graduates from high school, whichever is earliest.

But the implementation excluded athletes who began college careers during the 2022-23 season and completed four years. And those athletes, including some who have played for professional teams, are now suing to play their fifth season in college.

The ruling in Kentucky came one day after the Ohio Supreme Court kept in place a ruling from earlier this month allowing two dozen players involved in an eligibility case there to remain available for their teams. The lead plaintiff is Filip Borovicanin of Xavier, which opens its season Monday, while other basketball players involved include Gonzaga’s Javon Bennett and MJ Collins of Cincinnati.
The NCAA legal office sent a memo to its members late Thursday saying it was “deeply disappointed” by the outcome in Ohio.

“Every minute played by an ineligible player is an opportunity deprived to an eligible student-athlete — sometimes in the pinnacle events of a season,” the NCAA's letter said. “And it provides a significant competitive advantage to schools rostering experienced players who exhausted their eligibility.”

title: Love throws 3 TD passes as the Packers beat the Panthers 27-19
summary: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to defeat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night
story: Jordan Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Green Bay Packers withstood three turnovers to defeat the Carolina Panthers 27-19 on Thursday night
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- Jordan Love realizes the Green Bay Packers need to finish better.
They started out well enough Thursday night that their fourth-quarter struggles didn't really matter.
Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Packers withstood three turnovers and Carolina's late comeback attempt to beat the Panthers 27-19.
“Late in the game, it wasn't good enough," Love said. “We weren't able to finish the way we wanted. That's something we've got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”

Love went 30 of 41 for 288 yards with touchdown passes to Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Jacobs plus an interception. Although Jacobs rushed for only 39 yards on 21 carries against the NFL’s lowest-ranked run defense, he scored on a 4-yard catch and 1-yard run.
That was more than enough for the Packers on a night when they sacked Bryce Young six times. Green Bay hasn't allowed any of its last five opponents to exceed 20 points.
“This defense is really special,” safety Javon Bullard said.

After trailing 27-10 in the third quarter, Carolina cut Green Bay’s lead to 27-19 on Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker on a fourth-and-3 play with 5:37 remaining. Young’s ensuing 2-point conversion pass was incomplete.

The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 before losing the ball on downs at midfield with 2:41 remaining. Carolina got one last chance from its own 20 with 22 seconds and no timeouts remaining, but Dani Dennis-Sutton's sack essentially ended any comeback hopes.
“Love the fight in the group,” Panthers coach Dave Canales said. “Didn’t expect anything less. The guys kept battling all the way through, gave us some opportunities at the end.”
Young went 23 of 41 for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Carolina's Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards.

Green Bay’s Christian Watson returned to the game after hurting his chest while making a 53-yard catch in the second quarter, causing him to get taken to the hospital. Carolina cornerback Will Lee hurt his hamstring while diving to make a tackle on the same play, and he got carted into the locker room.
Watson said he got clearance to return to the game after a CT scan didn't show any internal bleeding. Watson did say he broke a rib on the play.

“I felt like I was watching ‘WWE Smackdown vs. Raw’ or something, seeing the cameras on me when I was coming out of the ambulance,” said Watson, who caught eight passes for 113 yards. “That was a little crazy. It was a surreal experience, no doubt.”
Carolina already has three other cornerbacks on injured reserve: Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), Mike Jackson (groin) and Jaycee Horn (quadriceps).

After fumbling the opening kickoff to set up a Carolina field goal and going three-and-out on their first series, the Packers (5-3) scored touchdowns on three of their next four possessions to take command.
Love threw a 12-yard touchdown pass across the middle to Kraft on a third-and-8 play to put Green Bay ahead 6-3, as struggling rookie Trey Smack’s extra-point attempt bounced off the left upright.

Watson’s 53-yard catch set up a Jacobs touchdown run that put Green Bay ahead for good, 13-10 early in the second quarter. One play after dropping a potential touchdown pass, Golden caught a 24-yarder in the left corner of the end zone on third-and-13 to make it 20-10.

Carolina got the ball to start the second half, but Chris McClellan and Evan Williams stopped Hubbard a yard short on fourth-and-2 from midfield. On Green Bay’s ensuing drive, Love found Jacobs to extend the lead to 27-10.
Green Bay led 27-13 and had the ball on Carolina’s 28 in the opening minute of the fourth quarter when Love threw a pass to Golden that Zakee Wheatley intercepted in the end zone.
That turnover sparked Carolina’s comeback attempt, but the Panthers ultimately couldn't break through against Green Bay's defense.
“I said at the beginning of the year, and I still feel this way: I think the sky is the limit for this defense,” Packers linebacker Isaiah McDuffie said.

Several members of the Milwaukee Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, received a huge ovation as they arrived at Lambeau Field one night after winning the first World Series title in franchise history.

Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff held the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft as he emerged from the tunnel during a timeout before the second quarter. A few of them attempted a “Lambeau leap” into the crowd, with outfielder Sal Frelick having the most success.
Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”

The Packers honored former president/CEO Bob Harlan during a halftime ceremony in which his name was unveiled on Lambeau Field’s northeast façade alongside that of former Packers general manager Ted Thompson. Harlan, who was the Packers’ president/CEO from 1989-2008, died March 5 at the age of 89.
Panthers: OG Corey Bullock hurt his quadriceps in the second half.
Packers: TE Josh Whyle was evaluated for a concussion in the first half.
Panthers: Host Denver on Nov. 8.
Packers: At New England on Nov. 8.

title: Ailing Kimi Antonelli nears F1 title in Mexico and will make history as youngest champion
summary: Kimi Antonelli arrives in Mexico with the Formula 1 title within his grasp
story: Kimi Antonelli arrives in Mexico with the Formula 1 title within his grasp

MEXICO CITY -- Kimi Antonelli arrived in Mexico with the Formula 1 title well within his grasp. Despite a viral infection which was keeping him away from the track, he is set to be crowned the youngest champion in the series’ history on Sunday.
Antonelli missed Thursday's media session while recovering but Mercedes expects him back for Friday's first practice session for the Mexico City Grand Prix.
To secure the title and break the record set by Sebastian Vettel — the youngest champion to date at 23 in 2010 — Antonelli can finish as low as ninth.
Antonelli wants to seal the deal with another big result, but he could also do it without scoring another point if someone other than Lewis Hamilton or George Russell wins Sunday's race.

“I’m very excited. I would love to clinch the title in style with a great result,” Antonelli said after taking his ninth win of the season in Texas last week. “That’s the mindset. That’s always the mindset, and that’s what it will be from now until the end of the season. I’m just going to try to enjoy every moment because they’re moments that will always be remembered.”

Antonelli can also become the first Italian driver to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Mercedes can clinch the constructors' title on Sunday for the first time since 2021 — though that would need a big points haul for Antonelli and Russell, combined with a disastrous race for second-place Ferrari.
Mercedes hit the ground running under this season's new regulations, with George Russell’s victory at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix.

Defying predictions this would be Russell's year, Antonelli surged ahead by winning five consecutive races as his teammate faded. Russell struggled to explain his lack of pace after finishing eighth in Austin last week.

“I think, at least in terms of my own approach, we’re not like boxers in a ring fighting directly against someone else,” Russell said of his relationship with Antonelli. “We’re essentially competing against ourselves. It’s the work and preparation you put in personally that makes the difference to a good performance”.
Colton Herta will take the wheel of Valtteri Bottas’s Cadillac for Friday's first practice, with Bottas' future still unclear.
Cadillac has yet to score a point since joining F1 this year, and its debut season has included some painful learning experiences included a long-running problem with the brakes overheating.

Sergio Pérez recently signed a two-year contract extension through 2029, but Cadillac has yet to confirm whether Bottas will stay with him. Herta would give the American team an American driver, but the former IndyCar prodigy has had a disappointing year in Formula 2 and is just 19th in the standings.

“I think he is doing a good job. He is bringing good feedback to the team, good information, which is all that we need of him,” Pérez said of Herta on Thursday. “Obviously, it’s very difficult to showcase your speed or your true level during FP1 sessions. But now that he’s had a bit more time in the car, we’re starting to see more of his speed.”
Pérez, who reaches the milestone of 300 Grand Prix starts on Sunday, declined to express a preference.

“Obviously, it’s not my decision; it’s up to Marcin (Budkowski, team principal) to decide who they want in the car,” Pérez added. “I’m also working really well with Valtteri. I think he’s been quite unlucky in a few races. It’s not an easy decision for the team.”

The 2,240-meter (7,350-foot) altitude above sea level in Mexico City will pose a challenge for participants in the Mexico City Grand Prix. According to Mercedes’ George Russell, the Ferrari team could have an advantage.
At this altitude, thin air starves the engines of oxygen—resulting in a loss of power—and makes it more difficult to prevent vehicle components, such as the brakes, from overheating.

“It’s going to be very interesting,” said Russell. “I think turbo lag is going to be a major factor for many teams this weekend. It’s no secret that teams like Ferrari use a smaller turbo than most, so they likely have a significant advantage in this regard.”

title: Nakase and Valkyries are determined to avoid another slow start in WNBA Finals Game 7 against Dream
summary: There should be no problem with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream approaching the first WNBA Finals Game 7 in league history with a sense of urgency
story: There should be no problem with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream approaching the first WNBA Finals Game 7 in league history with a sense of urgency
ATLANTA -- There should be no problem with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream approaching the first WNBA Finals Game 7 in league history with a sense of urgency.

Then again, that's what Golden State coach Natalie Nakase thought about Game 6. She was baffled that her team somehow left behind its defensive intensity at the start of Thursday's 80-69 loss to the Dream that forced Game 7 at “Ballhalla” in San Francisco on Saturday night.

While the Valkyries were missing their defensive edge that was so important in their 64-55 Game 5 win, the Dream seized the opportunity by making 73.3% of their shots in the first quarter and racing to a 32-15 lead. The 32 points are the most by either team in a quarter in the series.
Atlanta kept the lead in double figures most of the remainder of the game.
“Can’t let that happen right out of the gate,” Valkyries guard Veronica Burton said. “There needs to be a sense of urgency. It’s the WNBA Finals.”

Even after the Valkyries showed fight by attempting a second-half comeback, Nakase was still struggling to comprehend the lackadaisical start so she could make sure it's not repeated in Saturday night's decisive game. She said she planned to have conversations with her players about the issue on the flight back to California.

“I put that on me of like, what did I not say, what did I not get to my team of the sense of urgency that we knew they were going to play?” Nakase said of the Dream. “We knew they were going to play desperate. We knew they were going to play like their life depends on it. For us not to match that is disappointing and frustrating. So, yeah, I need to make sure my team is prepared.”
Added Nakase of her plan to seek answers: “For me, I need clarity. I need some information.”
The Dream and Valkyries each will be playing for their first WNBA title.
Atlanta's Allisha Gray scored 23 points and Rhyne Howard had 21 in Thursday's win when Golden State's only lead was 2-0. Angel Reese added 15 points and 14 rebounds for the Dream.

“Our job is not done,” Reese said. “We definitely could be happy about it for now but we have more work to do. I think we definitely have another level that we can get to, like (Gray) was saying. We shot a lot better this game, for sure, but I think we just continue to grow from this.”
The format for the WNBA Finals was a best-of-five series until the first best-of-seven series in 2025, when the Las Vegas Aces swept the Phoenix Mercury 4-0.
The Dream lost in the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013. The Valkyries reached this year's Finals in only their second season of existence.

Despite Thursday's Game 6 being scheduled for a much-criticized 12:30 p.m. EDT tipoff that created concerns about fans' obligations to work and school, Atlanta supporters delivered a sellout of 17,099 at State Farm Arena.

“Shout out to the crowd, being able to come here at 12:30 on a Thursday and so many things going on in the world from school to work, to everything else,” Reese said. “We’re just super thankful. We fed off their energy. They were loud from the beginning. So we’re definitely thankful for that.”
Reese knows another packed house will be supporting the Valkyries on Saturday night.

“I think that the crowd doesn’t really get to us much but I think, obviously, Game 7 is going to be a lot louder,” Reese said. “The energy is going to be electric in there. So just honestly staying poised, staying together, and I think we’ll be fine.”

Golden State's Tiffany Hayes was called for her fifth foul in a collision for a loose ball with 5:01 remaining. Hayes was left laying on the court following the collision. She slowly walked off after receiving attention from a trainer.
Nakase said she wanted to check in again with Hayes but added “she looked good to me. Yeah, she looked fine.”
Nakase and her players firmly denied the early start — 9:30 a.m. by California time — was a factor in the Valkyries' slow start.
“No. That had nothing to do with it,” Nakase said. “We played at 1 o’clock last week. No.”
Added Gabby Williams: “They played at the same time as us, right? So it’s not an excuse. We have to be better.”

title: Kings beat Senators 6-5 in OT after blowing a 4-goal lead in the 3rd period
summary: Quinton Byfield scored at 3:37 of overtime and the Los Angeles Kings beat the Ottawa Senators 6-5 on Thursday night after blowing a four-goal lead in the third period
story: Quinton Byfield scored at 3:37 of overtime and the Los Angeles Kings beat the Ottawa Senators 6-5 on Thursday night after blowing a four-goal lead in the third period
LOS ANGLES -- Quinton Byfield scored at 3:37 of overtime and the Los Angeles Kings beat the Ottawa Senators 6-5 on Thursday night after blowing a four-goal lead in the third period.
Byfield beat goalie Samuel Ersson with a snap shot from the high slot, with Drew Doughty picking up his third assist of the night on the play.

Erik Haula tied it for Los Angeles on a first-period power play and Trevor Moore, Mikey Anderson, Joel Armia and Artemi Panarin scored in the second to make it 5-1. Panarin capped the run on a power play after Ottawa's Hayden Hodgson was tossed for boarding defenseman Brandt Clarke.
Clarke missed the rest of the game because of an upper-body injury.
Ottawa roared back in the third, with Shane Pinto tying it at 5 with 1:40 left and Ersson off for an extra attacker.

Dylan Cozens scored twice in the period and Drake Batherson also connected. Cozens and Batherson struck in a 33-second span, and Cozens cut it to a goal with 7:26 remaining. Tyler Kleven opened the scoring for Ottawa in the first period.
Darcy Kuemper made 17 saves for Los Angeles.
Jonas Johansson stopped 12 of 16 shots before giving way to Ersson in the second. Ersson made 20 saves on 22 shots.

title: Defending champ Laopakdee salvages 71 for 2-shot lead in windy Asia-Pacific Amateur
summary: Defending champion Fifa Laopakdee of Thailand salvaged a 1-over 71 in strong wind Friday in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship to take a two-stroke lead into the weekend at Te Arai Links
story: Defending champion Fifa Laopakdee of Thailand salvaged a 1-over 71 in strong wind Friday in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship to take a two-stroke lead into the weekend at Te Arai Links

TOMARATA, New Zealand -- Defending champion Fifa Laopakdee of Thailand salvaged a 1-over 71 in strong wind Friday in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship to take a two-stroke lead into the weekend at Te Arai Links.

A day after opening with an 8-under 63, Laopakdee began his morning round on the seaside layout bogey-bogey-birdie-bogey-bogey in 35 mph wind. The Arizona State senior also bogeyed the 10th, then birdied Nos. 12, 13 and 17.

“I had a 5‑footer two holes in a row and the ball just snapped 90 degrees,” Laopakdee said. “I aimed a foot left from 5 feet and it went like 3 feet right. It’s pretty tricky. Overall, it was a grind out there and I would take 7 under for the first two rounds.”
The winner will receive spots in the Masters and British Open. Last year in Dubai, Laopakdee won the third hole of a playoff to become the first Thai champion in event history.

Three players from New Zealand followed on the leaderboard. Cooper Moore (70) was second at 5 under, Ryan Xie (71) was 4 under, and Zack Swanwic (67) 3 under. Kaito Sato of Japan was 2 under after a 72.
Seven players were under par after two days, with Japan's Taishi Moto (71) and China's Qiyou Wu (72) at 1 under. Moto had a hole-in-one on the par-3 eighth.

“I couldn’t make any putts because it was super windy out there so the hole-in-one definitely helped a lot," Moto said. “It was super difficult on the greens. Like ridiculous. My ball was moving. My body was moving.”

title: Boozer posts first career triple-double in Grizzlies win over Blazers
summary: Cameron Boozer had the first triple-double of his NBA career with 18 points, 12 rebounds and 12 assists, and the Memphis Grizzlies beat the Portland Trail Blazers 124-103 on Thursday night to move to 5-0
story: Cameron Boozer had the first triple-double of his NBA career with 18 points, 12 rebounds and 12 assists, and the Memphis Grizzlies beat the Portland Trail Blazers 124-103 on Thursday night to move to 5-0

PORTLAND, Ore. -- Cameron Boozer had the first triple-double of his NBA career with 18 points, 12 rebounds and 12 assists, and the Memphis Grizzlies beat the Portland Trail Blazers 124-103 on Thursday night to move to 5-0.

The Grizzlies had seven other players in double-figures, including three players off the bench. Isaiah Stewart led the Memphis reserves with 18 points. Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 24 points, nine rebounds and seven assists.

Ja Morant had 14 points and three assists in 23 minutes in his first game against his former team but left the game in the fourth quarter with a hamstring injury and did not return. One game after hitting a game-sealing 3-pointer against the Lakers, Damian Lillard went 3 of 13 from the field on Thursday.
With the Grizzlies holding a 2-point lead, they went on a 10-0 run to make it 87-75 with 2:09 left in the third quarter.
A 3-pointer by Zach Edey with 9:47 left gave the Grizzlies a 96-85 lead, forcing a Blazers timeout.
Morant cut the lead to 96-87 out of the timeout, but the Grizzlies kept the pressure on with back-to-back baskets by Western Conference Player of the Week Ty Jerome to the Memphis lead to 101-89.
Jerome scored 10 points on just 3 of 12 from the floor in the win and has cooled after a hot start to the year.
Memphis pulled away once the teams both emptied the bench and outscored Portland 33-20 in the fourth quarter.

title: Bournemouth in pinch-me territory as another underdog success story in English soccer
summary: These are pinch-me times for Bournemouth
story: These are pinch-me times for Bournemouth
Held aloft by Bournemouth supporters at one end of the club’s cozy, 12,000-seat stadium was a giant tifo that posed a simple question: “How did we end up here?”

Their team was about to play AC Milan, one of the most famous names in world soccer, in the Europa League and cruise to a 3-0 win. Three days later, it would steamroll Manchester United — another global superpower — by the same score in the Premier League.

Indeed, these are pinch-me times for fans of a team from England’s south coast which was playing in the second-tier Championship just five years ago and, 18 years ago, went into bankruptcy protection, leading to demotion to the bottom tier of the English Football League.
That year — the 2007-08 season — Milan started out as the Champions League titleholder and Man United finished it by winning Europe's biggest club trophy.
Bournemouth? It was on its knees, barely able to survive.
How different things are now.

The Cherries are owned by U.S. billionaire Bill Foley, have a raft of top international talent in its squad including U.S. captainTyler Adams, and have just finished in their highest ever end-of-season position — sixth place in the Premier League — to qualify for European competition for the first time.

In almost every transfer window Bournemouth’s best players are typically poached by the heavyweights of the European game, like Dean Huijsen going to Real Madrid, Illia Zabarnyi moving to Paris Saint-Germain and star winger Antoine Semenyo signing for Manchester City. Even its previous manager, Andoni Iraola, left to join Liverpool during the last offseason.
Yet so well-run is the club and so astute is its recruitment team — much like another upwardly mobile south-coast club, Brighton — that it isn’t turning out to be a problem.

OK, this season started slowly in the Premier League, with Bournemouth not winning any of its first six matches under newly appointed coach Marco Rose — chiefly because good performances were undermined by letting in sloppy late goals.

But the team has just had five straight wins, culminating in a magical past week containing the Milan-United double that would have had dyed-in-the-wool Bournemouth fans rubbing their eyes in disbelief and then Wednesday's 3-0 win over Aston Villa — one of England's Champions League entrants this season.
“It feels at the moment that we are in a flow but it is hard work — that’s what we have to know and we have to continue the hard work to stay in it," Rose said.

Sitting in 13th place in the 20-team Premier League but clearly with sky-high confidence, Bournemouth next faces Leeds at home on Saturday and has a benign run of games coming up, after its tough schedule to start the season.

France Under-21 star Eli Junior Kroupi, the team's biggest young talent and possibly its next big money sale, is fit again after a three-month layoff with a foot injury. Rayan, an imposing 20-year-old winger and another potential superstar-in-the-making, joined from Vasco da Gama only in January but is already in the Brazil squad and is a fearsome opponent to handle. Portugal defender Antonio Silva, signed from Benfica in the summer, is settling in nicely. Brazilian striker Evanilson has hit form with goals in four of his last five games.
No wonder Rose has high expectations.
“I want to win every game and we want to be competitive in every competition,” said the coach who has managed two of Germany's biggest clubs — Borussia Dortmund and Leipzig.

Win the Europa League — just like English clubs Tottenham and Aston Villa have done the past two seasons — and Bournemouth will be in the Champions League next year, marking the next extraordinary chapter in its rise from the depths of English soccer.

Manchester City, which is continuing to play under a cloud after being found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking, and Arsenal are tied on points at the top of the standings and both have tough games in the ninth round.
City hosts Brighton on Saturday — a repeat of their English League Cup meeting on Wednesday, won by City on penalties — and Arsenal visits Liverpool in Sunday's only match.

Under-fire Michael Carrick appears to be in charge of Manchester United only on a match-by-match basis after back-to-back heavy losses to Como in the Champions League and Bournemouth in the league. Next up for United is Chelsea away on Saturday.

Erling Haaland was rested by Man City for the cup in midweek, so will be fresh as he continues to chase history. Haaland has scored in each of his last seven league games, meaning he is closing in on Jamie Vardy's record of scoring in 11 consecutive matches for Leicester in the 2015-16 season.

Chelsea striker Joao Pedro is out for several weeks with a thigh injury and that's a problem for manager Xabi Alonso. The Brazil international has missed two games this season and Chelsea lost both and didn't score in either of them.

Man United might be missing its leading specialist striker for longer. There has been no confirmation from the club but reports in the English media, including the BBC, say Benjamin Sesko is expected to be out until at least January with a shin injury. He hasn't played since mid-September.

title: Osaka knocked out in Pan Pacific Open 2nd round as Rybakina advances
summary: Four-time major winner Naomi Osaka has been knocked out of the Pan Pacific Open by 18-year-old Mia Pohankova of Slovakia
story: Four-time major winner Naomi Osaka has been knocked out of the Pan Pacific Open by 18-year-old Mia Pohankova of Slovakia
TOKYO -- Four-time major winner Naomi Osaka lost in front of her home crowd to Slovakian teenager Mia Pohankova in the Pan Pacific Open round of 16 on Thursday.
Pohankova, who turned 18 a week ago and was a wild card entry, upset No. 7-seeded Osaka 6-3, 7-5 to advance to the quarterfinals.
Pohankova will face Alycia Parks next. Pohankova was the 2025 junior singles champion at Wimbledon.
Osaka was coming off a win over Jasmine Paolini in the first round in Tokyo.
In other round-of-16 matches, top-ranked Elena Rybakina beat Yulia Putintseva 6-2, 6-3 and Leylah Fernandez defeated No. 14 Elise Mertens 6-2, 7-6 (8).
Second-seeded Maja Chwalinska and No. 4 Belinda Bencic pulled out of the tournament earlier with injuries. Chwalinska had an injured left thigh and Bencic had a right-ankle injury.

title: Griezmann has 1 goal, 1 assist for Orlando City in 2-2 tie with Fire
summary: Antoine Griezmann had a goal and an assist and Iván Angulo also scored a goal for Orlando City in a 2-2 tie with the Chicago Fire
story: Antoine Griezmann had a goal and an assist and Iván Angulo also scored a goal for Orlando City in a 2-2 tie with the Chicago Fire
CHICAGO -- Antoine Griezmann had a goal and an assist and Iván Angulo also scored a goal for Orlando City in a 2-2 tie with the Chicago Fire on Wednesday night.

Griezmann became just the fourth player in MLS history to record a goal or assist in at least 12 consecutive matches in a single regular season. The 35-year-old French forward has 14 goals and eight assists in 16 regular-season games since joining Orlando City after the World Cup break.

The Fire (15-10-7) are fourth in the Eastern Conference with 52 points, two ahead of fifth-place Charlotte with a little more than a week left in the regular season. Orlando City (12-13-7) is seventh with 43 points.

Jonathan Bamba had a goal and an assist and Maren Haile-Selassie put away a first-touch shot in the 69th minute for Chicago. Bamba subbed on for Sergio Oregel Jr. at halftime and scored on a header, off a cross played by Leonardo Barroso, in the 57th minute.

Angulo, on the counter-attack, held a defender on his right hip as they raced down the left side and then slipped a shot past goalkeeper Chris Brady and inside the back post to open the scoring in the sixth minute.
Griemann, on the counter-attack, calmly drilled a shot from 25 yards out to make it 2-0 in the 35th.
Orlando: Plays Saturday at Charlotte.
Chicago: Visits Colorado on Halloween.

title: Jasinski and Roberts each score a goal for Earthquakes in 2-2 tie with Rapids
summary: Jack Jasinski and Reid Roberts each scored a goal for the San Jose Earthquakes in a 2-2 tie with the Colorado Rapids
story: Jack Jasinski and Reid Roberts each scored a goal for the San Jose Earthquakes in a 2-2 tie with the Colorado Rapids
SAN JOSE, Calif. -- Jack Jasinski and Reid Roberts each scored a goal for the San Jose Earthquakes on Wednesday night in a 2-2 tie with the Colorado Rapids.

The Earthquakes (13-9-10), who are winless in five straight, have 49 points. San Jose is fifth in the Western Conference standings, behind Houston and St. Louis (tied for third with 51 apiece). The Rapids (12-13-7) are seventh with 43 points.
Morgan Whittaker scored in the 26th minute, his second consecutive game with a goal, and Darren Yapi added a goal in the 73rd, for the Rapids.
Timo Werner was shown a straight red card in the 71st minute and the Earthquakes played a man down until Colorado’s Kosi Thompson was also shown a straight red card in 75th.

Yapi, who subbed on for Whittaker in the 63rd minute, took a pass from Georgi Minoungou, cut back to evade a defender and then fired a shot from the left side of the area that slipped inside the near post to make it 2-1.
Whittaker rolled a low shot from the center of the area past Angus Gunn and inside the right post to make it 1-1 in the 26th minute.
Roberts went up high for a header, off a corner kick played in by Werner, that deflected off the crossbar into the net to open the scoring in the 15th minute.
Hansen had six saves for Colorado, which is unbeaten in five straight.
The Rapids had 54% possession but were outshot by San Jose 16-8, 8-2 on target.
Rapids: Host Chicago on Saturday.
Earthquakes: Hosts Salt Lake on Halloween.

title: Generations of anglers have made the pilgrimage to Montauk to catch striped bass
summary: Generations of fishermen have come to Montauk, New York, to fish for striped bass, but the fish are in the midst of a decline
story: Generations of fishermen have come to Montauk, New York, to fish for striped bass, but the fish are in the midst of a decline

MONTAUK, N.Y. -- On most October nights, fishing guide Bill Wetzel can be found navigating the shores of Montauk, New York, in a modified 4x4 pickup truck, rumbling over boulders and thick sand as he scans the surface of the Atlantic for signs of life.

He notes, and meticulously logs, where he spots seams in the water's currents, cuts in sandbars, points and coves, troughs along the shoreline or birds working over bait that was pushed to the surface by one of Montauk’s many predators. Any sign that a striped bass might be feeding beneath the waves, Wetzel will likely see it.
So, as he prepares for a mid-afternoon nap between nocturnal surfcasting customers, he tunes in his VHF radio to get the latest marine forecast. The squawking voice tells him something new.
“Northwest ...” he mutters aloud, pondering what the wind change might mean for his next outing.
He already knows the tides, the moon phase, and the best spots to fish under whatever conditions the ocean has to offer.
What he doesn’t know is if there will be any fish left to catch.

Some years, fishermen will make more than 17 million fishing trips seeking striped bass. But for countless anglers on the East Coast, that future is in danger. Scientists say the species is in decline because of a host of human-caused, environmental and ecological changes, putting the $8 billion industry in jeopardy, and threatening a generations-old tradition of standing on the ocean's edge and trying to catch a potentially humongous fish.
Here’s a look at Montauk’s anglers and what they’ve experienced amid a dramatic decline in striped bass.

Wetzel is obsessed with understanding and finding these fish, which can grow larger than 50 pounds (23 kilograms). Contrary to what one might expect, he doesn’t want to kill them. Instead, he wants to save them so future generations get the opportunity to enjoy the sport he loves.

He has led fishermen to Montauk in search of stripers for more than 25 years, and is one of the best known guides on Long Island. He also actively uses his platforms on social media to discuss conservation, and remembers the collapse of the stock decades ago that led to a fishing shutdown in the mid-1980s.
He doesn't want to relive those days. But he fears it's coming.
“I haven't seen a blitz in four years,” Wetzel said, referring to the chaotic feeding frenzies that were once a hallmark of Montauk's shores. “There's no small fish left. They're gone.”
More and more, he says, the only fish left are big ones. That's because the population isn't replenishing itself.

Jason Markowitz, an IT professional who lives outside New York City, is the former president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association. He is one of the intrepid anglers who still swim out to Montauk's offshore rocks, proven fishing grounds where strong waves can push you around and predators swim at your feet.
He said the chilly swim is worth it “if the fish are there.” Increasingly, he said, they aren't.
“You’ve got a lot of folks that are finding fish but it really is a case of ‘last of the buffalo,’” Markowitz said.

John Skinner is 65 and has been fishing for stripers on Long Island since he was a boy of 10 or younger. In the ensuing years, he has become one of the most respected and sought-after authorities on striped bass fishing.
Looking at the current state of the striped bass industry and the decline in population, two words come to his mind: “It sucks.”

Blunt, but the situation is devastating for Skinner, who runs a popular YouTube channel about striper fishing and authored a book on the subject. These days, he hits up his prime spots on Long Island's North Fork and sometimes leaves empty-handed.

Skinner is inclined to let the scientists come up with reasons for the decline, but he said he can't help but notice a lack of small fish like menhaden for the stripers to feed on. And he sees a lack of other large, predatory fish beyond just stripers.
It's about more than just fish. Sitting in his office, surrounded by decades-old fishing lures, he thinks back to his days on the family boat in the early 1970s, when the itch to fish first set in.
“What do you do with a little kid to keep him out of your hair,” Skinner said. “Give him a rod and some worms.”
With 40 years of fishing under his belt, Mahan says he’s nostalgic for a time when the fish were more abundant.
“What it was like, back in the later ‘80s and ’90s, was spectacular,” Mahan said.

Mahan, who sports a drooping white mustache and fishes from the rocks in a black hoodie and waders, fears the way to save the stripers might be to leave them alone entirely for a while. It would be hard, because striper fishing is in his blood, but sometimes it feels like the only way.
Read more about the science and regulatory issues facing striped bass here.
At “The End,” as it's known, of Long Island, Montauk’s waters are historically renowned for producing some of the best striper fishing in the world.

Part of the draw of Montauk has always been the danger and dynamic environment — there are sand beaches, boulder-strewn points and swift currents that pull bait into coves where fishermen can intercept the big predators chasing their forage.
“The lighthouse kind of draws you in,” said fisherman John Mahan on an October trip. “Beautiful conditions. There should be fish here right now.”
For a long time, Montauk's unofficial motto was “a small drinking village with a big fishing problem.”
“Not anymore,” says Wetzel, lamenting a change in culture.
But he's quick to say he still loves Montauk, and fishing.
“It's in me. If it's not in you, a lot of guys come and go. It's not in you. Plus, I mean, look at this. Look at this — that's why,” he said, motioning to the surf and the ocean beyond it.

Once a blue-collar fishing town, the community has become increasingly hard to distinguish from the nearby ultrawealthy enclaves of the Hamptons. It was a slow transformation that took place over decades and accelerated in the 2000s. But fishermen who have journeyed there for generations say it still maintains an identity all its own.
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine.

title: Graphika finds China-linked Spamouflage accounts posing as US voters on X
summary: Analysts at Graphika report that the influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections
story: Analysts at Graphika report that the influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- The long-running influence campaign known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the midterm elections, with accounts likely linked to China posing as U.S. voters and posting divisive content about U.S. politics, social issues and the elections, analysts say.

In a blog posted on Friday, Graphika, a New York-based firm that tracks online networks, said it had identified Spamouflage-linked activity on X that closely resembles tactics documented in 2024 ahead of the U.S. presidential election.
“The accounts post content questioning election integrity and the legitimacy of U.S. democracy,” the Graphika blog said.

Intelligence and national security officials have long warned that Russia, China and Iran have run online influence operations targeting U.S. voters ahead of elections. China, rather than supporting one presidential candidate over the other, has focused its efforts on undermining confidence in elections, voting and the U.S. in general, observers have said.
Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said in a statement that China “has never and will never interfere in the U.S. elections."

Darren Linvill, who co-directs Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub and has tracked Spamouflage activity, said there is “no chance it tips the balance in any real political conversation.”
“Spamouflage is famously bad at mimicking real Americans," Linvill said. “It's outside their wheelhouse.”

Rather, the network has been more effective in suppressing information, Linvill said, as the accounts linked to the influence operation “very frequently attack and harass members of the Chinese diaspora community” and are part of a wider effort by Beijing to silence views it dislikes.

In its blog, Graphika said it identified an account that appears to have replaced a removed account that was linked to Spamouflage and has posted divisive U.S. political content, including attacks on Democratic Party leadership during the U.S. government shutdown in October 2025 and criticism of immigration policy.

Graphika flagged four accounts with a history of Spamouflage activity that now amplify MAGA-styled personas and another account with more than 200,000 followers that presents itself as a Philippine culture blog but now posts pro-China and divisive U.S.-focused content.
Graphika said it could not determine whether the account was hijacked or whether the original operator sold or otherwise lost control of it.

title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
summary: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish
story: Striped bass are in decline on the East Coast and fishermen and scientists are in a race to save the iconic sport fish

MONTAUK, N.Y. -- Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.
Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.

“I’m part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon,” said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.
Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren't showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.

Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.

Factors like years of warming waters — a prime concern cited by many scientists — poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.
See a visual essay featuring anglers who were fishing the shores of Long Island earlier this month here.

“Stripers” are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine's coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.

Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they're measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action — including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s — is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.

“They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned,” said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. “People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass.”
Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms — it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U.S. alone.
And it relies on a fish whose future looks grim.

“Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse,” said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.
“Sometime around 2029, 2030 it’s going to go off a cliff,” he said, “and it’s going to be ugly.”

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them — specifically, cool, wet springs.

Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.
Conditions have been poor in recent years, and fewer fish have entered the population going back to 2019, said Chris Batsavage, chair of the commission's striped bass management board.
“Low precipitation and waters that warm quickly result in weak year classes,” Batsavage said. “It seems like it's environmentally driven.”
The conditions have led to a “slump of bad years” that have made it especially difficult for the fish to maintain their population in the Chesapeake, Versak said.

John Skinner, who wrote a book about striped bass fishing and runs a YouTube channel on the subject that has more than 100,000 followers, has been fishing off Long Island for more than 50 years and says once-reliable spots have completely dried up.
“I'm not saying the fishing is bad. I’m saying when you go there in perfect conditions, you catch nothing,” Skinner said. “Absolutely nothing.”

Many other striped bass fishermen across the Northeast shared a recurring story this summer and fall — the fish's once-plentiful schools are dried up, and the individuals that remain are clearly older, meaning years of reproduction failure are starting to take their toll.

Some fishermen said stricter rules or a fishing moratorium could be the only ways to prevent the fish’s population from becoming dangerously low. And they lament what they’re seeing on the waters — smaller schools of fish, many of them older and larger, with few young fish entering the population to provide a future.

They also see more factors than just the warming environment at play. Some see years of heavy fishing on striped bass becoming apparent today in the form of a lower population. Others blame the resurgence of sharks buoyed by years of conservation efforts, as a reintroduction of competition for the fish.

The Atlantic States commission considers the stock to be overfished, although it says overfishing is not occurring at the moment. The fish are caught commercially as well as recreationally, but recreational fishing is much larger.

Most of the recreational catch is tossed back into the ocean alive. Still, some fish don't survive the encounter. Regulators have historically expected 9% to die after release, while newer data shows the number could be less than 5%.

Limits on how large a striped bass can be caught and kept are typically in the range of 28 to 31 inches (71 to 79 centimeters), with rules varying by state and location. Striped bass are popular with catch-and-release fishermen, and these days, it’s more common to catch larger bass, many well over 31 inches.
Paquette, the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association coordinator and a longtime angler himself, said that without drastic action he fears the end of striped bass fishing.
“If you’re a guy who thought he was going to retire and striped bass fish, and you’re planning on retiring soon, get a different plan,” Paquette said.
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine. Associated Press video journalist Mingson Lau contributed.

title: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
summary: The provost of Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found that he used artificial intelligence in his writing, including in a Washington Post guest column on AI cheating
story: The provost of Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found that he used artificial intelligence in his writing, including in a Washington Post guest column on AI cheating

A top administrator at Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, including in a guest column in The Washington Post on AI cheating.

The announcement Wednesday of Provost Santiago Schnell’s departure from the Ivy League university comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools.

Dartmouth touts itself as the birthplace of AI, saying the field got its start at the school in Hanover, New Hampshire, in 1956 when a small group of scientists gathered for a summer research project on the topic. A conference commemorating the 70th anniversary — titled “What Must Remain Human?” — began Thursday.
University President Sian Leah Beilock said in a written statement that keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI means “leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing.”

“That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars,” the president wrote, adding that Schnell’s departure was "his decision” and that the school wishes him well.
Schnell referred questions to his attorneys, who didn’t immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Issues arose after the news outlet Semafor ran guest columns in major newspapers through an AI filter. Schnell’s August column in the Post, titled “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem," was found to be entirely written by AI.
Schnell defended himself, saying at the time he used ChatGPT to "refine a few arguments” but that the column was based on his “own thinking.”

The college paper, The Dartmouth, then ran other publications from Schnell through an AI detector. Writing that predated ChatGPT’s 2022 public release was found to be human-written, but high rates of AI use were detected in his recent writing.

Schnell told the paper in an email last month that he uses AI for “language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organization and making writing processes more efficient.” The paper ran the statement through an AI-detector and found it was AI-written.
In a follow-up statement, Schnell told the paper that he “developed the substance and wrote a draft” of the email, then “used an AI tool to assist with language and clarity.”
An investigation ensued, and the faculty committee found that Schnell used AI to “meaningfully alter his writing” and “was not forthcoming about his AI use.”

Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously taught and held leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan and Indiana University, according to his LinkedIn profile.
