title: South Korea fines Google and Apple over unfair app market practices
summary: South Korea on Wednesday fined Google and Apple a combined $47.6 million, saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews
story: South Korea on Wednesday fined Google and Apple a combined $47.6 million, saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet’s Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country’s media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Apple said it “respectfully” disagrees with the decision, arguing that its current practices comply with South Korean law and that it is evaluating its legal options. Apple said its in-app payment system allows users to make secure transactions while protecting them from predatory tactics and fraud and that such safeguards that could potentially be lost when paying through alternative methods.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

title: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions
summary: The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
story: The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing

ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.

Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.

The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.

In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.

Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.

Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.

All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.

Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.

The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.

Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.

Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

title: New York enacts ban on 'unsafe' chatbot behavior with kids
summary: New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions ban on certain chatbot behaviors to protect children using artificial intelligence
story: New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions ban on certain chatbot behaviors to protect children using artificial intelligence

HARRISBURG, Pa. -- New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions on companion chatbot behavior, as states increasingly move to protect children who use artificial intelligence, regulate how employers deploy AI systems and push developers to prevent an AI-caused catastrophe.
Legislation signed Wednesday by Gov. Kathy Hochul outlines a dozen definitions of “unsafe AI companion features” that will be prohibited when a companion chatbot interacts with a child under 18.

A violation could expose a chatbot developer to a lawsuit by the state attorney general's office. Penalties could include monetary damages, shutting down the chatbot and destroying data. The law takes effect Jan. 1.

Hochul, in the thick of her reelection campaign, signed the bill amid growing warnings about the existential risks posed by the rapid development of AI technology and calls for bold action by a reluctant Washington.

With Congress doing little to regulate AI, state legislatures are packed with efforts to wield state consumer protection laws to make AI use more transparent and rein in chatbots and rogue AI frontier models.
New York and California are at the vanguard of such laws that also are targeting social media platforms.

In September, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring chatbot developers to assess a model's risk to children, show how they tried to eliminate those risks and submit to an independent audit to determine whether they are complying with the law.
He also signed legislation to prohibit social media platforms from deploying addictive features for users under 16.

Meanwhile, eight states sued AI giant OpenAI earlier this month, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what one activist called “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”

However, governors acknowledge that Congress and the federal government have farther-reaching abilities to clamp down on AI-posed threats, even as President Donald Trump has brushed off concerns and warned states not to regulate AI.

Under New York's law, outlawed chatbot behavior with children under 18 includes suggestions that the chatbot is a real person that has emotions, opinions or an actual relationship with the child. It also outlaws chatbot messages that use flattery, involve sexually explicit material or encourage secrecy or unhealthy behavior.
Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of watchdog group Common Sense Media, called New York's law "the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country."

Justine Gluck, policy analyst at the Future of Privacy Forum, a nonprofit focused on data protection and AI governance, said the different regulatory approaches by California and New York could be models other states adopt after legislatures reconvene next year.

New York's law, she said, underscores how quickly chatbot regulation is evolving, as states move beyond basic disclosures and crisis-response protocols to regulating the underlying design and operation of chatbots.
Still, several categories in New York's law are broadly worded or undefined, Gluck said.
That raises questions, she said, about “where ordinary conversational responsiveness ends and prohibited behavior begins,” and could complicate how it is enforced.
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: FDA scientists opposed the Trump administration's effort to ease peptides access
summary: Food and Drug Administration scientists did not support an effort by President Donald Trump's administration to loosen rules on unproven peptide drugs
story: Food and Drug Administration scientists did not support an effort by President Donald Trump's administration to loosen rules on unproven peptide drugs

WASHINGTON -- A plan to give Americans easier access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was opposed by most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff members, who had limited input in drafting the policy, according to six people familiar with the policy's development.
The document, which covers certain injectable peptides popular within the wellness industry, recently underwent regulatory review at the White House, typically the final step before publication.

The effort on peptides, driven by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s longstanding mission of keeping unproven health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development.

The policy would direct the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell certain widely used peptides — substances that would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they haven’t gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness, according to three of the people.
The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. An HHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.

The chemicals subject to the new policy haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. They include BPC-157 and TB-500, which are promoted to help heal injuries and build muscle. Both are considered doping substances by international sports authorities.
Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and recently described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.
The guidance document reviewed by the White House represents a step back from HHS' original plans, according to two of the people who discussed its development.

Initially, HHS officials wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.

But FDA officials warned that the agency's scientific staffers had major safety concerns and wouldn't support a regulation deeming them safe. So HHS officials moved to a different approach that would direct the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.

Ultimately, FDA staffers provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-regulated factories.
Kennedy has said repeatedly that U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans are turning to “gray market” products imported from China and other countries.

Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting Americans from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.

The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.

It’s extremely rare that HHS would take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials have said. However, federal law technically gives HHS authority over essentially all drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.

Many Americans using peptides today don’t deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections. Instead, they often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only,” since the FDA doesn’t regulate research chemicals.

In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.
At a meeting in July, FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.
The policy pending at the White House avoids a direct confrontation with FDA staffers because it only directs the FDA not to enforce certain rules.

HHS ultimately included several safety measures suggested by FDA staffers, according to two of the people. Besides sourcing ingredients from FDA-registered facilities, compounders will be directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the chemical identity of peptides.
Those measures are supported by some industry groups, including the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which recently met with White House officials about the proposal.

title: Fire briefly triggers emergency at South Carolina lab on former nuclear weapons site
summary: A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is on a site that once made key parts for nuclear bombs has triggered an emergency response that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area
story: A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is on a site that once made key parts for nuclear bombs has triggered an emergency response that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area

A fire at a national lab in South Carolina that is in a complex where key parts for nuclear bombs were once made triggered an emergency declaration Wednesday that shut down incoming traffic and restricted air and rail service in the area.

The fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory on the U.S. Department of Energy’s Savannah River Site was extinguished by Wednesday night and the site returned to normal operations. No detectable levels of contamination were found, according to a Savannah River Site statement.

The Savannah River Site is a massive complex where the federal government once produced materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily tritium and plutonium-239. The lab is in its northwest corner, near the edge of the site.

The site was opened in the early 1950s as the Cold War was heating up. Today it is used for environmental stewardship and cleanup, along with nuclear waste management and disposition of nuclear materials, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

The lab currently does experiments with nuclear materials and also does processing work with radioactive material, including operating a facility for radioisotope recovery from used nuclear fuel, said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
Lyman said it is reassuring that officials said there has been no off-site contamination, noting that there is a buffer zone between most of the facilities and the public areas.

But if you have a fire where there is radioactive material, “you need to take extreme precautions because of the potential dispersal of that material and the potential for contamination, potential for the public to be exposed,” he said.

The emergency declaration put out Wednesday is the second-highest of three categories of emergencies at the site and indicates “something more serious has occurred,” according to the site’s community preparedness information. The emergency declaration ended Wednesday night after the fire was extinguished.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
summary: DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery
story: DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery
DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart to supercharge its grocery delivery business in what would be a big consolidation in grocery delivery.

DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

title: Google misses revenue expectations, Alphabet stock sinks in early after-hours trading
summary: Alphabet Inc., Google's parent company, reported strong revenue growth in its third quarter, but it fell short of Wall Street expectations
story: Alphabet Inc., Google's parent company, reported strong revenue growth in its third quarter, but it fell short of Wall Street expectations

Google parent company Alphabet Inc. came up short of Wall Street expectations despite strong revenue growth in its third-quarter results, which sent its stock falling in after-hours trading Wednesday.
The Mountain View, California-based company said its net income was $26.17 billion in the July-September period. That’s down from $34.98 billion in the same period a year earlier.

Revenue grew 25% from the same period last year to $127.58 billion, but that was shy of analysts' expectations. Analysts, on average, were expecting revenue of $127.97 billion, according to a poll by FactSet.

The company earned $2.12 per share. Results were impacted by an $8.7 billion loss on equity investments in the quarter. It was not immediately clear if the reported earnings per share are comparable to the analyst estimates, which were around $3.01 per share.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, said in a statement that the quarter was strong and that the company is “now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate. Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business,” he said, pointing to the 25% revenue growth year-over-year.
Pichai also said the Gemini app, its artificial intelligence assistant, has reached one billion users, which makes it the fastest-growing product in Google’s history.
Alphabet’s shares fell about 9% to $295.20 within an hour after the market closed.

title: To make AI morally good, tech companies turn to religion. Some say it's not so simple
summary: Some are asking how to teach a chatbot right from wrong.
story: Some are asking how to teach a chatbot right from wrong.
LOS ANGELES -- As tech companies race to build the most powerful artificial intelligence, some are also asking how to teach a chatbot right from wrong. Their answer? Religion.

“These are not questions a lab can answer,” Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah said earlier this year at the Vatican’s presentation of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on AI. “They are questions traditions like yours have carried for millennia.”

Amid this much-discussed turn to faith, there has been little public scrutiny surrounding what exactly these technology companies think religion is — and, perhaps more important, what they hope to get out of it.

As executives sound the alarm about AI's destructive potential and debate the need to develop morally good models, they are increasingly seeking input from philosophers and faith leaders. The executives' philosophy goes something like this: that religion can help inform AI to be morally good in an environment where fears about it — founded and unfounded — are hopscotching across the culture.

Because these companies are not bound to a particular religion, the goal is often quite broad — an aggregate of moral ideas that can inform their models. “What I think ChatGPT should do is reflect that weighted average, or whatever, of humanity’s moral view,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last year.

But experts and adherents alike warn that this idea fails to reckon with how different traditions and worldviews can often contradict one another. In short, they say, it's not exactly how religion works.

For decades, scholars have pushed back against a widespread view of religion as a set of rules or principles that can be divorced from the “messy, practical, ad hoc” ways adherents live, argues Webb Keane, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan.

The idea that religion can be separated from things like culture and politics remains entrenched, even though it suffuses both in many ways. Some worry that AI companies, as they ask various faith leaders to answer ethical questions, will further perpetuate a theory of religion that fails to recognize the importance of doctrine, ritual and relationships.

Here's the issue, Keane argues: If you assume that religion overall can offer a distinct set of extractable moral principles, using it to train AI risks prioritizing certain traditions and distorting others — particularly when it comes to faiths that do not see themselves primarily as a system of ethics.

“There’s a very conventional way of thinking of religion as a rule book,” he said. “It is certainly very tied to scriptural religion, and the scriptural religions at the end of the day really turn out to be the Abrahamic religions.”

That’s not to say these meetings have lacked diverse representation. Nor does it suggest that their engagement with religion hasn’t been thoughtful from the perspective of those in attendance, like Meghan Sullivan, a philosopher of religion who leads an initiative on ethics and AI at the University of Notre Dame.

Though it doesn't enumerate the traditions it has consulted, Anthropic said in a May blog post that they’d met with “scholars, clergy, philosophers and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural groups” — a pool they hope to broaden in the future.

Earlier this year, Sullivan went to Anthropic for one of their meetings, which included Christians from different denominations. In contrast to conversations she’d had with other tech companies, she was impressed by the rigorous engagement with religion at Anthropic, which is widely seen as the AI company taking ethics and safety most seriously.

“The culture inside the company is similar to that on a good college campus in the sense that you’ve got a collection of very intellectually curious people,” she said. “These meetings are pretty nerdy — I don’t know if that’s the best way to put it — in a good way.”

Their meeting was split into two parts. First, the company explained their models “in layman’s terms” to those in attendance. Next, the faith leaders responded with feedback and discussions, Sullivan said. “Every kind of moral question that this technology raises — everything from, ‘Do humans have souls?’ to ‘Should third graders be able to access a chatbot for literacy education?’”
Representatives from Meta, Google and Amazon have also met with the Vatican, while Microsoft has been vigorous about its religious outreach.

Religion is generally considered both ancient and universal. And while experts like the late influential scholar of Jonathan Z. Smith concede that is true in some ways, they say it's also not the full picture.

“Man has had his entire history in which to imagine deities and modes of interaction with them. But man, more precisely Western man, has had only the last few centuries in which to imagine religion,” Smith wrote in 1982.

Many scholars of religion today share Smith's view of their field. They call into question the idea that religions are a set of distinct, comparable systems, saying it's a modern notion that can be traced to as late as the 19th century.

Buddhism and Hinduism, for example, were not recognized as clearly bounded traditions by the people who practiced them prior to the arrival of European scholars, says Tomoko Masuzawa, a religious studies scholar who wrote “The Invention of World Religions.” Says Mazuzawa: “All these categories were not native."
Western academics solidified those categories for years, only beginning to seriously reexamine them in the latter half of the 20th century.

Those entrenched ideas about religion — that it is easily comparable across cultures — help explain why Silicon Valley might not feel the need to define its own understanding of it. In an effort to represent various viewpoints, religion is often an obvious way to showcase diversity of thought.
“Somehow, religion becomes a way of kind of mapping out the world," Masuzawa said. “It’s as if the whole world has kind of bought into it.”
Some people want companies to further define terms and intentions to better understand what exactly they hope to gain from religion.

"This work isn’t about aligning our models with any one tradition’s worldview. We want Claude to draw from a full range of viewpoints — religious, secular, political — with equal depth and rigor,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “What we’re after in these conversations is careful, accumulated thinking on how good character actually forms.”
Large language models work by repeatedly guessing the next word in a sentence after having “learned” the patterns of a huge trove of human-written works, including religious texts.

Paolo Carozza, a member of the independent Meta Oversight Board and a legal expert who studies Catholic social thought and technology, worries that in the quest for accumulation, there is potential for a given tradition's defining characteristics to be lost — in effect, homogenized into something that pulls toward the middle or even favors Western religions.

“Any living, sophisticated tradition over time is capable of interacting with others outside of it and absorbing some new knowledge and growing. But it does so in this organic way," he said. “What AI, I think, often does and potentially does, is not in an organic way, but in a way that just throws it all together, mixes it all up, and therefore makes sense of none of it.”

title: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
summary: Anthropic expands its support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares publicly for the first time
story: Anthropic expands its support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares publicly for the first time

Anthropic expanded its support for the nonprofit sector Monday, even as the artificial intelligence company filed to sell shares to the public for the first time. The maker of the AI assistant Claude said the moves are all part of its broader strategy for “compounding good.”

Anthropic launched a new Claude for Nonprofits plugin created with 30 nonprofits to be more responsive to their specific needs. It will also broaden its Claude Corps program that embeds fellows with nonprofits to help them better utilize AI by also making consultants available to help organizations with smaller, shorter-term projects.

“This work is so core to who we are as a public benefit corporation,” Elizabeth Kelly, Anthropic’s head of beneficial deployments, told The Associated Press. “We were founded to ensure that we’re both developing AI safely and responsibly and that we’re deploying it in a way that really benefits everyone, including those who are too often left behind.”

Earlier this month, Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund that could be used for large scale donations to nonprofits or directly distributed to groups of people adversely impacted by AI. The fund still needs to be approved by shareholders once Anthropic completes its IPO, which could come as early as November.

Critics say AI companies are using donations and nonprofit pledges as an attempt to generate goodwill with the public at a time when so many are worried about the potential dangers of the technology and its impact on jobs.

However, Anthropic says that as a public benefit corporation, it balances its commercial interests with the interests of the public good. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei told The Associated Press in a May interview that the company works to make that balance clear. “I think there’s something really valuable about that as a construct just to help investors and employees and outside people understand what our intentions are and hold us accountable to them,” she said.
Other public benefit corporations include eyeglass maker Warby Parker, insurance company Lemonade, and Amalgamated Bank.

Bella DeVaan, director of the Charity Reform Initiative at the Institute for Policy Studies, said that public benefit corporations can be meaningful, but the federal government doesn’t currently properly regulate corporations. Without tax reform and a change in what she calls “the public permissiveness toward billionaire power in America,” DeVaan said there is no guarantee that even public benefit corporations will act in the public interest.

“Their wealth belongs to the public in the first place -- it’s created by the country and there’s a sort of social wage owed to people who use their products,” she said. “I hope that when people use the ethos of Silicon Valley that gave birth to these companies that have grand designs of changing the world that they’ll also think about how philanthropy could actually achieve charitable aims.”

Kelly said Anthropic’s work with the nonprofit sector is part of the company’s mission. The bulk of the 25,000 nonprofits currently using Claude for Nonprofits have less than 10 people on staff, so its impact on the organizations is often great. She points to Allies Against Slavery, the Texas-based nonprofit fighting human trafficking, as an example of what is possible, after its only government affairs staffer used Claude to analyze more than 750 state-level anti-trafficking policies and turned them into recommendations for advocates.
“This is basically compounding good,” she said. “That’s the kind of work that we’re so excited to support here at Anthropic.”

Montgomery County Food Bank President and CEO Scott Burns said his organization’s use of Claude has already generated significant savings that allow it to provide food to more people in his Texas county north of Houston.

“Costs have gone up for fuel,” Burns said. “Costs have gone up in every area – for proteins, in particular… I still want to be able to do more without adding a bunch of additional resources and (Claude) will enable me to do that.”

The Montgomery County Food Bank is one of the 30 nonprofits that has been working with Anthropic to better customize Claude for its specific needs. Burns said his team has already used it to optimize scheduling for food pickup and delivery and keeping better contact with donors.

He is looking forward to welcoming two Claude Corps fellows into the organization soon to tackle its outdated inventory system and the scheduling of its volunteers. Burns said he is also hoping to share his findings with other food banks.
“Nonprofits – we’re kind of an open book,” he said. “Why would I not share? It’s only going to help get more people fed, right?”
Taproot Foundation CEO Cat Ward said her nonprofit is excited about working with Anthropic to provide pro bono expertise to nonprofits for specific projects.
“Nonprofits are as lean as they come,” Ward said. “They’ve got the ambition. They’ve got the vision. This is about empowering them with tools that’ll help them go further faster.”

title: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
summary: With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings without alienating either and risking losing out
story: With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings without alienating either and risking losing out
HONG KONG -- With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.

As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the two AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the U.S.-led Pax Silica and the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization.
That could put many countries in a dilemma: Do they go with the U.S.’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?
Kazakhstan, a Central Asia nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.

Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the U.S. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China's initiative to shape the global AI agenda.

Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.

“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.
“We don’t want this binary choice,” Masalimova said.
Kazakhstan is benefiting from both U.S. and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” she said,
It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the U.S.
Earlier this year, Kazakhstan's government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.

Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.
Both China and the U.S. are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.

President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” U.S. officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.
Beijing has rejected those claims and says the U.S. is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.
Washington has signaled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.

“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the U.S. State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.

For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World AI Cooperation Organization. “As both major countries in AI, China and the United States should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement. “AI should not be owned by major countries.”

The two AI powers have different messaging largely because Beijing needs to court third countries in its bid to build an alternative coalition, whereas Washington already has a powerful network of allies, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.
That lends power to what he described as “swing countries.”

Like Kazakhstan, Indonesia has resources vital for AI and other technologies, such as nickel and copper. It's also seeking to make the most of both AI powers, having joined China's World AI Cooperation Organization.

Indonesia wants to benefit from both, Mari Pangestu, Indonesian National Economic Council's vice chair, told reporters at a University of Hong Kong Business School event. “We should be able to be part of both, put it that way. And choose the best system.”

U.S. AI firms are bringing investments to other countries like Singapore, where Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office. The city-state says it is also considering joining China’s AI organization.

In Saudi Arabia, the AI startup Humain unveiled in September a platform built on an open model by a Chinese AI company. The kingdom also has a deal with Nvidia to expand AI computing with its advanced chips.

France, one of the most ambitious AI developers aside from the U.S. and China, is attempting to go its own way with its startup Mistral, whose new model released this month outperforms some advanced Chinese models.

Japan is closely aligned with the U.S. on strategic and security issues, including advanced semiconductors, trusted AI and standards. But it will not reject the more affordable Chinese AI models for “lower-risk applications,” said Takahiro Tsuchiya, a professor at Kyoto's University of Foreign Studies.

For countries like the U.K. and Germany which have substantial economic and military capacity but no self-developed powerful frontier AI models of their own, aligning with the U.S. may be vital for their access to data centers and chip deals with U.S. companies, said Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Essentially, their access to advanced AI systems “depends on the whims of policymakers in Washington and Beijing,” they said, while those countries may have limited influence over AI’s future.

China, meanwhile, has been closing the technology gap with the U.S. when it comes to chipmaking and advanced AI capabilities, but it still trails top U.S. technological capabilities, at least for now.

Also, Beijing's open-source approach allows countries to be less reliant on the U.S., and China has been providing funding for developing countries to develop their own AI ecosystems, said Alberto Lemma, a research fellow at the think tank ODI Global.

To date, China has provided official sector grants and loans for project and activities that use or enable AI technologies in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, according to the AidData research lab at William & Mary, a public university in Virginia. Some top recipients include Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon, and Kenya. Public perceptions are also changing. Recent study results from Pew Research Center have shown that people in middle-income countries are becoming more positive and trusting of China when it comes to AI and the technology’s regulation.

All things considered, many countries “don’t want to pick a side ... because there are advantages and disadvantages to each technology stack,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Most countries may eventually lack a good option since they cannot compete on building AI frontier models, but “every country in the world in some way or another is thinking about AI sovereignty," he said. After all, “maybe no other country than the U.S. and China can really build these very large, powerful models.”
Tang reported from Washington.

title: Microsoft offers quarter of global workforce voluntary buyouts
summary: Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence
story: Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence
Microsoft has offered 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its global workforce, voluntary buyouts as the software giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence.

The company's voluntary exit offer was available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, the company's Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a blog post Monday.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman wrote. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
The company, which releases its quarterly financial results Wednesday, had approximately 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.
Shares of Microsoft Corp., based in Redmond, Washington, hit an all-time high this month. The stock rose about 1% on Monday.

In May, Microsoft planned to offer buyouts to about 8,750 people, or 7% of its U.S. workforce, according to two people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to speak about it publicly. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including a large number of workers at its Xbox video game business.

The gusher of investment in data centers — likely topping $700 billion this year — to power artificial intelligence has made memory chips, computer processors and other equipment, as well as electricity, more expensive. Economists expect it will continue to push up inflation at least through the end of this year.

Microsoft has been ramping up its AI capabilities for several years. In 2024 the company revealed a new class of AI-imbued personal computers that centered on fusing its AI assistant, called Copilot, into the Windows operating system for PCs, where Microsoft already has the eyes of millions of consumers.

And in October 2025 Microsoft introduced a new artificial intelligence character called Mico, a floating cartoon face shaped like a blob or flame that embodies the software giant’s Copilot virtual assistant.

title: Midterm elections live updates: Judge orders DOJ to halt threats to election workers
summary: The judge granted a temporary restraining order through Nov. 16
story: The judge granted a temporary restraining order through Nov. 16
The high-stakes midterm elections are just days away, and candidates are making their final pitches to voters.

There are several key House and Senate races that could determine the balance of power in Congress as well as significant races for governor around the country. The elections could ultimately determine how effective President Donald Trump's agenda is in the back half of his second term.

Judge orders DOJ to halt threats to election workers

A federal judge on Friday temporarily blocked the Justice Department from threatening state and local election officials, dealing yet another legal setback to the Trump administration as it endeavors to prevent vote-counters in California and elsewhere from setting aside thousands of ballots it claims belong to noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued the ruling as part of a lawsuit filed late Thursday by a coalition of civil rights groups and labor unions, including one that represents election workers in California.

The coalition’s attorneys requested a temporary restraining order halting the Trump administration’s threats to jail election officials who count ballots belonging to voters whom the Justice Department claims might be noncitizens.
On Friday, the judge granted the coalition’s request, issuing a temporary restraining order through Nov. 16.

The Justice Department "shall not threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by [DOJ] to be ineligible to vote,” she wrote in her eight-page order.
Thompson also ordered the Justice Department to inform the court of any pending grand jury subpoenas or search warrant applications.

This week, the Department of Justice issued grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in California as part of its criminal investigation into the state's voter rolls, multiple sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.
ABC News has reached out to the DOJ for comment on the judge's order.
-ABC News' Lucien Bruggeman
Trump says he was asked to resume in-person rallies
President Trump has confirmed he is going to conduct in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa this weekend ahead of the critical midterm elections, saying he wants to "make sure we win" in those states.
Asked about the recent schedule changes around his rallies ahead of Election Day, Trump said that he was pivoting back to in-person events because he was told "it would be better than a tele-rally."

"So I wanted to see if I could do tele-rallies because I'm very successful," Trump said. "You know, we're batting unbelievable at tele-rallies." But Trump said that he "got a call from Iowa," and from his "friends" asking him to revert to in-person rallies.
-ABC News' Isabella Murray and Nicholas Kerr
Federal appeals court rejects DOJ appeal in California ballots case

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an appeal Friday from the Trump administration seeking an emergency order for California to set aside 20,000 ballots belonging to individuals the Justice Department claims belong to "likely" noncitizens.

In a 2-1 ruling, Circuit Judges Mark Bennett, a President Donald Trump appointee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a President Joe Biden appointee, said the Justice Department failed to meet its burden that an emergency injunction was warranted and not counter to the Constitution's Elections Clause, which mandates states take the lead in administering their elections.
"If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts," the majority judges wrote.

Another Trump appointee on the court, Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, dissented from the decision describing the Trump administration's demands to set aside the ballots as "reasonable" given the potential risk of non-citizens casting ballots.
-ABC News' Alexander Mallin

title: Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage
summary: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
story: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
NEW YORK -- Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage, according to court records.
The case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in Brooklyn, New York, and is listed as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant.
Attorneys for Qualley and Antonoff did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The couple separated in July.

Qualley, 32, is an actor known for films including “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer who has worked with artists including Taylor Swift, Lana Del Rey and Sabrina Carpenter. He is also a member of the band Bleachers.
The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023.

title: Peltola denies knowing of 'any other candidate' on ballot besides herself, incumbent
summary: The DOJ is acting to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska said.
story: The DOJ is acting to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe.

Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied that she knew about an effort to recruit a candidate to be on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"I just want to clear the air. I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said during a rally in Juneau, Alaska, on Thursday, according to an Associated Press video.
ABC News has asked the Peltola campaign to clarify whether she is denying knowledge of the reported recruitment effort to find a spoiler candidate.
Peltola later added, "I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan."

Peltola's comments, just days before the high-stakes midterm elections, come after a New York Times report Wednesday that her campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee played a role in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan -- a Republican who almost has the same name as incumbent Sen. Sullivan -- as part of an effort to sow confusion and ultimately benefit Peltola's campaign.
At a separate campaign event on Thursday, Peltola called the New York Times' report "just another distraction."
"It's another diversion. Every day, it's some new, you know, 'look over here' moment,” Peltola said in a social media video verified by ABC News.

Meanwhile, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska held a press conference Friday afternoon to announce the Justice Department's efforts to "intensely and swiftly" escalate its probe into the Alaska Senate race following that New York Times report.

In the press conference, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman provided little in the way of details about what actions the department was specifically taking -- citing sensitivities surrounding ongoing criminal investigations.
"I do want to say that what we've learned recently has been deeply troubling," Heyman said. "We are acting on it intensely and swiftly."

Heyman said the new information reported on by the Times has resulted in a "significant surge" of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and other law enforcement "around the country" are also taking "investigative steps" regarding information from the article. Heyman said the office has already received "a number of new pieces of information" in just the last 24 hours that investigators are following up on.
Asked during the press conference what specific crime was being investigated, Heyman conceded the department hasn't made a determination one way or another.

"We investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories," he said. "So I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse. I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

Earlier this week, the Justice Department began issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal probe of Democrats' alleged efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. The Trump administration filed a separate civil lawsuit last week seeking an injunction against the state certifying the results of its election in the event Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses, which a federal judge is expected to rule on in the coming days.

Peltola’s campaign earlier this week told ABC News that it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." Former Peltola staffer Elisa Rios told the Times about the reported recruitment effort, saying Peltola wasn't directly involved but that she was "definitely aware."
ABC News reached out to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign for comment on the New York Times' report earlier this week, but has not heard back.

Alaska courts evaluated the dispute over Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy and found nothing illegal about his bid to be on the ballot -- even if it was not entirely in "good faith" or an attempt to "confuse and mislead" as the Trump administration and Republicans contend.

On Friday morning, President Donald Trump, who has claimed Pelota has committed "election fraud," said Alaskans would need to have a "190 IQ" to understand the ballot with two Dan Sullivans, despite the ballot's clear distinctions between the two candidates' names and other distinctive marks like party affiliation and incumbency.

On the general election ballot, Sen. Sullivan is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, a registered Republican, and it is noted that he is the incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. with no party affiliation.

"You need about 190 IQ to figure out the ballot. They put a ballot down where they're talking about incumbent Republican and the other one. Most people don't know in Alaska, in a lot of other states too, what does incumbent mean? They don't know what incumbent means," Trump said when he called into Kansas City's KMCO "Mundo in the Morning."
Peltola won the primary by a larger margin than adding Dan J. Sullivan in could have made up for: 48% to 2%, respectively; Sen. Sullivan earned 43% of the vote in the primary.

GOP Sen. Sullivan on Thursday criticized Democrats' alleged efforts to recruit another Dan Sullivan in the Senate race. Sen. Sullivan, on Fox News, claimed Peltola's campaign ran a "secret operation to put a fake Dan Sullivan on the ballot with the primary purpose, the only purpose, to trick Alaskans."

title: These House races could determine which party is in control in the next Congress
summary: All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3.
story: There are 16 races that ABC News rates as Tossup going into Election Day.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are on the ballot when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3. But spread across the political map, there are 16 races that ABC News rates as tossup in which the outcomes are expected to come down to the wire and will be crucial to determining the balance of power in the House for the 120th Congress.
Democrats must net at least a three-seat gain to take control.
Here are the races that ABC News rates as Tossup:
Alabama 2: Incumbent Democrat Shomari Figures vs. Republican Rhett Marques

In this newly drawn district, Figures faces Marques, a state representative, in a competitive race. The district was redrawn after the Supreme Court allowed Alabama to reinstate a 2023 congressional map that a federal court had previously blocked. Figures is counting on strong turnout among Black voters, who make up about 40% of the district’s voting-age population. President Donald Trump rallied in Mobile on Oct. 2 and urged voters to back Marques. Trump would have carried the new district by 14 points in 2024.
Colorado 5: Incumbent Republican Jeff Crank vs. Democrat Jessica Killin

Crank is locked in a tight race against Killin, an Army veteran and former chief of staff for then-second gentleman Doug Emhoff. The district, which includes Colorado Springs and nearly all of El Paso County, has leaned more left over the past three presidential cycles. However, Trump won this military-heavy district by about 9 points in 2024. The Iran war is a key issue in this race. Crank supports the war but believes Trump should have sought congressional approval.
Florida 14: Incumbent Democrat Kathy Castor vs. Republican Mike Beltran

Castor, a 10-term incumbent, is facing off against Trump-endorsed former trial lawyer Beltran. The seat became more competitive after Florida’s legislature redrew this district, putting Castor on the defensive.
Florida 22: Open -- Democrat Pia Dandiya vs. Republican Casey Askar

The battle for Florida’s newly drawn district spanning parts of Palm Beach and Broward counties and the city of Naples puts two political newcomers in the ring: Marine Corps veteran Askar against former teacher and U.S. Education Department official Dandiya.
Iowa 2: Open -- Democrat Lindsey James vs. Republican Joe Mitchell

As incumbent congresswoman Ashley Hinson runs for Senate, this historically red House seat in the Hawkeye State is now up for grabs. James, a state representative and chaplain, is running against Mitchell, a 29-year-old lobbyist and former state representative who worked on Trump’s transition team. Trump won this district by 10 points in 2024, but the economic impacts from the Iran war and tariffs on this agriculture-heavy district have made this race competitive.
Kentucky 6: Open -- Democrat Zach Dembo vs. Republican Ralph Alvarado

GOP Rep. Andy Barr’s bid to fill Mitch McConnell’s long-held Senate seat leaves his Kentucky House seat open. Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy JAG officer, faces Alvarado, a physician and former state senator. This district used to be more competitive, but redistricting in 2022 has made it friendlier to Republicans in recent years – though Barr was a consistent Democratic target since he was elected in 2012.
Michigan 4: Incumbent Republican Bill Huizenga vs. Democrat Sean McCann

Huizenga, who has served in Congress since 2011, is being challenged by McCann, a state senator. Huizenga does have incumbency advantage and outperformed Trump substantively in 2024, but his race appears to be tightening as many pollsters anticipate a sour political environment for the president’s party.
Michigan 7: Incumbent Republican Tom Barrett vs. Democrat William Lawrence

First-term congressman and former Army helicopter pilot Barrett, who has repeatedly bucked Trump by voting to limit his war powers in Iran, hopes to keep his seat and defeat progressive candidate Lawrence, a co-founder of the progressive Sunrise Movement. Despite the split, Trump has campaigned in favor of Barrett’s reelection in the competitive swing district, where Democrat Elissa Slotkin beat a Republican in 2018 to flip this seat before she ultimately won a bid for Senate in 2024.
Michigan 10: Open -- Democrat Christina Hines vs. Republican Mike Bouchard

As Rep. John James runs to be Michigan’s next governor, his open seat in Detroit's northern suburbs is up for grabs. The battle is between Hines, a former prosecutor, and Bouchard, an Army veteran. Trump carried this district by more than six points in 2024.
Montana 1: Open -- Democrat Sam Forstag vs. Republican Aaron Flint

Rep. Ryan Zinke’s retirement has left this Montana seat open with no incumbency advantage for Republicans. Flint, an Army veteran and conservative radio show host, is running against Forstag, a union leader and wildland firefighter smokejumper. Trump won this district covering western Montana by nearly 12 points in 2024.
New York 17: Incumbent Republican Mike Lawler vs. Democrat Cait Conley

Lawler is one of two Republicans running for reelection in Kamala Harris-won districts this cycle -- six others opted against another term in the House. Lawler has kept this seat in a blue state since 2022, outperforming Trump in 2024 by 2.8%. Lawler, who secured State and Local Tax (SALT) deductions during the Trump tax bill negotiations, is running against Conley, an Army combat veteran.
Ohio 7: Incumbent Republican Max Miller vs. Democrat Brian Poindexter

Miller’s reelection bid has been hampered by allegations of domestic assault against his ex-wife Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller, a former Trump aide, has flatly denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with any crimes and refused to drop out of the race despite widespread calls from Republicans. Trump stopped short of calling on Miller to withdraw last summer, calling the situation "sad.” He’s being challenged by Poindexter, a union organizer and ironworker.
Pennsylvania 1: Incumbent Republican Brian Fitzpatrick vs. Democrat Bob Harvie

Five-term incumbent Fitzpatrick, a former FBI agent, is the other Republican running for re-election in a district that Harris won in 2024. Fitzpatrick has repeatedly broken with the president on policy issues and was one of two House Republicans who voted against his mega tax and policy bill. He has established himself as a moderate in the House, helping boost his electoral performance in the competitive district, which includes Bucks County and Montgomery County. Harvie, has served as a Bucks County commissioner since 2020.
Texas 15: Democrat Bobby Pulido vs. incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz

De La Cruz, who was first elected in 2022, is seeking to keep her seat in a South Texas district that is nearly 80% Latino. Redistricting expanded the 15th into Hidalgo County and shifted some of her GOP voters into neighboring districts. Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, is challenging De La Cruz in a race that could test Trump’s standing with Latino voters.
Texas 35: Open -- Democrat Johnny Garcia vs. Republican Carlos De La Cruz

This East San Antonio seat, previously held by Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, is open after the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus changed districts because of redistricting initiated by the Republican-controlled legislature. Garcia, a deputy sheriff, hopes to keep the district blue and is running against Trump-endorsed De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran and brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz.
Virginia 1: Incumbent Republican Rob Wittman vs. Democrat Shannon Taylor

In North Virginia and the Middle Peninsula, 10-term Republican Wittman is battling to keep his seat against Taylor, Henrico County’s top prosecutor. It is one of a few districts across the country where Kamala Harris in 2024 outperformed Joe Biden in 2020, suggesting the district is trending left.

title: Voters weigh citizenship amendments as Trump fans fears of noncitizen election fraud
summary: Civil rights groups warn millions of Americans could get sidelined.
story: Civil rights groups warn millions of Americans could get sidelined.
Voters in six states on Nov. 3 will decide whether to approve ballot measures that would amend their state constitutions or state law to make U.S. citizenship a requirement for voting.
The closely watched popular referenda reflect a push by President Donald Trump to crackdown on noncitizen voting based on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud.
Voting-rights advocates warn they also raise the potential of sidelining millions of eligible American voters.

"Rather than strengthening democracy, [the amendments are] a political maneuver designed to justify future rollbacks of voting rights," said Rashane Hamby with the ACLU of Kansas in testimony last year.
Federal and state laws already prohibit noncitizens from voting in any federal or statewide election, but advocates for the constitutional amendments say even more protection is needed.

"Law can change, as we know,” said West Virginia state Sen. Patricia Rucker, a Republican, at a press conference last month. "This proposed amendment would ensure that no future legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill."

No state constitution currently includes a citizenship requirement for voting. Five states -- Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia -- have amendments on the ballot. An Alaska initiative would create a new state law.
Of particular concern to some supporters: major cities in three states plus the District of Columbia that do allow some noncitizens to lawfully participate in local elections.
"There's nothing that magically stops those bad ideas at that state's borders," said Arkansas state Rep. David Ray in a news conference last month.

Many civil rights groups and nonpartisan voter advocates fear the measures -- and accompanying regulations requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote -- could disenfranchise tens of millions of Americans.
Jemmie Lolita Pepper of Indiana, a former public-school educator who was born on U.S. soil but spent decades unable to prove it, says she empathizes with both sides of the debate.

"I understand the desire to require proof so there won't be voter fraud or anything like that. I truly support that: no voter fraud,” said Pepper, 63, in an interview. "But for those of us who had to live years of not having [any documentation], you couldn’t prove it. I couldn't."

With pro bono legal help, Pepper recently untangled a series of clerical errors in state records -- including a misspelling of her first name and faulty substitution of her last name -- that had prevented her from obtaining an official government ID and, in turn, casting a ballot. She now has one.
"They had my name listed as the boys' spelling, J-I-M-M-I-E," Pepper recalled of her legal odyssey. "I said, 'Well that’s still me. That's still me.'"

An estimated 21.3 million Americans -- or 9% of all eligible voters -- are unable to readily present documentation proving they are citizens because of misplaced or inaccessible records, financial hardship putting replacement fees out of reach, name changes from divorce or remarriage, and clerical errors in state databases, according to a 2025 study by the University of Maryland.
Only 48% of Americans have a valid passport as of 2023, according to the State Department.
Some voting-rights advocates say a proof-of-citizenship requirement would hit elderly, disabled and rural voters particularly hard.

"I’ve been through SCUD missiles, riots, sniper fire. To be unable to keep it together navigating all these processes makes me ashamed to say, but it would be really difficult," said Symmone Ford of Michigan, a 56-year-old Gulf War veteran with severe PTSD who has difficulty leaving her home.

"I can’t afford the money for a lawyer to change my name. I barely have enough to pay my bills," said Ford, whose last name does not currently match her birth certificate because of several marriages and divorces.

Additional paperwork requirements for voter registration could effectively shut down online access, some experts said. Even when people do have proper documentation, many may lack access to copiers, notaries and scanners to submit electronically.

Nine states currently have laws requiring state officials to verify a voter's citizenship status either by looking at documentary proof at time of registration, reviewing voter registration history, or cross-checking with other government databases, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Federal law requires voters in all states to attest with a signature -- under threat of imprisonment -- that they are, in fact, U.S. citizens when they sign up for a ballot.
Still, 83% of Americans, according to Gallup, say people registering to vote for the first time should have to provide documentation to show that they are eligible citizens.

Efforts by Trump and his Republican allies to institute a nationwide proof-of-citizenship standard stalled in Congress earlier this year and later got blocked by federal courts when he attempted to impose it by executive order.
An online tracker of major public claims of noncitizen voting compiled by the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research shows cases of noncitizen voting are extremely rare.

In Michigan, for example, the state attorney general identified 38 credible cases of noncitizen voting in the 2024 general election out of roughly 5.7 million votes cast. That's 0.0000066% of total votes cast.
Six of the Michigan cases have resulted in criminal charges, while 10 were closed without charges and 22 are still under review, according to state officials.

Eighteen states did not publicly disclose finding or removing any noncitizen from a voter registration list in the 2024 election, and no state uncovered any coordinated effort to get noncitizens to vote, according to CEIR records.

President Trump and the Department of Justice continue to push unsubstantiated claims of widespread noncitizen voting as the basis for tighter voter registration rules and ballot segregation in several states, including California and Washington.

The U.S. Supreme Court has previously struck down efforts to add a proof-of-citizenship requirement to federal voter registration forms. Later this year, in a major case from Arizona, the justices will decide whether states can mandate proof-of-citizenship on state forms and for voting in state races.

title: Vote Republican, or else: How Trump is dangling government help on the campaign trail
summary: President Donald Trump is signaling to states that his administration may be far less likely to help if their voters put Democrats in power on Election Day
story: President Donald Trump is signaling to states that his administration may be far less likely to help if their voters put Democrats in power on Election Day

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump says Georgia GOP Senate candidate Mike Collins can call him whenever he wants to ask for help for his state. But if Georgia reelects Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, Trump says it could be another story.

“There’s a big difference between that and Pee-wee Herman calling,” Trump said last week in Perry, Georgia, using his derisive nickname for Ossoff. The president acted out a hypothetical scenario at his rally where Ossoff called to ask for money for his state, with Trump responding, “I don’t give a damn what he wants.”

It’s been a recurring theme at Trump’s rallies this month: From North Carolina to Ohio to Kansas, the president has dangled the idea that his administration would be far less likely to help states where Democrats win in the upcoming midterm elections.

Trump has sandwiched the threats into rallies where he has announced goodies like new semiconductor investments, a submarine repair center and fewer limits on a certain type of diesel, underscoring to the audience the types of tangibles an all-Republican Washington could continue to deliver for voters should his party remain in power after November.

But the president’s utterances — part of a larger political strategy that’s anchored on making the midterms about himself and activating conservative voters — have also injected politics into processes that have traditionally remained apolitical, such as doling out disaster aid and providing benefits for veterans.

“It’s a losing strategy for the failed president to insult and threaten voters while he’s in town reminding them he made everything more expensive,” Ossoff told The Associated Press in response to Trump’s rally comments in Perry.

Asked for further elaboration on the pattern of remarks, the White House said Trump is committed to keeping a Republican majority in Congress so “he can continue to deliver on his winning, commonsense agenda.”

White House spokesman Davis Ingle cited Trump’s policies on taxes, prescription drugs, immigration and other policies and added, “Democrats have made it clear that they have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people.”
Yet some of Trump’s remarks have handed ammunition to Democratic candidates in key battleground races.

A sweeping 2022 veterans law signed by then-President Joe Biden allowed those facing health conditions linked to contaminated water at Camp Lejeune, a Marine Corps base in North Carolina, to file for compensation.

In Greenville, North Carolina, earlier this month, Trump announced that $1 billion in cash settlements had been delivered to veterans and their family members who had been affected by the Lejeune contamination, and that he would direct the Justice Department to settle all remaining legitimate claims expeditiously — “if we win the House and the Senate.”
“So, if we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said. “If we do win, you’re getting it.”

Questioned afterward at the White House, Trump said, “If we’re not there, then somebody else is going to have to settle” the Camp Lejeune claims and he “can’t speak for another administration,” although his own Justice Department is handling the claims.

It wasn’t the first time Trump had made that type of remark in North Carolina, where his handpicked Senate candidate, Michael Whatley, has struggled to gain traction against Democrat Roy Cooper, a well-known former governor.

During a September rally in Gastonia, Trump said North Carolina was still waiting on more Hurricane Helene recovery money and added, “Now, if Michael loses, I’m not sending it,” even though he immediately said he was kidding.

Cooper has described Trump’s Camp Lejeune threats as “insulting and frustrating” while his campaign has gone after Whatley for refusing to denounce them. (Whatley, asked in a local television interview about the president's comments, said caring for the affected veterans and families is a priority.)

The threat angered Jill Steen Dilgard, whose father and other relatives served at Camp Lejeune and were subsequently diagnosed with cancer and other health issues. She said in an interview with the AP that it was “totally unacceptable” for the president to condition care for those who had served in the U.S. military on the results of the midterms.

“It made me physically sick, and it infuriated me,” said Steen Dilgard, who helps advocate for other Camp Lejeune victims and their families. “You're playing politics and trying to bribe for a vote. So many hundreds of thousands have already lost their lives, and hundreds of thousands are suffering, and many have been given a death sentence.”

Trump has frequently announced state-specific perks at rallies, from protecting a steam-powered heat utility in Ohio to investing billions in Montana mortgages through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to pardoning truckers in Alaska who had pleaded guilty to violating federal environmental laws.
But sometimes, he takes it a step further.

During a trip to Kansas to shore up GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, Trump noted to the crowd that he had granted a waiver that would temporarily allow year-round sales of E15, an ethanol-blended gas that is usually restricted during the summer.

“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Trump said during a rally in Park City. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.”

Although there is legislation in Congress that would allow for permanent year-round sales of E15, it can also be done at an administration’s discretion through temporary waivers issued by the Environmental Protection Agency.
In response, Hamilton's campaign did not criticize Trump directly but said, “Kansans are tired of our broken politics that treats public service like it’s all about opposing teams."

“Roger Marshall has been in Congress for 10 years and never passed year-round E15,” said Tyson Brody, a spokesman for the campaign. "When Adam is senator, he will look forward to working with anyone — including President Trump — to finally deliver on this and other important priorities for Kansas.”
Other times, the president’s threats to not help Democratic-led states have seemed less about policy and more about personal relationships.

In Vandalia, Ohio, this month, Trump again was noting how Republican officeholders in the state were pushing him on disaster relief and added that “when you are president, you have a lot of power over states.”

If Democratic gubernatorial candidate “Amy Acton got in, I don’t know anything about her,” Trump continued. “She’s never gonna call me. I’m never probably gonna work the same way. You just can’t. It’s just human nature. But I’m not gonna help her probably.”
