title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Actor Walter Koenig (Sept. 14, 1936-Oct. 25, 2026) originated the character of Ensign Pavel Chekov, the Starship Enterprise's Russian navigator, during the second season of the TV series "Star Trek." After the original series ended in 1969, he continued playing the character, promoted to lieutenant, in seven theatrical features (concluding with 1994's "Star Trek: Generations"), and, as an admiral, in fan productions (including "Star Trek: New Voyages" and "Star Trek: Renegades").

Born of Russian Jewish immigrant parents, Koenig had several TV credits in the 1960s (including "Ben Casey," "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "Gidget," and Gene Roddenberry's "The Lieutenant") before auditioning to play Chekov in 1967. In a 2013 interview with the Television Academy Foundation, Koenig (who said he hadn't watched the first season of "Star Trek") said he was asked to read a very serious scene: "The ship is about to blow up," he said. "This is jeopardy, this is personal risk involved here, and I had to show some sense of command and that I was capable of being an officer at this moment. So, I read it with all of that in mind — the brows furled, the jaws clenched, the teeth tight, and the nostrils flared. And when I got done … they all kind of looked at their feet and said, 'Yeah, well, that's nice, Walt, but can you make it funny?'"

Chekhov would prove to be a lighter-hearted member of the Enterprise crew, speaking with a heavy Russian accent that underscored how 1960s political tensions didn't exist in the 23rd century. The insertion of the youthful Chekov was, Koenig said, inspired by the popularity of The Monkees. "They were looking for an actor or a personality that would appeal to the same demographic that Davy Jones did — kids 8 to 14 years old," he said. "And indeed, my mail was from people who are 8 to 14 years old: 'I think you're groovy,' 'I love your hair' (which was a wig by the way)." Koenig said he never got any hostile mail over the fact that he was a Russian on the Enterprise: "Because these were all kids; they didn't really know too much about the Cold War."

In 2005 Koenig described to the BBC the importance of the multi-cultural (and alien) crew of the Enterprise as they went boldly where no one had gone before: "We were stating tacitly that peoples of all races and creeds, nationalities, could not only co-exist but care for each other deeply, and in doing so we were heralding a future that was very optimistic, and one that I think appealed to the audience," he said. "We would like to believe that the future is not an Armageddon kind of situation, as has been so frequently depicted in film, but one where there's considerably harmony and a kind of one-world environment."

Koenig also wrote several "Star Trek"-themed books and an episode of the "Star Trek" animated series; the comic book series "Raver"; the graphic novel "Things to Come"; and scripts for TV series including "Land of the Lost," "Family" and "The Powers of Matthew Star." Other science fiction appearances were in "Moontrap" and "Babylon 5."

title: How punk rock and MTV inspired opera composer Missy Mazzoli
summary: "Lincoln in the Bardo," based on George Saunders' novel, is the first opera composed by a woman to premiere at the Metropolitan Opera. Missy Mazzoli talks about its creation, and the influence that punk rock and music videos had on her work.
story: On a recent Sunday night in Brooklyn, at a concert by the punk rock band Mannequin Pussy, we found the perhaps unlikely new face of the rarefied world of opera: 45-year-old classical composer Missy Mazzoli.

Asked what she loves about punk music, Mazzoli replied, "I love that it's extreme, that it wears its thoughts and emotions and politics on its sleeve, and that it is just this raw expression of human emotion."
Which sounds exactly like opera!

Mazzoli is taking on one of the biggest stages in the world, the Metropolitan Opera in New York, which is debuting her latest work, "Lincoln in the Bardo." With it, she becomes the first woman to have an opera premiered by the Met in its 143-year history.

Mazzoli's parents bought a piano at a flea market when she was seven. A few years later, she was writing her own music. But it wasn't just classical; she also played in punk bands – and inspiration came from everywhere. "MTV was there for me, when no one else was," she laughed. "And I would watch MTV for hours and hours every day. And so, I can look back to that and say like, 'Oh, my interest in opera makes a lot of sense, because I was watching Guns N' Roses or Sonic Youth, these videos that let you enter a whole different world.'"

"Lincon in the Bardo" is based on the novel by George Saunders, and tells the story of President Lincoln at a pivotal moment. "His 11-year-old son, Willie, died very unexpectedly," Mazzoli said, "and Lincoln was just consumed with grief, and would actually go to the graveyard and visit with his son's body in the days and weeks after his death."
I have no power here.And now I must accept it.My boy is gone!My boy is gone!Peaceful, resplendent, in a new form of being.Willie is dead.My dear little chap, good-bye. – From "Lincoln in the Bardo"

Mazzoli says the opera asks big questions that speak to our time, too. "This is a story that takes place at the height of the Civil War when America is at its most divided," she said. "And the idea of making a work set in a very divided America felt extremely relevant."

To prepare, Mazzoli spent time in actual cemeteries herself.  "For me, opera is the way to explore things that are difficult to talk about," she said. "Think about life and death. We can sing songs about it. But I think that we can sort of get at what the questions are. So, when someone is singing their heart out about love or betrayal or grief, I think words don't do those emotions justice, but singing and music really can."
True to form, "Lincoln in the Bardo" is an enormous production, with elaborate costumes, puppetry, special effects, and even a very large horse who makes a brief appearance at the end of the show.

Royce Vavrek has written the lyrics to Mazzoli's music in six operas. "We really bond because of our shared love of storytelling and theater," he said, "and so I am in charge of sort of the word drama and she is in charge of the musical drama, and together I think we just combust into something way bigger than the sum of our two parts."

Just this summer, they premiered another new work, "The Galloping Cure," which looks at the opioid epidemic. It's a personal topic for both. "I have two cousins who died," Mazzoli said, "one of an OxyContin overdose, and one of a heroin overdose after becoming addicted via Oxycontin. And Royce's father passed away and succumbed to his addiction."

With two major operatic premieres, and an upcoming piano concerto commissioned by the New York Philharmonic, Missy Mazzoli is having a moment. "I joke with my partner, everything in my life is happening in this three-week span," she said. "But I'm just really trying to ride the wave and enjoy it."

Mazzoli says, as a young composer, there were unequal expectations in the industry: "With male creators, they're looking for potential. They're like, 'Oh, he has great potential to do this.' But when it come to hiring a woman, they're like, 'Oh, but she hasn't written an opera yet.' And it's like, But she has the potential."

So, ten years ago, Mazzoli co-founded a non-profit organization called Luna Lab, to mentor and provide performance opportunities to teen composers. "I want to inspire future generations to pursue music as a career and to continue to express themselves in this medium," she said.

While Monday's premiere marked Mazzoli's Met debut, it's also a return of sorts. She first came to the Met when she was 18. The only seat she could afford was in the last row of the highest section: "And it was this seat, right here, and I sat here, and it changed my life!"

title: "The Mosquito Bowl" and the human cost of war
summary: Director Peter Berg discusses his new film, the true story of All-American football stars who volunteered for the Marines and fought in the Battle of Okinawa, the last and costliest World War II battle in the Pacific.
story: Okinawa proved to be the last and costliest battle of World War II in the Pacific – and it's a name director Peter Berg wants us all to remember. His new movie, "The Mosquito Bowl," captures that battle. "It is a film that I hope asks us all to look at what we ask of our young men and women," he said.

"The Mosquito Bowl" is based on the book by Buzz Bissinger, who also wrote "Friday Night Lights," which became Berg's breakout movie. But don't let the title fool you – it's not a movie about a football game. "No, it's not; it's a movie about the cost of war, the human cost of war," said Berg.

The human cost of war as told through the true story of four All-American football players who volunteered for the Marines after Pearl Harbor, and reported to boot camp at Parris Island, South Carolina, which is where we interviewed Berg. "They came down here and they joined the Marine Corps, thinking, Hey, we'll go win this thing. We'll go whup some butt and win this thing, like we win our football games," Berg said. "Then they come across an enemy, the Japanese, who are instructed by their emperor, who they believe is a god, to not surrender."

They first encountered the Japanese on a tiny speck of coral called Tarawa. When footage of American dead on the beach at Tarawa reached the United States, the public saw for the first time the human cost of war. It's the first battle sequence in the movie.
"I wanted it to be as hard and as intense as I could possibly make it," Berg said. "I wanted it to feel terrifying, because that's how I believe it was."

Berg's immersive style of filmmaking uses real flame throwers and real explosions. It's also his style of research. For "Friday Night Lights," he spent a season with a high school football team in Texas. For "Lone Survivor," he spent a month with Navy SEALs in Iraq.

He wrote most of the script for "The Mosquito Bowl" on Parris Island. "Just gets into your blood," he said. "And then I carry that, I try to, onto the set. And that's why I don't worry about the marks, I don't care if your jacket looks perfect, I don't care about the lighting; I want the soul."
For Berg, these recruits at Parris Island are the human cost of future wars. "It's a very, very powerful force," he said. "It's a very dangerous group of human beings. And I do feel responsibility."

To understand Berg, you need to understand that his father was a Marine who served during the Korean War. "My father's buried at Arlington," he said. "And I love my father very much. I go to his grave and I have conversations with him now. They're great, because I get to talk, and he has to listen!"

He said he'd already told his father about "The Mosquito Bowl." When asked what he told him, Berg choked up and excused himself. "Very emotional for me," he later explained. "I told him I was sorry that he couldn't see this film. He would have loved this film."

It's named after a football game played on the island of Guadalcanal shortly before the Marines shipped out for Okinawa. "A football game which really, to me, only matters as an opportunity for these young men to remember what's good about life," Berg said.

"That football game was a big event. That was a big deal," said Neal McCallum. Now 99, he hadn't turned 18 yet, but he was there. He'd joined the Marine Corps ten days after his 17th birthday. "I wanted to get in the war and do my part," he said.
McCallum's memory, plus a photo of the opening handshake and a mimeographed program, are all that remain of the game between two Marine regiments, each loaded with college football stars.

"Oh, it was a great game, back and forth, so it was a tie," said McCallum. The final score: 0-0. "They wanted to play again, but the colonel of the 4th Marines said he could not take that chance and hurt his Marines, because he knew we were going into battle soon."

The battle was Okinawa, and Berg, who started out as an actor, plays the commanding general, telling his Marines, "There's nothing I would like more than to tell you it's going to get easier. It's not. I would love to tell you there will be no more casualties, no more deaths. That's not true."

Berg recreated the hellscape of Okinawa in a quarry in Australia, although nothing can recapture the horrors of that 82-day battle. "The casualties on Okinawa [were] just insufferable, and it was a great sacrifice, a big sacrifice," said McCallum. "Of course, these young guys, their lives were ended. They didn't have opportunities like I did. I survived the war."

More than 12,000 Americans were killed, including 15 of the football stars who played in the Mosquito Bowl. And, as Berg shows, the loss of life for Japanese soldiers and the civilians of Okinawa was almost unimaginable.
"How can you forget something like that?" McCullum asked. "It was so intense, you're not going to forget about it."

You might not remember the exact numbers, but Berg has tried hard to make sure you never forget the human cost of war. "I want you to feel like you're going through it," he said. "I want people to say, 'I felt that. I felt it. I didn't think about it, but I felt it.'"

title: Parker Posey: "I have felt in the right place at the right time"
summary: In the 1990s actress Parker Posey was dubbed "The Queen of the Indies." The Emmy-nominated star of "The White Lotus," and the new film "Wild Horse Nine" talks about her Southern upbringing, and how her parents inspired her acting.
story: This was actress Parker Posey's first headshot as a teenager. "How cute is this?" she laughed.
It's been a long time, but I still see this girl. "I'm still that girl, are you kidding?" she said.

I met that girl in 1985, when we were both 16, at the North Carolina School of the Arts in Winston-Salem. "We were serious young performers," she said. It was a decade before Parker Posey became one of the breakout stars of the 1990s independent film heyday.

We met at a loft which was the very first place she stayed on a trip to New York City. But she's very much a product of her Southern upbringing – and the two people she calls the stars of her family. "My dad would take my mom on dates," she said. "They would go to the grocery store, 'cause they didn't have money, and he would make up stories of the people going in and out of the grocery store to make my mom laugh. So, entertain yourself! And if you can't, work on it, you know?"

And that's what Posey has been doing with particular relish throughout her career. Whether the part is big or small, there's always the sense that she's having fun with it, whether it's "Dazed and Confused," "You've Got Mail," "Josie and the Pussycats," or "Scream 3."

Parker Christian Posey and her twin brother were raised in Monroe, Louisiana, and Laurel, Mississippi. Her mother Lynda was a chef, and her late father Chris owned a car dealership. Her Southern roots came in handy for season three of "The White Lotus," where Posey was Emmy-nominated for her portrayal of the pill-popping and much-quoted North Carolina matriarch Victoria Ratliff.

Was any part of that character her mom? "Oh, my God, of course!" she laughed. "It was all the women in my family, and some people that – I mean, I love the drama that the South brings. I remember being in a grocery store and I just thought this woman was hilarious, and she goes, 'Do you have the ROH-maiiiiiine lettuce?' You're just like, Wow! 'ROH-maiiiiiine'!"

Posey spent several of her summers working at her father's car dealership: "I was always imitating people and putting on accents. I liked speaking over the speaker. And I'd say, "Good morning. Chris Posey Chevrolet Nissan. How may I help you? Mike Wally, you're needed on line one. MIKE WALLY, LINE ONE!!!!!!' Every time would be just, like, start with this, and then just start yelling. I laughed."

While attending the acting program at State University of New York in Purchase, Posey was cast as Tess Shelby on "As the World Turns." "I auditioned on a Monday, and by Tuesday I was packing my bags, and Wednesday I was on camera acting on plastic rocks and AstroTurf, and getting all this wonderful help from the great actors that I was working with," she said.

Her first big lead was in the 1995 film "Party Girl." Plum roles in a slew of lower-budget, critically-acclaimed movies followed, such as "Clockwatchers" and "The Daytrippers." That led to a 1997 Time magazine article proclaiming Posey "The Queen of the Indies" – just as the independent film scene itself was going into decline.

So, was that moniker a mixed blessing? "I don't know. Maybe," she said. "When someone's called a name, it's not a great thing. You're labeled and you're in some corner, right? And then you're not that cool anymore. There's something about being on the pedestal that must be knocked down."
Still, she kept on working, notably as part of Christopher Guest's ensemble, in movies like "Waiting for Guffman" and "Best in Show," where pretty much all of the dialogue was improvised.

"Chris saw that people weren't having children anymore; they were having dogs," Posey said. "And then we started seeing kind of the marketing of dogs, and they just seemed to be more prevalent than they had been. And I'm part of that generation. I had a dog that was like my child.""

She's also been getting lots of young fans, "which feels good, because I don't have kids of my own. So, I have these 19- and 20-year-olds coming up, talking about 'Party Girl' or movies that their parents [watched], or 'The Daytrippers,' these independent movies that they're really enjoying. And that feels so good."

Posey is having yet another moment: hosting a new reality show called "The Mob," and starring alongside John Malkovich and longtime friend Sam Rockwell in the movie "Wild Horse Nine." She's in two scenes and, as always, makes them count. "If I like something, it doesn't matter if the part's big or not, if it's resonating for me as a whole," she said, "which 'Wild Horse Nine' just really felt like. It was like a play … as an actor, you enjoy the whole play."

But I wanted to go back to a moment much earlier in her life, when our acting teacher at the North Carolina School of the Arts said this about a teenage Parker Posey: "She's better than she realizes." "She's gonna make it." And also, "She's more beautiful than she knows."

"That's so sweet," she laughed. "I loved my teachers, yeah. I still, oh, now I can't believe now I'm crying! So grateful I had that guidance. But also my family, I had that guidance, too. Like, I feel like my life has been such a path. It's not been easy at all, but I have felt in the right place at the right time."

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: RFK Jr. to ease access to unapproved peptides, draft policy states
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps Wednesday that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.
story: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps this week that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.

In a draft policy filed Wednesday, Kennedy said he had determined that compounding pharmacies could prepare six specific peptides — BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, TB-500 — even though they do not have approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
"By allowing limited compounding of the substances addressed in this guidance under appropriate safeguards, the policy provides patients with a more controlled alternative," Kennedy wrote.
Compounding pharmacies mix ingredients to prepare customized medications for individual patients.
Although they are not FDA approved, the six peptides in Kennedy's new policy are often still marketed with health claims.

The Department of Health and Human Services "did not intend to take action" against licensed pharmacies or physicians that compound "a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product," Kennedy's policy said.

Peptides are small proteins that can have powerful effects. There are several, such as insulin, that are FDA approved as being safe and effective. GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and to treat diabetes also contain FDA approved peptides.

In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend allowing the six unapproved peptides to be used in compounding, although that decision did not constitute FDA approval. That vote, however, went against the recommendations of the FDA's own scientists, who said there isn't enough evidence of safety and effectiveness for each of the six peptides to make such a determination.
Kennedy cited that panel's recommendation in his decision, saying he had determined the policy "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety."

In a statement provided to CBS News, an HHS spokesperson said that pharmacies will have to do quality testing and safety reporting, and that should help patients know what is in these peptide drugs that are currently being sold by unregulated sources.

"The policy does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness," the HHS spokesperson said. "It requires patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing, and safety reporting to hold compounders accountable and give patients an alternative to unregulated sellers."
The draft policy requires an FDA-registered ingredient maker, a lab certificate for the raw ingredients, and reports of serious side effects.

In a CBS News investigation published last week, a laboratory test was conducted on an experimental peptide weight-loss drug known as retatrutide that was purchased from a bodega in Brooklyn, New York.
The lab test, however, found that the sample of retatrutide purchased from the bodega did not contain a peptide at all.

A CBS News investigation last summer found that dozens of clinics across the country, staffed by licensed physicians and nurse practitioners, have been openly advertising retatrutide even though it has not been reviewed by the FDA and remains in clinical trials by drug giant Eli Lilly.

Kennedy's draft policy will be open to public comment beginning Friday through Nov. 13. The policy will remain in place until the FDA finalizes a rule regarding compounded peptides. However, at this point, the FDA has not proposed one.

title: Nearly 75% of ex-NFL players who died from 2008-2023 had CTE, study finds
summary: Nearly 75% of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE, a new study out of Boston University finds.
story: Nearly 75% of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a new study led by Boston University researchers finds.

CTE is a degenerative brain disease that is found in people who have suffered repeated blows to the head. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death. CTE has been discovered in football players as well as other athletes, first responders and military members.
The study published in JAMA Network Open shows how CTE, rarely seen in the general population, is far more common among deceased NFL players, lead author Julia Gallini said in a statement.

"With CTE consistently found in less than 1% of donors to community brain banks, an estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms," Gallini said.
CTE study findings
B.U. said the new findings build on a study released in August, which estimated that anywhere from 25% and 98% of ex-NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE.

"The wide range reflected uncertainty about how representative brain donors were of the overall NFL population," B.U. said in a statement. "Brain donors are more likely to have symptoms believed to be related to CTE, a concept known as selection bias."

In the new study, 362 of 387 deceased ex-players were found to have some form of CTE. But to counter the selection bias, researchers factored in that former NFL players with cognitive symptoms were five times more likely to have their brains donated to science.
"They used this estimated selection ratio to adjust the 94% prevalence of CTE observed among brain donors to an overall estimate of 74.5%," B.U. said.
The authors noted that the study only involved NFL players who have died and does not predict how many living former or active players might have CTE.

"It's hard to learn what the guys who built the game have suffered through," former NFL quarterback Matt Hasselbeck, an ambassador for the study, said in a statement. "We have to learn from this data to make the game safer, because we can't accept these numbers for the next generation of players."
NFL and NFLPA respond to CTE study

The NFL said in a statement that it "continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts." It pointed toward the introduction of better equipment like Guardian Caps and rule changes designed to keep players safe.

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust - and expanding - set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," the NFL said. "We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."
The NFL Players Association said the study is one of many that are "critical" to understanding the long-term health impacts of football.

"The NFLPA remains committed to supporting scientific research, investing in resources that aid players' physical and mental well-being, and expanding access to care so that they can experience improved health outcomes during and after their playing careers," the union said.
Asked about the findings on Wednesday, New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel says he and other football players "knew what the risks were."

"Your kids are going to have to see you maybe be knocked out on the field and laying there unconscious, or getting another surgery, or breaking your arm or breaking your leg," the former linebacker said.
The former linebacker said he thinks the NFL should be doing everything it can to protect players' quality of life.
"I do think that the league in being conscious and trying to make the game safer and better is good," he said. "But I also knew what I was signing up for when I decided to play the game."

title: How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
summary: Security experts are calling it the "largest bank robbery in human history." Getting all of the stolen crypto funds won't be easy.
story: After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.

"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.

Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."

TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.

"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.

The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.

Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.

"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.

"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."

Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.

"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.

Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.

"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

title: Nasdaq sheds more than 700 points as tech stocks slump
summary: Disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears on Friday that the AI trade could unravel.
story: The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 700 points on Friday, a rocky close to October trading amid growing investor concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.

The rout followed a series of earnings reports from major tech companies that fell short of Wall Street's expectations. Intel's stock tumbled nearly 29% on the day, the chipmaker's biggest single-day drop since 1974. Shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, also continued to struggle following a 12% slide on Thursday that erased roughly $500 billion in market value.
Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, fell 4.2%.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.
The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 sank 140 points, or 1.8%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572 points, or 1.1%.
Debt reckoning?

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."
Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.

The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.

Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.
A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: $6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
summary: A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was likely carried out by North Korea, according to a blockchain intelligence firm.
story: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?

In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.

Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"

Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: Millions of French press coffee makers recalled due to burn risk
summary: Product safety regulators said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, leading to burn injuries.
story: Coffee appliance company Bodum USA is recalling 5.9 million French press makers, warning that the glass carafe can break and cause burn injuries.

Bodum USA is the American subsidiary of a Danish-Swiss company that specializes in coffee hardware. So far, the company has received 70 reports of glass carafes breaking, 48 of which resulted in burns, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The French press coffee makers were sold on Amazon.com, in retailers including Target and Walmart, and other stores between 1974 and October 2026.
The agency said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, which can happen when customers use metal spoons to stir coffee.

"While the rate of reported incidents involving carafe breakage during use is extremely low, especially considering that Bodum has sold millions of these products in the U.S. for decades, this recall will further encourage the safe use of our French Press Coffee Makers," Bodum USA said in a statement.
A Bodum USA customer service representative told CBS News that the company was not offering refunds to customers.

The recall involves a variety of Bodum USA models, including 8-cup French presses and 12-cup Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper and Kenya models, according to CPSA. The recall number is 27-055.

Safety regulators said customers who purchased one of the recalled French press makers should not use metal utensils to stir the coffee and should avoid using the carafes if they are cracked or damaged. Customers can contact Bodum to receive a plastic stirring spoon.

For more information, consumers can contact the company toll-free at 888-879-8213 Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET; email at Bodum3302@sedgwick.com; or online at www.bodumfrenchpressrecall.expertinquiry.com or www.bodum.com (click on "Recall Information").

title: Midterm elections put Social Security funding gaps on the ballot
summary: With Social Security's main trust fund on course to be depleted in 2032, Congress will face mounting pressure to find remedies and avert benefit cuts.
story: Next week's midterm elections could prove momentous for Social Security, with time running out to put the program on solid financial ground. Social Security trustees' most recent report projects that the program's main trust fund is on course to be depleted by late 2032, after which Social Security recipients would face a more than 20% cut in benefits.

In effect, that means the burden of repairing Social Security will fall on both sitting and newly elected lawmakers. If Congress wants to avert what would amount to a devastating financial blow for millions of Americans, it will need to solve an issue that previous generations of legislators have punted on for decades.

"The pressure on Congress is going to just be tremendous going forward," said Martha Shedden, president of the National Association of Registered Social Security Analysts, an organization that trains Social Security advisers. "Every time that the annual trustees report comes out, there's more and more consternation about what lawmakers are doing."

Social Security's funding is running low largely due to demographic factors, as the U.S. population ages. More baby boomers are claiming benefits while comparatively fewer workers are paying into the program, forcing the agency to draw down its trust funds.

Concerns over the future of Social Security — a key issue for older Americans, a powerful political constituency — have surfaced in multiple electoral races across the country, including in key battleground states.

In the Michigan Senate race, for example, Republican candidate Mike Rogers highlighted the importance of eliminating fraud when asked to outline possible fixes to the program during an Oct. 25 debate. Rogers' opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, expressed support for removing the cap on income subject to employee payroll taxes "so that the rich pay their fair share."
The current payroll tax income limit is $184,500, with any earnings above that amount exempt from payroll taxes. The tax is 12.4%, with employers and workers each contributing 6.2%.

Other candidates around the country have also endorsed scrapping the cap, which would require high-income workers to pay the Social Security tax on a greater share of their income. In a recent analysis of 20 Senate races by economist Jon Schwabish, around half of the candidates said they would support raising or eliminating the cap.

Others have been more vague about their plans to shore up Social Security, simply committing to ensuring that Americans collect their full benefits rather than offering detailed policy proposals. Previous proposals have floated gradually raising the retirement age or means-testing benefits, according to Boston College's Center for Retirement Research.
Battleground battle

Social Security reform is also a hot-button issue in the battleground state of Maine, which data shows has the oldest population of any U.S. state. Around 390,000 Maine residents were collecting Social Security as of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration, more than a quarter of the state's total population.

In a September AARP poll of nearly 1,000 likely Maine voters aged 50-plus, 81% said Social Security is one of the issues that will factor into their vote. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, have each proposed possible ways to stabilize Social Security.
Jackson, a logger who previously served in Maine's state senate, has committed to eliminating the payroll tax income cap.

"People who work hard their entire lives should be able to retire with dignity," Jackson said in a statement to CBS News. "While Susan Collins has repeatedly voted to weaken Social Security, I'll work to scrap the cap because billionaires should pay into Social Security at the same rate teachers and loggers do. Social Security is a promise, and I intend to keep it."

Collins has painted herself as a champion for reform, having co-sponsored the Social Security Fairness Act with Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio. The bill, which passed in 2025 under former President Joe Biden, eliminated federal policies that barred employees with a public pension from collecting their full Social Security benefits and that reduced benefits for those workers' surviving spouses and family members.

In a television interview last week with News Center Maine, a local media outlet, Collins suggested creating a bipartisan commission to develop solutions to the projected Social Security shortfall, "such as potentially raising the earnings cap for Social Security taxes." She also vowed not to cut benefits, a proposal that has gained traction among some Republicans.

"As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, the author of the Social Security Fairness Act, and a longtime advocate for Maine's seniors, I remain committed to keeping the Social Security program strong for current and future generations," she said in the interview.
Shedden said Maine's Senate race could signal where the national debate over Social Security is heading after the midterms.

"The question is increasingly shifting from whether higher-income Americans should contribute more to how much more, and whether Congress can turn that emerging agreement into bipartisan legislation before the trust fund deadline forces the issue," she told CBS News.

title: AI deepfakes pose risks to consumers and voters, experts warn
summary: "When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," said one cybersecurity expert focused on political campaigns.
story: Advances in artificial intelligence are making it a cinch to create so-called deepfake images, videos and audio recordings, raising concerns that bad actors could bombard people with hyper-realistic scams and spread disinformation.

Deepfakes that use the voices and likenesses of public figures, including celebrities or political candidates, can also deceive the public in various ways, security experts told CBS News. By one measure, fewer than 10% of people can recognize an audio deepfake, according to Doppel, a social engineering defense platform for detecting AI-enabled threats.
"In a test, only 8% of people realized an AI agent was calling them, whereas 92% of people thought they were speaking to a human," said Doppel co-founder Kevin Tian.

AI's capacity to churn out deepfakes at scale is a pressing issue in the political arena, according to security experts. AI-generated advertisements featuring deepfakes of politicians have already surfaced across the internet and social media ahead of the midterm elections.

In one such incident in Texas, a phony, AI-manipulated social video targeting Senate candidate James Talarico purported to show a former student accusing the Democrat of sexual misconduct, according to The Poynter Institute's PolitiFact service.

"When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," Michael Kaiser, CEO of Defending Digital Campaigns, a nonpartisan organization that provides free cybersecurity services to political campaigns, told CBS News.

As of mid-October, political campaigns had spent more than $137 million on at least 220 AI-generated ads, some of which feature deepfakes of candidates, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks ads by political candidates.

"AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year. For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle," Erika Franklin Fowler, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, said in a statement this month. She noted that in most cases, the creators of the ads don't disclose that they were made using AI.
Even when someone suspects an ad is AI-generated or features a deepfake, the ad's visuals still can make an impression and shape opinion, the project's co-director, Travis Ridout, told CBS News.
"Even if we know it's not real, that sticks in one's mind," he added.
Prompting for deepfakes

Deepfakes are a kind of synthetic media that replicate a private individual's or public figure's image and likeness. Examples include a voice that sounds like a colleague or relative on the other end of a phone line, or a political figure appealing to voters for support or donations.
Raul Liive, a deepfake expert at Veriff, an AI-powered identity verification company, said the ease and speed with which deepfakes can be made and deployed today pose major risks.

"Every day that goes by, the generation of deepfake data gets easier and easier," he told CBS News. "If you wanted to fake someone's face years ago, you needed to make an effort to create fake data and use Photoshop. But now, to generate a fake face, you can just prompt your AI tool."

Veriff has documented a 300% increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts against businesses this year, compared with 2025. Liive outlined several examples of how bad actors use the tech to target businesses and unsuspecting consumers.
"A purported friend of yours calls and asks for a loan, but you know that person, and they've never made that kind of request before," he said.
Other types of scams center around medical emergencies. A caller could say they have a medical bill they urgently need help paying.

"Ask yourself what is the chance that someone you know would actually ask you something like that?" he said. "You can also hang up the phone and call the contact back on the number you have for them, or use another channel to validate their identity, if the request seems suspicious."

Veriff research on deepfakes found that consumers struggle to spot deepfakes, leaving them vulnerable to manipulation. In one test the firm conducted, 70% of people misidentified a deepfake video of a female character as being real.

The old telltale signs that something was a deepfake, like a human having six fingers or three hands, are also disappearing from AI content. Veriff found that people look for unreliable visual cues, such as unnatural skin or oddities in a subject's hair or teeth, which AI is increasingly eliminating from the content it generates.

Meanwhile, eroding public confidence in what they see could also undermine trust in legitimate content. Kaiser pointed to a photo of Sen. Mitch McConnell posing with his wife from his hospital bed, released amid speculation that the senator had died following a medical emergency earlier this year. Although the photo was authentic, some Internet users suggested it had been manipulated.

"That's an example of people just not trusting what they are seeing," Kaiser said. "People don't know if what they are looking at is legitimate, or if requests for donations are real. They're questioning everything that's going on and that disadvantages and erodes trust in the whole system."

title: DoorDash gobbles up Instacart in $17 billion deal
summary: DoorDash's purchase of Instacart for $65 per share will unite two of the country's largest grocery and food-delivery companies.
story: DoorDash said Thursday that it will buy Instacart for $17 billion, uniting one of the nation's top grocery delivery services with a major food delivery company.
DoorDash, which will pay $65 per share for Instacart, said the acquisition will benefit communities by enabling more supermarkets to use Instacart's platform to run their websites.

"Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said in a statement. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
Consumers will benefit by having more stores to choose from, speedier delivery options and access to savings when they shop locally, DoorDash also said in announcing the acquisition.
"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," DoorDash said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada.

DoorDash was founded a year later in San Francisco as a restaurant-delivery business and expanded into grocery delivery in 2020 amid a pandemic-induced surge in demand. The San Francisco-based company later teamed with the supermarket chain Kroger in 2022 and with Costco last month.
The deal will beef up DoorDash's grocery delivery services, making it a more potent competitor to Amazon and Walmart.

DoorDash's most recent earnings report, released on Wednesday, shows its revenue grew 34% from a year ago. Its total number of orders rose 28%, a sign the company is continuing to grow in the highly competitive delivery business. By the end of 2024, DoorDash held nearly 61% of the food delivery market share, topping Uber Eats and Grubhub, which held around 26% and 6%, respectively, according to Consumer Edge.
Survival of the biggest

The acquisition is the latest sign of consolidation in the delivery services industry, which is increasingly dominated by larger players. As competition intensifies, companies like Instacart have struggled to maintain their market share. Instacart now commands 18% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms, down from 26% five years ago, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company.

DoorDash's acquisition of Instacart  also comes as more people migrate from in-person stores toward apps to order their weekly groceries. Nearly 150 million Americans grocery shopped online as of 2025, according to Capital One.
As online shopping becomes more prevalent, some companies are experimenting with personalized pricing, which involves using AI and consumer data to charge shoppers different prices for the same item.

The advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative has slammed the practice as unfair and predatory. In a months-long investigation last year, the group found that identical grocery items on Instacart could differ in price by as much as 23% from one customer to the next.

Federal regulators are now scrutinizing such practices. The Federal Trade Commission on Thursday said it has opened a probe into DoorDash and Instacart, along with seven other companies across retail and transportation, to examine how they set prices.

DoorDash, which has a market value of $73 billion, said the companies will operate as separate entities until the merger is finalized, which is expected in late 2027 or early 2028. After the deal closes, DoorDash said it plans to maintain Instacart's brand, technology and app.

title: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains high
summary: The U.S. central bank left borrowing costs unchanged this month after hiking rates in September for the first time in three years.
story: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday after hiking borrowing costs in September to clamp down on inflation.
The central bank left the federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4%, keeping it unchanged after raising rates last month for the first time in three years.
In a statement, the Fed said economic activity is growing at a "strong pace" while acknowledging that inflation remains elevated.
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal," Fed officials said.
Wall Street had forecast that the Fed would stand pat on rates. Investor reaction was muted, with the three major indexes remaining essentially flat after the Fed's announcement.

The Fed's benchmark rate is its main weapon for stabilizing consumer prices, which have crept up in recent months. The latest rate decision comes less than a week before Americans head to the polls for the midterm elections, where affordability issues will be top of mind for voters. President Trump has long urged the Fed to ease borrowing costs.
Stubborn inflation

During a press conference after the rate decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said economic indicators are moving in the right direction, citing robust consumer spending, a low unemployment rate and healthy overall economic growth.

He also said credit conditions — the terms lenders set for borrowing — have tightened for businesses and households since the Fed's September rate hike, a sign the economy is heading toward a "more durable period" of growth and price stability.
At the same time, he said inflation remains "too high" and acknowledged that the Fed hasn't yet succeeded in bringing inflation under control.

"On the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive, and yet Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the committee's objective for close to six years," he told reporters. "It's our responsibility to get inflation down."
Two dissents

Ten members of the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rates, voted to hold the benchmark rate steady. Two FOMC members — Fed Board Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank President Beth Hammack — voted to raise it by 0.25 percentage points.
"We just came out of a heck of a family fight, a serious, sober discussion," Warsh said Wednesday. "I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment."

Investors and Wall Street analysts widely expected the Fed to remain on hold in October, but many economists think policymakers will raise rates at their last meeting of the year in December and again in 2027.

"The two hawkish dissents, the wording of the policy statement, and prior comments from officials all suggest the central bank will hike rates in December," Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist for forecasting firm Oxford Economics, said in an email following the Fed's decision.

Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at investment advisory firm Pantheon Macroeconomics, said financial markets are pricing in an additional 0.75 percentage points of tightening over the next year as the Fed tries to douse inflation.
Warsh stays tight-lipped
Warsh demurred when asked if Fed officials would raise rates at their Dec. 8-9 meeting, citing his stated reluctance to telegraph his policy views.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now," he told a reporter.

The Iran war has kept global energy costs elevated, making it harder to bring down prices in the U.S. Last month, the closely watched Consumer Price Index rose at a 3.7% annual rate; core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.6% from a year ago. Both measures were above economists' expectations.
Solid economic growth and steady consumer spending are also exerting upward pressure on prices, complicating the task of taming inflation, according to economists.
What does this mean for your money?

The federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — influences the cost of borrowing across the U.S. economy. A rate hike can spur higher borrowing costs for bank loans, credit cards and auto loans, while boosting returns for savings accounts.

The Fed's pause in rate hikes could provide borrowers with some breathing room, Bankrate home lending expert Linda Bell said, citing potential relief for home equity rates. Still, consumers may be in for higher borrowing costs down the road. Matt Schulz, a chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, said it's possible some loan rates could continue to climb heading into the holiday shopping season.

"Even though the Fed is leaving rates alone this month, it might raise rates again at its last meeting of the year in December," Schulz said in an email ahead of the Fed's decision. "That is far from guaranteed, but it is something that Americans should be aware of. It means that the debt they run up during the holidays could get a little more expensive to pay off before the year ends, through no fault of their own."
A surprise change
While the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged was widely expected, Warsh elicited surprise by announcing changes to the central bank's meeting schedule.

Policymakers will continue to meet eight times throughout the year. But starting in 2027, one of those meetings will be reserved for discussion and strategizing on monetary policy, Warsh said. At that meeting, the Fed will not vote on interest rates or issue a policy statement.
By 2028, Warsh said he expects two meetings to be dedicated to policy discussion and six to issuing rate decisions.

The change aligns with Warsh's broader vision for the Fed. He has been vocal in arguing for more limited communication from Fed officials, known as forward guidance, to preserve their flexibility in setting policy.

"Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals," he said. "But it's equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point."

title: Caregivers face soaring costs, taking a toll on income and jobs
summary: Caregivers spend an average of $11,500 per year looking after an aging parent, relative or friend, up roughly 60% since 2021, according to AARP.
story: Wendy Mayo knows firsthand how expensive and time-consuming caring for an aging parent can be. The 44-year-old Connecticut resident and her two siblings help look after their mother, who has Alzheimer's disease and requires around-the-clock supervision.
The siblings split the cost of care, which includes employing a professional caregiver, paying their mother's rent, and spending to adapt the home to accommodate her condition.

"We pay her rent and bought stuff to prevent bedsores, plus bed alarms because she was getting out of bed and wandering around," Mayo told CBS News. "So we also invested in cameras to watch her, and all those things add up when you're a caregiver."
Mayo estimates she spends $15,000 annually caring for her mom, while the siblings spend a combined $45,000.

Caregivers for aging relatives and other loved ones have seen their out-of-pocket costs skyrocket over the past five years, according to a new study from AARP. On average, caregivers today spend more than $11,500 per year looking after people who need support, up roughly 60% from 2021, the group found.
For households that earn less than $40,000 a year, caregiving costs consume more than three-quarters of their annual income, on average, according to AARP.
The hardships can also be significant for members of the "sandwich generation" — middle-aged adults who are raising children while also caring for aging parents.
AARP based its findings on a survey of more than 2,500 people who provided care for an adult relative or friend in June and July.
The toll on caregivers

Family caregivers' financial commitment to caring for a loved one can affect their own economic security, AARP noted. For her part, Mayo said she never hesitated to offer care for her mom, but acknowledged it wasn't a cost she had budgeted for.
"It's a role you're thrust into. It's not like retirement, which we plan for," she told CBS News, noting that supporting her mother has forced her to pull back on saving for her own retirement.

Housing and other household costs — which often include food, rent, mortgage payments and property taxes — are the largest expense for caregivers, according to AARP. The group estimates that people spend an average of nearly $4,800 a year on those expenses.

Healthcare costs are the second-largest financial burden for caregivers, including insurance premiums, copayments and payments to hospitals. Other major costs include nursing homes, medical equipment and supplies, and prescription and over-the-counter drugs.
Megan O'Reilly, AARP's vice president of government affairs for health and family, told CBS News that such costs can drain caregivers financially and make it hard for them to retire.
"The financial outputs they provide for their loved one have implications for their own retirement security," she said.
Impact on jobs

Along with the financial toll that often accompanies looking after a loved one, caregivers may also experience an impact on their jobs or income. Nearly two-thirds of working caregivers surveyed by AARP said that those added responsibilities had affected their work lives.

Sometimes the added costs required them to work additional hours, while the time commitment in offering care sometimes forced them to reduce their work schedules or even quit altogether, affecting their earnings.
"They have to make decisions about staying in the workforce or leaving, and increasing or reducing their hours to meet caregiving needs," O'Reilly said.
She also highlighted how many additional unpaid hours caregivers can spend assisting patients.

"There is the financial component, but there's also the time that caregivers spend navigating the healthcare system for loved ones," O'Reilly said. "They are spending time finding providers, making appointments, and providing transportation to and from those appointments."

title: Apple's first foldable phone broke within hours, some owners say
summary: "I didn't even make it through setup," one consumer said after his new iPhone Duo cracked shortly after he bought it.
story: Apple's first foldable iPhone went on sale on Oct. 23, and some new owners report that their devices are already broken.

Within days of the new iPhone Duo hitting stores, photos and videos of cracked screens began popping up online. Consumers said the device's inner screen broke down the middle near the hinge where the phone folds, leaving a line across the display.
The Duo, whose price starts at nearly $2,000 and tops $3,000 for higher-end models, represents Apple's biggest bet in years and the first major product rollout under new Apple CEO John Ternus.
"Loud pop"

Jesse Dalton, who lives near Frisco, Texas, bought the Duo the day it came out. He told CBS News he had just put a case on the phone and went to open the device when it "just got super tight about halfway up the hinge."

"Just pushed past it, assuming it was just stuck on the case or something for some reason, and the whole thing just snapped. I just heard a loud pop, and the screen just cracked right in the middle," Dalton said.
"I didn't even make it through setup," he added.
Dalton said he paid about $800 for the 512-gigabyte model after an AT&T trade-in promotion, bringing the full retail price to around $2,200.
A local Apple Store had a replacement on hand, he noted. "So they had one, and they were able to swap it out immediately. So I was in and out like 30 minutes."
But Dalton voiced concern about the phone's durability.
"Every time I open it, I kind of have a little pause where I'm waiting to see if it catches that same way," he said.
Justin Smith bought a Duo as a graduation gift for his wife, Roneshia. She said it cracked the following morning, less than 24 hours after purchase.
"We both woke up, and like most people, I grabbed my phone off the nightstand. I went to open it up like a book, and I realized I just could not get it open. It was a lot of resistance," she said.

"When I finally was able to get it opened, that's when we heard the crack noise, like an egg cracking. We just totally just started laughing basically because we were, like, no way, it's been less than 24 hours," Roneshia added.

After taking her device to an Apple Store, she said the staff said they were unable to fix it and that the only option was a replacement. But because the phone is backordered, she's unsure when she'll receive a new Duo. "I'm kind of stuck in this limbo."
What Apple says
Apple told CBS News it is aware that some Duo owners are reporting problems with the phone.

"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," the company said in a statement. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

Lance Ulanoff, editor at large at technology news website TechRadar, said the Duo's folding screen consists of multiple layers, including an OLED panel, glass, a plastic covering and a mechanical hinge. The ultra-thin glass could be the most fragile part, he said.
Apple's quick acknowledgment of an issue with the device is also unusual, Ulanoff noted.
"I honestly was shocked that Apple responded and acknowledged that they had seen a small number of these things. That's not typical of Apple to do that," he said.

Ulanoff, who said he had been using a Duo for a week and a half, hasn't had trouble with his own device. "I think that this right now looks like a blip. We'll keep an eye on it if it becomes more than that."
Ulanoff said owners with a damaged Duo should go to Apple, and he recommends making an appointment at an Apple Store rather than walking in.
"I would be making a beeline right back to Apple," he said.
The reports came as Apple prepared for another product event in Los Angeles this week, where the company is expected to unveil a touchscreen laptop.
