title: Midterm elections put Social Security funding gaps on the ballot
summary: With Social Security's main trust fund on course to be depleted in 2032, Congress will face mounting pressure to find remedies and avert benefit cuts.
story: Next week's midterm elections could prove momentous for Social Security, with time running out to put the program on solid financial ground. Social Security trustees' most recent report projects that the program's main trust fund is on course to be depleted by late 2032, after which Social Security recipients would face a more than 20% cut in benefits.

In effect, that means the burden of repairing Social Security will fall on both sitting and newly elected lawmakers. If Congress wants to avert what would amount to a devastating financial blow for millions of Americans, it will need to solve an issue that previous generations of legislators have punted on for decades.

"The pressure on Congress is going to just be tremendous going forward," said Martha Shedden, president of the National Association of Registered Social Security Analysts, an organization that trains Social Security advisers. "Every time that the annual trustees report comes out, there's more and more consternation about what lawmakers are doing."

Social Security's funding is running low largely due to demographic factors, as the U.S. population ages. More baby boomers are claiming benefits while comparatively fewer workers are paying into the program, forcing the agency to draw down its trust funds.

Concerns over the future of Social Security — a key issue for older Americans, a powerful political constituency — have surfaced in multiple electoral races across the country, including in key battleground states.

In the Michigan Senate race, for example, Republican candidate Mike Rogers highlighted the importance of eliminating fraud when asked to outline possible fixes to the program during an Oct. 25 debate. Rogers' opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, expressed support for removing the cap on income subject to employee payroll taxes "so that the rich pay their fair share."
The current payroll tax income limit is $184,500, with any earnings above that amount exempt from payroll taxes. The tax is 12.4%, with employers and workers each contributing 6.2%.

Other candidates around the country have also endorsed scrapping the cap, which would require high-income workers to pay the Social Security tax on a greater share of their income. In a recent analysis of 20 Senate races by economist Jon Schwabish, around half of the candidates said they would support raising or eliminating the cap.

Others have been more vague about their plans to shore up Social Security, simply committing to ensuring that Americans collect their full benefits rather than offering detailed policy proposals. Previous proposals have floated gradually raising the retirement age or means-testing benefits, according to Boston College's Center for Retirement Research.
Battleground battle

Social Security reform is also a hot-button issue in the battleground state of Maine, which data shows has the oldest population of any U.S. state. Around 390,000 Maine residents were collecting Social Security as of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration, more than a quarter of the state's total population.

In a September AARP poll of nearly 1,000 likely Maine voters aged 50-plus, 81% said Social Security is one of the issues that will factor into their vote. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, have each proposed possible ways to stabilize Social Security.
Jackson, a logger who previously served in Maine's state senate, has committed to eliminating the payroll tax income cap.

"People who work hard their entire lives should be able to retire with dignity," Jackson said in a statement to CBS News. "While Susan Collins has repeatedly voted to weaken Social Security, I'll work to scrap the cap because billionaires should pay into Social Security at the same rate teachers and loggers do. Social Security is a promise, and I intend to keep it."

Collins has painted herself as a champion for reform, having co-sponsored the Social Security Fairness Act with Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio. The bill, which passed in 2025 under former President Joe Biden, eliminated federal policies that barred employees with a public pension from collecting their full Social Security benefits and that reduced benefits for those workers' surviving spouses and family members.

In a television interview last week with News Center Maine, a local media outlet, Collins suggested creating a bipartisan commission to develop solutions to the projected Social Security shortfall, "such as potentially raising the earnings cap for Social Security taxes." She also vowed not to cut benefits, a proposal that has gained traction among some Republicans.

"As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, the author of the Social Security Fairness Act, and a longtime advocate for Maine's seniors, I remain committed to keeping the Social Security program strong for current and future generations," she said in the interview.
Shedden said Maine's Senate race could signal where the national debate over Social Security is heading after the midterms.

"The question is increasingly shifting from whether higher-income Americans should contribute more to how much more, and whether Congress can turn that emerging agreement into bipartisan legislation before the trust fund deadline forces the issue," she told CBS News.

title: Meteorite found in the Sahara Desert turns out to be piece of Mars
summary: A meteorite found in the Sahara Desert has been determined to be 4.1 billion years old and from Mars.
story: A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert in 2022 has been identified as a 4.1-billion-year-old chunk of the Red Planet, a NASA study determined.
The nearly two-pound meteorite was found in Mali. It was named Teghaza 001, after the salt plain where it was discovered, NASA said in a news release.

Study of the meteorite allowed NASA scientists to determine it was one of roughly 435 from Mars. Meteorites can be verified as having been part of Mars by comparing their chemical and mineral makeup to samples and data collected by NASA's Martian missions.

Age-dating of the meteorite led researchers to conclude it was about 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth, NASA said. That provides "a rare snapshot" of the planet's crust and formation, the agency said.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the lead author of a paper detailing the age-dating process and related discoveries. Liu is part of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Previous ancient Martian meteorites provided narrower glimpses into the planet's history. But Teghaza 001 shows how Mars' crust formed from cooling magma and was then changed by water on the planet's surface.

The meteorite is made of a unique mix of volcanic minerals, including zircon crystals, NASA said, matching samples observed by the agency's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's southern highlands. Francis Tissot, a geochemistry professor at Caltech, helped the researchers use a pioneering age-dating method that studied a piece of meteorite smaller than a fingernail. The precise method allowed scientists to analyze single grains of minerals.

That analysis showed the rock had been altered by Martian water about 4.1 billion years ago. The rock itself may have been formed even earlier, NASA said. The data also showed that early Mars may have had a more dynamic water cycle than scientists previously believed.

Paper author Lee Saper said that the meteorite "records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." Another study of the meteorite, published in June, focused on the rock's water content and considered how water might have shaped the early topography of Mars.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," Lee, a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center, added.
Liu said that further research on the meteorite is likely.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.

title: Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
summary: Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate​ impacts that will persist for centuries, the U.N. says.
story: Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.

"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.

WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.

"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.

The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

title: Spacewalkers begin final phase of a space station upgrade
summary: Two astronauts stepped outside the International Space Station for the first of two spacewalks, one week apart, to complete a complex upgrade to the aging power system.
story: Two astronauts stepped outside the International Space Station Thursday for the first of two spacewalks, one week apart, to install a final pair of roll-out solar blankets that will complete a complex, years-long upgrade of the lab's aging power system.

Running well ahead of schedule, NASA's Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed the first set of ISS roll-out solar arrays, or IROSAs, on the left side of the lab's power truss as planned.
As a safety precaution, they waited until the station was in orbital darkness, with no sunlight generating any power, before connecting cables tying the new IROSA into the lab's power circuits.

Four hours and 23 minutes after the spacewalk began, as the space station moved back into orbital daylight, Menon used a power tool to unbolt a final restraint, and the IROSA slowly unrolled, stretching out to its full length of 60 feet in about 10 minutes.

"Engineers and electrical officers here in mission control are happy with what they're seeing from the new array, which will add eight kilowatts to the overall power capability of the complex," said NASA commentator Rob Navias.

With the seventh IROSA successfully installed, Menon and Kutryk carried out a few "get-ahead" tasks, preparing the final IROSA for installation next week, and returned to the Quest airlock, bringing the seven-hour 11-minute spacewalk to an end at 3:08 p.m. EDT.

"Well, being outside, I can say that it is always sunny in space, except for a few orbits, and quite incredible what we've been able to do to provide new solar arrays to space station," Menon said from the airlock. "In fact, we've been powering our efforts in space and doing complex operations like this for over 26 years."
It was the fourth spacewalk for Menon but the first for Kutryk.
"We knew you're going to absolutely crush it," Menon said to his partner. "Everyone had those high expectations for you, and you absolutely delivered."

The new IROSA and the final unit that will be installed during a spacewalk next Thursday will complete an upgrade that began in 2021 when the first of eight ISS roll-out solar arrays was installed at the base of an existing solar wing.

The IROSAs are needed to offset age-related degradation that has reduced the power output of the station's original arrays. The new panels are smaller, but they are more efficient, featuring state-of-the-art solar cells.

Before the first IROSA was installed, the original arrays were generating about 152 kilowatts of power. The six IROSAs installed to date have boosted that up to about 200 kilowatts. With the final two sets, some 215 kilowatts of power will be available to sustain the lab through its planned retirement and de-orbiting in 2030, supporting life support systems, research and visiting vehicles.
The final two IROSA's were delivered to the station aboard a SpaceX Cargo Dragon capsule earlier this month with each one folded in half and stowed in the ship's unpressurized trunk section.

The station's robot arm, operated remotely by flight controllers at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, pulled the IROSAs out of the Dragon and stowed them on the left side of the lab's power truss to await installation.

Floating in the station's Quest airlock, Menon and Kutryk switched their suits to battery power at 7:57 a.m. to officially kick off the 285th spacewalk since station assembly began in 1998. The spacewalk began in orbital darkness, prompting Kutryk to observe, "the night is dark and full of wonders."

Menon and Kutryk unbolted the first of the two stowed IROSAs from its carrier so Menon, anchored to the end of the station's 58-foot-long robot arm, could carry it over to its mounting point farther outboard along the power truss.
"They are around 750 pounds in that folded configuration, they're about 10 feet long, and so it's a lot to handle," said Garrett Hehn, a spacewalk flight director.

He said flight controllers developed "a pretty elegant series of maneuvers" to move Menon and the IROSA on the robot arm "where we've tried to rotate around the actual center mass of the arrays rather than the crew member. It was a lesson learned from previous EVAs of how we could make it a little less tiring on Anil when he's got to hold that array in his hands."

All of that went well, and the seventh IROSA, still folded in half, was installed on a previously assembled support fixture at the base of one of the station's left-side inboard solar wings. The two halves then were unfolded and bolted together.

Working when the station is on Earth's night side and the arrays weren't generating any power, the spacewalkers connected four electrical cables tying the IROSA into power channel 2A. Once that work was completed, the array was unrolled.
The IROSAs deploy somewhat like a tape measure winding home, with "stored energy" built in that lets the blankets unroll without motors or other drive mechanisms.

"These arrays, I kind of think of them like a snap bracelet, if you remember that time," Hehn said. "They basically have a series of magnets up the side where they deploy with enough energy that it just continues rolling out steadily. That process will take about 10 minutes."

Menon and Kutryk plan to float back outside Nov. 5 to install the final IROSA on a solar wing at the far right end of the power truss. The robot arm does not have the reach to carry Menon and the new blankets to the far end of the truss, so he and Kutryk will hand it off to each other leap frog fashion to get it all the way to the waiting support frame.
From there, installation and deployment will mirror the work done Thursday.

"ISS is building towards future exploration missions in deep space and beyond," Kutryk said after re-entering the station's airlock. "That's why we're doing this. And so today was a step forward for the future of the space station. But it's also another step of many towards the EVAs that teams will hopefully be doing on the surface of the moon."

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.
A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: Data center health worries animate midterm campaigns
summary: Opposition to the rapid emergence of data centers in states such as Ohio and Arizona has ginned up activism and unified voters. A range of public health issues have played into the resistance.
story: Page, Arizona — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health.
"I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers."
"There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said.

Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction.

The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building.

Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes.

It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds.
"Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio.
"That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending."

The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI, with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists.

Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies.

Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside.

Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing.

Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands.

"We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now."

A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts.
"Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition.
It cuts across politics
Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth.
Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.

Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned.

Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Mr. Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won.

Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Mr. Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support.
"This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in."
In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards.

The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Mr. Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new construction in their district.
The House seat they're vying for is considered competitive, and the contest could be pivotal in determining which party gains House control after the Nov. 3 midterms.
In Arizona, 57% of registered voters oppose construction of more large data centers, according to an August opt-in online poll of 1,040 registered voters by Noble Predictive Insights.
More than costs
Photos from across the nation featuring politicians at groundbreaking ceremonies for data centers held only a year or two ago are now campaign fodder.

That has become a big problem for some elected leaders in Ohio, where more than a dozen local referendums or initiatives related to construction of the facilities will appear on ballots — the most of any state.

The issue has forced its way to the forefront of the state's marquee U.S. Senate race. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is hoping to return to Congress with pointed attacks against Republican Sen. Jon Husted over the matter.

Roughly $2.5 billion in state and local tax breaks over the last decade have prompted Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech companies to erect dozens of data centers across Ohio. That boom has spurred protests across the state, organized by local residents who are worried about the health, environmental, and financial impact of the structures.
Brown has pinned the blame on Husted directly with ads airing widely across Ohio that call him "the face of data centers."
"They're devouring our farmland, sucking up our water, and using our energy," Brown says in one recent video.
A memo circulated by the National Republican Senatorial Committee in August and obtained by Politico described Brown's critiques as a big problem for Husted.
"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck," warns the Aug. 18 memo, which was shared with artificial intelligence companies.

Husted has rebuffed these critiques by framing the construction of data centers as a local issue. More recently, he has said he wants to make sure that the companies building data centers pay for infrastructure costs, including energy.
In a statement, Husted spokesperson Tom Evans reiterated that point, saying the senator believes "data centers should remain a local decision."

It's not just costs that voters care about. An early-October opt-in survey of 1,650 Ohio adults by Ohio Northern University and SurveyUSA found that 55% were opposed to data center construction. About two-thirds had a negative opinion of data centers' impact on their community's environment, and about half said the same about their impact on quality of living.
Opponents of data centers cite noise, air, and water pollution as a concern, according to a Gallup poll. Americans are more opposed to data centers in their area than nuclear power plants.

The air pollution comes from gas turbines and diesel generators that have been linked to cardiovascular problems, asthma, and other health risks. Cooling system chemicals, heavy metals, and construction runoff can enter the water supply or rivers.

"When they are fired up and powered by diesel, they emit a lot of air pollution like nitrogen oxide, and this pollutant can travel around the community and to those downwind," said Shaolei Ren, an electrical and computer engineering professor at the University of California-Riverside.

In Page, residents in July voted out the mayor amid backlash over the Council's approval of the land sale for the data center. Opponents of data centers say it's a warning to candidates in the midterm elections who back new construction.

Some residents in this picturesque town of about 7,000 people remain worried that the health effects could plague them if the project goes forward. Jan Boehme lives in a neighborhood close to the proposed site. From her front lawn with its "No Data Center" sign, she said she is concerned that a data center could become her new neighbor — and cause harms such as hearing loss.
"We're against it," she said. "In this area, there are a lot of houses, and I'm concerned about all the noise."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Apple's first foldable phone broke within hours, some owners say
summary: "I didn't even make it through setup," one consumer said after his new iPhone Duo cracked shortly after he bought it.
story: Apple's first foldable iPhone went on sale on Oct. 23, and some new owners report that their devices are already broken.

Within days of the new iPhone Duo hitting stores, photos and videos of cracked screens began popping up online. Consumers said the device's inner screen broke down the middle near the hinge where the phone folds, leaving a line across the display.
The Duo, whose price starts at nearly $2,000 and tops $3,000 for higher-end models, represents Apple's biggest bet in years and the first major product rollout under new Apple CEO John Ternus.
"Loud pop"

Jesse Dalton, who lives near Frisco, Texas, bought the Duo the day it came out. He told CBS News he had just put a case on the phone and went to open the device when it "just got super tight about halfway up the hinge."

"Just pushed past it, assuming it was just stuck on the case or something for some reason, and the whole thing just snapped. I just heard a loud pop, and the screen just cracked right in the middle," Dalton said.
"I didn't even make it through setup," he added.
Dalton said he paid about $800 for the 512-gigabyte model after an AT&T trade-in promotion, bringing the full retail price to around $2,200.
A local Apple Store had a replacement on hand, he noted. "So they had one, and they were able to swap it out immediately. So I was in and out like 30 minutes."
But Dalton voiced concern about the phone's durability.
"Every time I open it, I kind of have a little pause where I'm waiting to see if it catches that same way," he said.
Justin Smith bought a Duo as a graduation gift for his wife, Roneshia. She said it cracked the following morning, less than 24 hours after purchase.
"We both woke up, and like most people, I grabbed my phone off the nightstand. I went to open it up like a book, and I realized I just could not get it open. It was a lot of resistance," she said.

"When I finally was able to get it opened, that's when we heard the crack noise, like an egg cracking. We just totally just started laughing basically because we were, like, no way, it's been less than 24 hours," Roneshia added.

After taking her device to an Apple Store, she said the staff said they were unable to fix it and that the only option was a replacement. But because the phone is backordered, she's unsure when she'll receive a new Duo. "I'm kind of stuck in this limbo."
What Apple says
Apple told CBS News it is aware that some Duo owners are reporting problems with the phone.

"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," the company said in a statement. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

Lance Ulanoff, editor at large at technology news website TechRadar, said the Duo's folding screen consists of multiple layers, including an OLED panel, glass, a plastic covering and a mechanical hinge. The ultra-thin glass could be the most fragile part, he said.
Apple's quick acknowledgment of an issue with the device is also unusual, Ulanoff noted.
"I honestly was shocked that Apple responded and acknowledged that they had seen a small number of these things. That's not typical of Apple to do that," he said.

Ulanoff, who said he had been using a Duo for a week and a half, hasn't had trouble with his own device. "I think that this right now looks like a blip. We'll keep an eye on it if it becomes more than that."
Ulanoff said owners with a damaged Duo should go to Apple, and he recommends making an appointment at an Apple Store rather than walking in.
"I would be making a beeline right back to Apple," he said.
The reports came as Apple prepared for another product event in Los Angeles this week, where the company is expected to unveil a touchscreen laptop.

title: Jury selection begins in Meta, Snap social media addiction case
summary: The plaintiffs allege that features on the companies' social media platforms, like endless scrolling, kept them hooked and harmed their mental health.
story: Jury selection begins today in Los Angeles for a trial against Meta and Snap brought by two plaintiffs who claim the companies' platforms were designed to be addictive — the latest in a wave of cases focusing on social media's impact on young people's mental health.
The plaintiffs sued in 2023, alleging that endless scrolling, Snapstreaks and other features on social media platforms kept them hooked and harmed their mental health.

The first, a 16-year-old from Illinois identified in court documents as S.J., started using Snapchat as a young child and alleges the app's features led to compulsive use and contributed to depression, reduced sleep, anxiety, an eating disorder, suicidal ideation and self-harm. The other plaintiff, K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, said her use of Meta's platforms and Snapchat from a young age also contributed to mental health issues and self-harm.

"Defendants defectively designed the platforms to specifically appeal to and addict minors and young adults, who were particularly unable to appreciate the risks posed by the platforms, and particularly susceptible to harms from those products," the plaintiffs' lawyers argued in the complaint, filed in a Los Angeles trial court.
TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube were part of the original lawsuit, but settled ahead of the trial. Meta also settled with S.J., the Illinois plaintiff.
A spokesperson for Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said the company disagrees with allegations brought by K.D.B.

"A young person's mental health is shaped by many factors, as the evidence in this trial will show," the spokesperson said in an email. "The plaintiff used TikTok far more than Instagram or Facebook, and her personal circumstances were a substantial factor in her struggles."
A spokesperson for Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, also disputed the claims and defended the company's actions.

"We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs' experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed," they said in a statement.
The companies are expected to argue that other factors, not their platforms, were responsible for the plaintiffs' mental health issues.
Plaintiffs are seeking an unspecified amount in compensatory and punitive damages.

"This will be the first case against Snapchat and the first time the public has a chance to see some of their documents," Mark Lanier, the founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in an email.

Instagram head Adam Mosseri, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel are all expected to take the stand during the trial, which the plaintiffs' lawyers say will likely run until mid-December. Opening statements are scheduled to begin in early November, with Judge Carolyn Kuhl presiding.
Earlier this week, Meta and Snap requested that the cases be split into two separate trials — a matter Judge Kuhl has yet to rule on, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The case was selected as one of several bellwether cases for a trove of similar claims brought against social media players in recent years. It could intensify scrutiny of social media platforms at a time when many are already wary of the technology's impact on young people. Nearly half of teens said they're online almost constantly, according to a 2024 Pew Research Center survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17.

In a separate landmark case earlier this year, Meta and YouTube were ordered to pay $6 million after a jury found they were liable for creating products that led to harmful and addictive behavior by young users.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Judge orders DOJ to stop trying to "intimidate" California election officials
summary: A federal judge ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots and threatening criminal prosecution for noncompliance.
story: A California judge late Friday ordered the federal government to stop demanding that state and local election officials separate out ballots or not count certain votes from alleged noncitizens, and to stop threatening officials with criminal prosecution if they do not comply.

The ruling from U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson came in response to a lawsuit filed a day earlier by labor unions and other groups, accusing the Trump administration of intimidating California election workers and interfering in the administration of the midterms.

The Justice Department has pressed officials in California this month to separate out mail ballots for roughly 20,000 people it alleges are not U.S. citizens, and has issued grand jury subpoenas for officials in Los Angeles County — part of a sweeping campaign by the Trump administration. Federal officials have also suggested for months that election workers could be prosecuted if they fail to stop noncitizens from voting.

The lawsuit cited the head of the Justice Department Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, sending letters to all 50 states and Washington, D.C., threatening to criminally prosecute local election officials in July, and the department's latest demand for lists of names of voters they believe are possibly noncitizens, as examples of unlawful conduct.

The judge on Friday found federal officials have likely violated the Voting Rights Act of 1965's prohibition on "attempting to intimidate, threaten or coerce" people who help others vote. She also said the government was acting outside its legal or constitutional authority.

"One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation," she wrote. "Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy. It requires safeguarding to ensure full participation and public trust in our elections."

Thompson also wrote: "Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters."
The judge issued a temporary restraining order that expires on Nov. 16, and scheduled the next hearing for Nov. 13.

In addition to blocking the Justice Department from threatening criminal prosecutions or demanding that officials separate out ballots, Thompson ordered the Justice Department to inform the court of any pending search warrant applications or subpoenas.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

The ruling was issued after another California federal judge on Wednesday denied the Justice Department's request to compel California to set aside more than 20,000 ballots for alleged noncitizens. He found that it violates "longstanding constitutional principles" giving states the authority to administer their own elections. The Trump administration appealed the matter to an appellate court, which also rejected a request to segregate the ballots on Friday.

title: DOJ calls Alaska Senate allegations "troubling," asks to segregate ballots
summary: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska did not specify what crimes are being investigated by the Justice Department, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."
story: Anchorage, Alaska — The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska said new reporting on the origins of an independent candidate's Senate campaign "has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets" to the state, as federal officials in a separate civil case seek to segregate some of Alaska's Senate ballots.

Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for the District of Alaska, called the allegations about how Daniel J. Sullivan — a man with the same first and last name as incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan — ended up on the ballot "troubling."

"We are aware of the recent New York Times reporting regarding the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, that they orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate, and we are taking that extremely seriously," he said in a press conference in Anchorage.
But Heyman declined to detail what specific crimes are being investigated, saying he's "not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not."

"That's what we do, is we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I'm not going to comment on what those theories are, and I'm also not going to put the cart before the horse," he said.
Asked by CBS News why the Justice Department is choosing to escalate the case ahead of the election, Heyman said, "We're not escalating anything except to the extent that a new article came out."

"This has been going on sort of quietly for several months, with the intent not to escalate anything," he said, adding that investigators are going to take allegations involving election integrity seriously, even if a few days before the election.

Republicans have claimed that Daniel J. Sullivan is a plant by Democrats to confuse voters and boost the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country.

Peltola and national Democrats have strongly denied any involvement in his campaign. Peltola said Thursday she is "not interested in tricking voters" and "knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has argued Republicans have been linked to their own efforts to stack the Alaska ballot in order to help their preferred candidates, including in this year's Senate primary and in other elections.

State election officials initially determined Daniel J. Sullivan was not eligible to appear on the ballot, accusing him of a "deliberate attempt" to confuse Alaska voters. But the decision was overturned by state courts, which ruled that state officials didn't have the authority to exclude a candidate based on their interpretation of "good faith."

The controversy drew renewed scrutiny after the New York Times reported that operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into the matter and the Justice Department has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials.
In a separate civil case, the Trump administration has sued to block Alaska from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses because of "voter confusion."

On Friday, the Justice Department asked for a preliminary injunction, saying it wants to "ensure the preservation and segregation of ballots that may be impacted by voter confusion." The government also asked for expedited discovery for the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and requested that a judge rule on the matter by Monday. The filings heavily rely on The New York Times' reporting.

"Daniel J. Sullivan does not seek to serve in the U.S. Senate but rather seeks to confuse voters," the filing says. "Accordingly, there will indeed be voter confusion caused by this frivolous candidacy."

Federal government lawyers said they want to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."

The state of Alaska opposed the request, arguing the Justice Department's lawsuit "lacks any merit." They also said votes are "comingled in the ballot box on Election Day" and therefore can't be segregated without violating ballot secrecy requirements, and noted that "the ballots (whether segregated or not) will not reveal any voter's reasons for voting for Daniel J."
And they said an order to preserve ballots is unnecessary since the state already saves ballots for 22 months.

"The United States' delay further undermines its request for expedited consideration. It waited until two weeks before Election Day to file a lawsuit about issues that arose months ago," the state said.

During the news conference, Heyman also said that he had been recused from the matter some time ago, but that the recusal "has officially been rescinded." Heyman said he had been recused because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, which is no longer the case.

title: El-Sayed and Stevens feud ahead of key Michigan Senate race
summary: Stevens has demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad and apologize for comments he made about Israel. El-Sayed said Stevens is "intent on relitigating" their primary.
story: Washington — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, clashed Friday ahead of a Sunday campaign event where both were expected to make a rare appearance together.

The public rift between the two Democrats comes just days before one of the country's most hotly contested Senate races, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers seeks to peel off centrist Democratic voters. El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.
In a statement Friday evening, El-Sayed said Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago."

The dig came hours after Stevens demanded that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for suggesting during the campaign that "Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care."
"Abdul promises to get money out of politics," Stevens said in the statement. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford."

She also urged El-Sayed to condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. The video ad features a couple in a grocery store talking about needing to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf because "we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." The man and woman in the ad then complain about the billions in military support that the U.S. has provided Israel.
El-Sayed's campaign said earlier this week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad, which was created by the political action committee Rebellion PAC.
"No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign," his campaign said in a statement.
In her Friday statement, Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down his own ad featuring the far-right podcaster and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson.
It's unclear what the dustup means for their Sunday appearance.

Stevens said she planned to appear with El-Sayed at a Detroit church, alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. An announcement from El-Sayed's campaign about his appearance with Clyburn did not mention Stevens.

Earlier this week, Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Later that day, Stevens said in a CNN interview that she would vote for El-Sayed, saying "we're a household divided," but she called on his campaign "to shut out the hate and to call it out."

title: How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
summary: Security experts are calling it the "largest bank robbery in human history." Getting all of the stolen crypto funds won't be easy.
story: After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.

"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.

Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."

TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.

"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.

The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.

Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.

"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.

"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."

Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.

"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.

Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.

"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

title: ATF's top lawyer, who oversaw overhaul of its firearms regulations, resigns
summary: Robert Leider was appointed as the ATF's top attorney last year, shortly after former Attorney General Pam Bondi abruptly fired the agency's former chief, claiming without evidence that the bureau was "targeting gun owners."
story: Robert Leider, the chief counsel at the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, who has been overseeing a major overhaul of the agency's firearms regulations, announced Friday he is stepping down from his role, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Leider was appointed as the ATF's top attorney last year shortly after former Attorney General Pam Bondi abruptly fired the agency's former chief, claiming without evidence that the bureau was "targeting gun owners."
Shortly after CBS News sought comment, the ATF said it had released a short press statement announcing Leider's resignation.

Leider, who previously clerked for Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, is expected to return to his previous role as a law professor at George Mason University 's Antonin Scalia Law School, the ATF added.

Leider will technically remain employed with the ATF through January until he returns to his teaching post, but will remain on administrative leave starting Monday, a source with direct knowledge said.
Leider could not be immediately reached for comment.

Leider has been in charge of overseeing an overhaul of dozens of different firearm-related regulations that were unveiled by the Justice Department in April, in what it called an effort to "reduce unnecessary burdens on law-abiding citizens and businesses while modernizing regulatory frameworks that no longer reflect current law, agency practice, or court precedent."

Among the various proposals was one that would repeal a Biden-era "engaged in the business" rule that broadened the definition of who was required to obtain a firearms dealer license and undergo a background check.
That rule was intended to prevent online sellers and sellers at gun shows from evading licensing requirements that would subject them to background checks.

Although Leider was a political appointee at the ATF and a staunch supporter of Second Amendment rights, he did not always see eye to eye with the Justice Department leadership's legal positions on litigation brought against the ATF by pro-gun groups, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News.

The most recent dust-up inside the Justice Department revolved around a decision by senior leadership not to appeal a court ruling in Texas that loosened regulations for short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and silencers under the National Firearms Act.

Sources told CBS News in September the decision not to appeal the ruling was directed by President Trump, and ran counter to the legal advice of numerous career and politically appointed attorneys at the Justice Department.
A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Leider's decision to step down was not related to the Justice Department's decision not to appeal the court ruling on the National Firearms Act.

title: Nasdaq sheds more than 700 points as tech stocks slump
summary: Disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears on Friday that the AI trade could unravel.
story: The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 700 points on Friday, a rocky close to October trading amid growing investor concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.

The rout followed a series of earnings reports from major tech companies that fell short of Wall Street's expectations. Intel's stock tumbled nearly 29% on the day, the chipmaker's biggest single-day drop since 1974. Shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, also continued to struggle following a 12% slide on Thursday that erased roughly $500 billion in market value.
Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, fell 4.2%.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.
The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 sank 140 points, or 1.8%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572 points, or 1.1%.
Debt reckoning?

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."
Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.

The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.

Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.

title: Judge skeptical of administration's defense of Trump's proposed arch
summary: The Justice Department and a group of veterans faced off in court over the fate of the 250-foot arch that President Trump wants to build.
story: Washington — The Justice Department and a group of Vietnam War veterans faced off in a Washington, D.C., courtroom on Friday over the fate of the 250-foot arch that President Trump wants to build between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan heard arguments over a preliminary injunction that would stop the arch's construction. Attorneys representing three Vietnam veterans and a historian who sued earlier this year to stop construction argued that the project has been rushed and lacks proper congressional approval, while defending their legal standing to bring the suit.

Chutkan said at the outset of the hearing that standing was the most important issue for her to consider. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court found that a group of plaintiffs who brought a similar suit to block the White House ballroom construction likely did not have the legal right to sue.
In court filings, the Justice Department called the plaintiffs' motions "breathless" and urged Chutkan to follow the Supreme Court's decision in the White House ballroom case.

Two of the plaintiffs in the case, Vietnam veterans Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told Chutkan that the arch construction would impact their experience in visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery, and said they would be harmed by the arch's size and purpose.

Lemmon, who appeared via Zoom, told the judge that he found the concept of the arch as a tourist attraction outside of Arlington National Cemetery "almost blasphemous." Lemmon said he walks from the Vietnam Veterans Memorial to the Lincoln Memorial and then to Arlington Cemetery, where he visits the graves of those who served in the Vietnam War.
"It means an intense amount to me to be able to continue to do that," he said, adding that the proposed arch looming over the gravesites "changes the entire experience in a profoundly negative way."
Byrnes, who appeared in-person, said in a declaration to Chutkan that he would reconsider being buried in Arlington if the arch is built.

The group challenging the project also argued that recent renderings show it would disrupt the symbolic connection between the Lincoln Memorial and the Robert E. Lee Memorial, a carefully considered sightline meant to convey unity after the Civil War.

According to court filings by the Justice Department from earlier this month, construction on the arch could begin as soon as Nov. 5 if the National Capital Planning Commission issues final approval of the plan the same day.

Justice Department attorney Robert Stander asked Chutkan to deny the motion to block the construction and grant a government motion to dismiss the case, arguing that "it's easier than the ballroom case" to dismiss because of the veterans "deep personal disagreement" at the concept of the Arch.
Stander called the project a "high-priority project" from the White House, and suggested that the plaintiffs should bring their motion again once construction begins.
Chutkan then pushed Stander on the project's funding, which so far has remained vague.

"I don't even know who is paying for this thing," Chutkan said, later adding that she was skeptical to allow construction to begin on the project, and questioned what harm the government would face if the project was temporarily delayed "apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city."

Chutkan also pressed Stander on the Trump administration's claim that there are national-security justifications for the arch, which were raised by the government for the first time in a filing Wednesday. She pointed to a declaration from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, in which he said the arch could have sensors, communications equipment and defense capabilities and noted that, according to the government, the arch would also host between 2,000 and 22,000 tourists each day.
"We're not talking about plans for a cafeteria," the judge said.
Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social in September that he converted plans for the arch to make it, in part, a "top grade Military Complex," equipped with snipers and drones.

The Trump administration also submitted two sworn declarations from top Cabinet officials, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Hegseth, stating that the arch would allow for the military and Secret Service to use the structure to defend the nation's capital against unmanned drone attacks and other potential threats.
In his declaration, Hegseth said that the proposed arch "is a generational national defense opportunity" to stop future threats.

Stander, however, declined to provide more details as to how the arch would provide national-security benefits, but noted that there have been several assassination attempts against Mr. Trump since 2024.
"The arch is somehow intended to prevent assasination attempts against the president?" Chutkan responded. "It's going to be completed three years from now."

While the Supreme Court allowed construction to continue on the White House ballroom in part due to what the Trump administration said were national security implications if the project were to be paused, Chutkan said that in this case, the high court's reasoning "does not make the mention of national security to be talismanic."

Critics of the project have raised concerns that it could interfere with flights in and out of nearby Ronald Reagan International Airport. Arlington County, adjacent to where the arch would be located on a currently empty traffic circle, sued in federal court in Virginia to block the project.

The Federal Aviation Administration determined that the arch would not pose a hazard to flights coming into and departing from the nearby airport despite those concerns, but the county argued that the arch would necessitate changes to the flight paths of planes traveling in and out of Reagan International Airport, and asked for a federal judge there to order an environmental review of the arch.

Kaia  Hubbard and 
                                                  
                                  Arden  Farhi
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Trump meets with Stephen Hubbard after release from Russian jail
summary: Stephen Hubbard was imprisoned in Russia for over four years until gaining release last week.
story: Washington — President Trump met with Stephen Hubbard, the American recently released from a Russian prison, at the White House on Friday.
Inviting reporters to join them in the Oval Office, the president called Hubbard a "very special man" who "suffered greatly." CBS News was first to report plans for the meeting.
Hubbard was jailed in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher, returned home to the U.S. last week.
Mr. Trump said to Hubbard, "I think I could say that you were treated reasonably well, right?" Hubbard said "yes," and that he he was even treated "sympathetically by some of the guards."
CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs asked Hubbard about the moment he learned he was being released.

"I had heard it many times before, and I reached the state where seeing is believing," Hubbard said. "Actions speak louder than words. I never trusted what they said. Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison. I went out and I saw the car and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians. Then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St. Petersburg, 'I'm really going somewhere.'"
Hubbard said he wouldn't have lived another year in that prison.
Hubbard's release was announced during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
Mr. Trump said there was no "swap" for Hubbard, but appeared to tie Hubbard's release to his decision to exempt Russia from sanctions passed by Congress.

"We were in the midst of negotiating," the president told reporters last week. "And a lot of stupid people said, and people that don't know how life works, they said, 'Why aren't you putting Russia sanctions and all this' in the midst of a negotiation to try to get a long-term hostage back from Russia. If I would have done that, you would not have Mr. Hubbard coming back."
The president has not reimposed those sanctions since Hubbard's release.
