title: ICE officer charged in Texas after allegedly hitting man with vehicle
summary: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was charged with a felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle earlier this month.
story: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer was charged with a felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle in Houston earlier this month, a Texas district attorney announced Friday.
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said ICE Officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Teare said if convicted, the punishment would be a prison sentence lasting between two and 20 years.

Teare accused Morales of hitting Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who the district attorney said has been living in Texas for more than 30 years without documentation. Parra-Hernandez doesn't have a criminal record and didn't have a deportation order against him at the time of the incident, Teare said.

The district attorney said Parra-Hernandez, who is in ICE custody, is missing court dates for deportation proceedings because he isn't able to leave a rehab facility where he is recovering from his injuries.
Teare expected that Morales would be taken into custody relatively soon, but possibly not on Friday. Prosecutors have been in contact with Morales' attorney, Teare said.

Morales engaged in a pursuit of a vehicle being driven by Parra-Hernandez on Oct. 10. During the pursuit, Parra-Hernandez and another person fled the vehicle on foot. At a news conference Friday, a video was played showing the moments when Teare said Morales hit Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.

Footage from what Teare said was Morales' body camera showed Parra-Hernandez groaning in pain on the ground after he was hit by the vehicle, which the district attorney said was a 2025 Jeep Grand Cherokee. Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg in the incident.
"Like, I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," the officer wearing the body camera said in the footage to someone else.
In the immediate aftermath of the incident, an ICE spokesperson had said in a statement to CBS News that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the ICE vehicle.
"Morales aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra-Hernandez," Teare said Friday. He also said that Morales ran over both of Parra-Hernandez's legs.
Parra-Hernandez is heard screaming in the background of Morales' 911 call for an ambulance in a recording played during the news conference. He told a dispatcher that Parra-Hernandez hit his vehicle.
"We're following this guy, trying to pull him over, he jumped out of the vehicle, I tried to get around him, and he hit my car," Morales said in the recording.
ICE told The Associated Press that the indictment against Morales was "a political stunt" and that local officials lack the authority to investigate federal officers for performing their duties.
"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement to the AP.

During the news conference, Teare said that the district attorney's office has the "utmost respect and admiration for law enforcement," and that his office will prosecute any officer who violates the law.

"An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill or violate the constitutional rights of anyone," Teare said. "My hope is that this prosecution will do more than just seek justice for the Parra-Hernandez family and Mr. Parra-Hernandez. I hope that it also sends a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorize our streets. The time to stop is now, and if you don't, you will be held accountable."

Teare noted that ICE had said agents were pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant. Teare said Friday that Mendoza-Cervantes has apparently been dead for nine years.

title: Appeals court rejects DOJ bid to set aside disputed California ballots
summary: The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots​ received in the midterm election.
story: Washington — The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit on Friday rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.

The panel's 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to assert control over state-run elections. Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez said in an unsigned decision that the Justice Department failed to meet its burden in showing that an injunction pending appeal is warranted.

"Major concerns remain that granting the United States's requested relief might result in immense hardship to Defendants and harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy," they wrote.
Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented.

The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department's demands could disenfranchise citizens.

"As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system," the appeals court wrote, adding that the relief requested by the Trump administration is "simple only in the abstract."
The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can't be matched back to the voters who submitted them.

The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. The Justice Department has also provided a list of alleged noncitizen voters to officials in Washington state.

Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to share the disputed list of names with lawyers for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the UCLA Voting Rights Project. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.
It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.
Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

The two groups sued the Department of Homeland Security in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government's data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.
A coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government's efforts.

The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with their demands.
The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that "any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy."

On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. At least three L.A. County election officials have been asked to appear before a grand jury on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The lawsuit accuses the Justice Department of issuing threats against election officials that could interfere with their ability to process votes.

It is unclear whether the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. The department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.
A spokesperson for the Lanier Law Firm, which is representing the plaintiffs, said they will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," the spokesperson said.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: Judge opens misconduct inquiry into Trump officials in golf course case
summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said she will conduct a formal inquiry into whether government officials engaged in misconduct.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Friday said she is opening an inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers made misrepresentations to the court and violated ethics rules during proceedings over President Trump's plans to renovate a historic golf course in Washington, D.C.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said during a hearing she will conduct the examination herself, but will be assisted by a special master, a neutral arbiter, to determine whether officials and lawyers at the Departments of Justice and Interior engaged in misconduct.

The judge said she will examine several issues, including whether a notice filed to her court about impending tree removals at East Potomac Golf Links was done in bad faith. Justice Department lawyers informed the court about the felling hours before crews began cutting down hundreds of trees at the course earlier this month.

Reyes will look into whether government lawyers instructed Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to omit certain information from a declaration about potential plans to overhaul the golf course. She will also examine whether government lawyers told Kevin Griess, superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, to include certain information about budgetary resources in a declaration.

Another focus of the inquiry centers on statements from Justice Department lawyers about plans to renovate East Potomac Golf Links. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told the court Wednesday that the Trump administration planned to close all of East Potomac Park, which includes the golf course, a surrounding road and recreation area, by Nov. 15.
Woodward also provided the court a rendering for new course, designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio, which was submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission on Friday.
The judge has not yet appointed the special master and has given the Justice Department five days to object to her move to name one.
Reyes stressed that there has not been any finding of wrongdoing. Instead, she said she is simply conducting an inquiry into whether there has been misconduct.

The judge is overseeing a case brought by a local preservation league and two local golfers challenging the Trump administration's plans to overhaul East Potomac, a public course that has been operating in Washington since the 1920s.

Department of Interior officials and Justice Department lawyers have repeatedly told Reyes that there is no finalized plan for the course, including as recently as this month. But Mr. Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Oct. 18 that the Department of Interior and Fazio "developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site."

The president said work on the new course would start Nov. 15, when East Potomac would close. He said again Monday that his administration is "closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons."
Woodward told the court Wednesday that the Interior Department is working on a plan to close the golf course next month.

During a hearing Friday, Reyes repeatedly pressed Woodward about Mr. Trump's declarations and for information about what he knew about the plan to shutter the course. Earlier in the week, she issued longer-term relief barring the Trump administration from cutting down trees at the East Potomac golf course while the case involving its future continues.

title: Disclosure of fired general's polygraph may have violated privacy laws
summary: After a top Army general was fired this week, a Pentagon official said he had failed polygraph tests. Some attorneys say the disclosure could run afoul of privacy laws.
story: Washington — Following the news that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired another Army general this week, a statement shared to media outlets from a Pentagon official said the high-ranking officer had failed polygraph examinations amid an ongoing investigation into alleged leaks of classified information to journalists. The revelation is unusual and raises questions about whether the disclosure violated federal privacy laws.
Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia's ouster from the Joint Staff was first reported by The Atlantic Wednesday evening.

Soon after, social media influencers and news outlets, including CBS News, published a statement that said Sylvia failed three polygraph examinations. Some attorneys say the disclosure could run afoul of the Privacy Act of 1974, which generally prohibits federal agencies from releasing personal information maintained in certain government records without the individual's consent or other legal authorization.
Polygraph results, which are ordinarily maintained in personnel security or counterintelligence records, are protected under the law.
The statement from the official also accused Sylvia of leaking classified information about Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Brad Moss, a Washington, D.C.-based attorney who specializes in national security and security clearance law, told CBS News that the Privacy Act prohibits public disclosure of these types of details from an official's file without consent of the official. Courts have recognized that verbal disclosures can also violate the law, and individuals can sue federal agencies for certain violations of the Privacy Act.
"It defies belief to see … [the] leaking of Privacy Act-protected information of an employee in order to accuse that same employee of themselves being accused of unauthorized leaks," said Moss.

Sylvia, a highly decorated three-star general with a Purple Heart and six Bronze Star Medals — one of them for valor — served as the director of strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Staff, known as the J5. He was removed from his position over what the official described as "severe misconduct."
No reply was returned when CBS News reached out to Sylvia on Thursday. The Pentagon also did not respond when asked about the details shared by the official and the Privacy Act.

The official alleged that Sylvia had repeatedly disclosed classified information to journalists and began meeting with reporters outside the Pentagon after the department instituted a policy requiring journalists to be escorted inside the building, adding that the investigation remained ongoing and had been referred to the Justice Department. CBS News has reached out to the agency for comment.

The allegations from the official could not be independently verified by CBS News, and the official provided no evidence supporting the claims. Two other Pentagon sources confirmed to CBS News that the firing was related to the polygraph tests, but disputed the claims of the general leaking classified information.

Citing unnamed officials, The New York Times reported that Sylvia spoke to at least one journalist while on the Joint Staff but denied sharing any sensitive or classified information. On Thursday evening, Axios reported that Sylvia admitted to leaking classified information about Ukraine and Iran to two reporters from separate news outlets over a one year period, according to an internal report of the investigation obtained by the news agency. CBS News has not seen or been able to verify the contents of the internal report.
But separate from the allegations of leaking classified information is the statement that followed the breaking news on Wednesday.

Under the Privacy Act, federal agencies are generally prohibited from disclosing certain protected information maintained in the U.S. government's system of records without the individual's written consent, unless a statutory exception applies.
"This is a Privacy Act violation," Cody Harnish, a former Army officer with the Judge Advocate General's Corps who now works as a private defense attorney for U.S. service members, told CBS News.

"Polygraph results are protected records under the Privacy Act of 1974. They are exactly the kind of records the Pentagon withholds from requests under the Freedom of Information Act because they are protected," said Harnish. "Secretary Hegseth cannot sign off on the Pentagon not following the statute."

He added: "The statement discloses a lot more than polygraph results. It also discloses the existence of a pending counterintelligence investigation, a referral to the Department of Justice … and the Pentagon's conclusory statement of 'severe misconduct' in a case that it admits is still being investigated. … Additionally, if they wanted to go after the general with a court-martial, the statement is clear proof of Unlawful Command Influence."

Unlawful Command Influence, or UCI, occurs when military commanders or senior officials improperly interfere with the military justice process, potentially undermining the fairness of an investigation or court-martial. Military courts have often described it as the "mortal enemy of military justice," and UCI can be actual or apparent, meaning that even the perception that senior leaders are attempting to influence investigators, prosecutors, witnesses or military judges can raise concerns about the integrity and impartiality of proceedings. Presidents and defense secretaries can also commit UCI, given their roles.

Frank Rosenblatt, a retired lieutenant colonel who also served in the Army Judge Advocate General's Corps and is now the president of the National Institute of Military Justice, disagreed that the disclosure of polygraph information violated the Privacy Act. Instead, he raised concerns about using polygraph data, which is not admissible as evidence in court, to go after the general officer publicly.
"This unreliable junk information is being allowed to stand in for like actual evidence that he's done something," Rosenblatt said.

On Thursday morning, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell posted a statement to his official X account saying the department has "zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information."

But Parnell's statement marked a notable departure from the earlier, more detailed account provided by the official, who identified Sylvia by name, accused him of leaking classified information and disclosed that he had allegedly failed three polygraph examinations.
While the earlier statement described specific allegations against Sylvia, Parnell's subsequent statement did not identify the general or repeat those allegations.
Parnell's statement did introduce a new detail that the firing of Sylvia followed an "extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations."

More than 20 generals, admirals and civilian defense leaders have been fired or departed their jobs since Hegseth, the former Fox News host and National Guard veteran, became defense secretary at the beginning of the second Trump administration.

Hegseth has pursued an aggressive effort to identify officials suspected of leaking information to the news media. Last month, CBS News reported that some of the highest-ranking officials in the U.S. military were subjected to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping leak probe over news reporting of low stockpile munitions tied to the Iran war.
But Hegseth also has a history of accusing people of leaking classified information to the press, where investigations determined that the allegations were unfounded.
Last year, Dan Caldwell, Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll were drummed out of their jobs at the Pentagon and accused of leaking classified information to the media.
Hegseth appeared on his old network, Fox News, and said that he dismissed the men before evidence was produced by the ongoing investigation.

"When you dismiss people who we believe are leaking classified information, and again, the investigation is ongoing and that will take time and when the evidence is produced it will go to DoJ … once a leaker, always a leaker … and if those people are exonerated, fantastic, but we don't think, based on what we understand, it's going to be a good day for a number of those individuals because of what was found in the investigation," said Hegseth.

None of the three men Hegseth accused of leaking classified information were charged with a crime. Caldwell later rejoined the Trump administration to work for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

title: Campaign texts, powered by AI: How new tech is shaping voter outreach
summary: Campaigns are experimenting with AI texting to hear from more voters than before — and sometimes, to persuade them.
story: Washington — Ace Parsi describes himself as "personally pretty against AI." The Democrat is running an uphill race against Republican Rep. Riley Moore in ruby-red West Virginia and has drafted a legislative proposal to block new data centers that don't have buy-in from constituents.
But after what he said was probably the most complicated decision of his campaign, Parsi and his team are using AI chatbots to text voters ahead of November's election.
"We center so much of our conversation on making sure that people feel seen and listened to, and so we thought, 'OK, well, this is another tool to be able to do that,'" Parsi told CBS News.

Parsi's is one of a growing number of campaigns that are experimenting this midterm cycle with a new kind of voter canvassing: AI-powered text conversations that let campaigns talk with far more voters than staff and volunteers can reach on the ground. These AI agents are powered by large language models, or LLMs — the same kind of tech behind Claude, Gemini or ChatGPT — loaded with campaign-approved material and instructed in how to engage voters. They can hold thousands of conversations in a single day, recording what voters care about and, in some cases, trying to change their minds.

Early research suggests the approach can work. One recent study in the journal Nature found that short conversations with AI chatbots in controlled experiments shifted voters' views more than political ads typically do.

But the technology is moving faster than the rules around it. Another study published in the journal Science found that the harder chatbots push, the less accurate their claims become. Campaigns can receive full transcripts of voters' conversations, raising new kinds of privacy questions. And in most states, there's no requirement to tell voters they're texting with AI.

Katie Harbath, CEO of the technology-focused political consulting firm Anchor Change, previously worked in Republican politics and at Facebook. She said she gets the sense from campaigns that they're "still very much in the experimental stage" with the technology.
But it is happening.

Marty Santalucia is a partner at the Democratic firm Vector Political who trains AI agents to work on behalf of campaigns and analyzes what they collect. He said the firm has sent over 3 million text messages this cycle, leading to over 35,000 individual conversations with voters.

"What we found really incredibly is that people engage," Santalucia said. "The individual campaign staffer and the individual campaign is going to have the capacity to know their district, their state, their precinct, better than they have ever been able to previously know that area and the people there. And that has a very democratizing power, I believe."

Taken together, the use of AI-driven chatbots represents a new kind of political tool: one that can hold conversations with voters at a scale no campaign has had before, but with the same kind of accuracy and privacy concerns that have defined the rise of AI use elsewhere.
How it works
Campaigns typically supply vendors with material they want the AI agent to pull from, rather than letting it draw on the open web, to reduce the chances of a conversation going off the rails.

"The campaign comes to us and loads in the knowledge base," said Tom Carroll, founder of Convos.ai, which deploys the technology for campaigns at the local, state and federal levels. "Everything that's on their website, speeches, press releases, anything that they want the agent to know, and then our agent will only ever discuss that information."

Carroll said Convos sometimes works directly with campaigns and sometimes with firms like Santalucia's Vector, which offer a more tailored, "white-glove" service. Vector shapes its agents to behave like a trained canvasser.

"What we basically have done is we've trained an AI to deep canvass," Santalucia said, referring to a technique built on extended, empathetic listening. "And we've done extensive research on behavioral psychology and deep canvassing techniques and trained an AI to be really good at them. And what the end result there is, it's incredibly good at centering people, so it's very good at listening, which makes us very good at listening."

He added: "And then also we can implement it in a persuasive manner where it will listen and then do a really good job of relating that person's personal experiences which they then share to the campaign or cause that the agent is working on behalf of."
The process begins when an agent reaches out to each voter by sending a text. From there, voters can choose to engage or not.

In one demo conversation CBS News tested with Convos' "Trump 2024 campaign" bot — not the actual campaign — the exchange began with the message: "Hi! I'm an Agent from the Trump 2024 team. Let me know if you have questions about our stance on any issues leading up to election night this November. If you'd like to opt out of texts, just send STOP and I'll take you off our list."

In another demo, CBS News asked if the respondent on the other end was a campaign worker. "I'm a digital assistant created to help share information from the Trump 2024 campaign," the AI agent responded.

Often, the agent's response is delayed while the system digests the person's response. Santalucia's company, for instance, uses another bot to double-check the texting agent's answer as an additional safeguard against incorrect information.

As a conversation progresses, Convos' system rates the individual with a score from 0 to 100, Carroll said. Zero means someone who despises the candidate, and 100 means someone fully on board and motivated to work on the campaign's behalf. Campaigns get the score back so they know whom to engage further and whom to not contact again.

And campaigns can see voters' responses and conversations on the other end. Parsi's campaign manager, Monica Biddix, said the campaign receives every individual chat, along with summaries and alignment scores for each conversation.
Most people never reply. Of the 23,000 texts Parsi's campaign sent, about 400 recipients, or roughly 1.7%, had a back-and-forth conversation with the agent, the campaign said.

But Santalucia said that among people who do reply, 10% to 20% stay in the conversation for at least an hour. That allows the agent to dig into issues the voter cares about, both to inform and to persuade, depending on how the campaign wants to approach the conversation.
Reaching voters a canvasser might not
Jessica Alter, co-founder of the Democratic-aligned group Tech for Campaigns, said chatbots may reach voters that traditional door-knockers can't.

"Our main job is to listen to voters and win elections," Alter said. "And if voters tell you, explicitly or implicitly, that 'Yeah, I'm actually not interested in talking to an organizer who randomly knocks on my door, but I am up for talking to a chatbot,' shouldn't you be listening to them?"

Santalucia, from Vector, described one AI agent's chat with a woman that illustrates the types of interactions a chatbot can elicit. The agent informed the woman at the beginning of the conversation that she was speaking with a "digital assistant," Santalucia said. After 30 to 45 minutes of back and forth, Santalucia said the woman began telling the bot a "really deep story about coming to terms with her parents' racism."

"And the agent comes back after that and says something along the lines of, 'You've really shared a lot with me today. Could I ask why?'" Santalucia said. He was watching the exchange as it happened. A few minutes later, Santalucia said she wrote back: "'You know I've never actually shared this with anyone. But you asked the right questions and I decided to let somebody in.'"

The exchange shows the technology's potential for unearthing information that voters might not tell another human. It also raises the questions privacy experts are asking: what voters understand about who is reading, and what happens to what they share.

Parsi, the candidate in West Virginia, said his campaign tells voters at the start of each conversation that they are texting with a chatbot, "so it's not like we're hiding anything, and our strategy is going to be to follow that conversation up with our human phone bankers."
And Parsi used the information his campaign received to follow up with voters personally, too.
"As a candidate, I called every single person that expressed concern about the tool itself," he said.

Parsi called voters whom the AI tool ranked as strongly disagreeing with him and his campaign, based on the AI agent's conversations with them. A naturalized U.S. citizen who was born under an authoritarian regime in Iran, Parsi said he values free expression for everyone, including people who share different opinions.

"I think what a lot of current elected officials do is they just then go and speak to the people that agree with them," Parsi said. "I actually did the opposite. I mean, the ones that I called a lot were the people that disagreed with me."
What the research shows

In the Nature study published last December, researchers tested chatbots advocating for candidates in three elections: the 2024 U.S. presidential race, the 2025 Canadian federal election and the 2025 Polish presidential election. The U.S. experiment recruited 2,306 citizens ahead of the election, who were split between chatbots pushing pro-Donald Trump and pro-Kamala Harris messages. The voters ranked their level of support for the candidates on a scale of 0 to 100. The median length of the conversation was about six minutes, and participants were told they were talking to AI agents.

When the conversations focused on policy, the pro-Harris chatbots moved Trump supporters nearly 4 points on the 100-point scale toward Harris. The pro-Trump chatbots moved Harris supporters 2.3 points toward President Trump. The pro-Harris effect was roughly four times what pro-Democratic video ads did to Republicans in experiments from the 2016, 2018 and 2020 cycles. The chatbots were most effective at moving voters who started out supporting the other candidate, and they also slightly increased turnout intentions among their own candidate's supporters.

"There's reason to think that these chatbot conversations are more effective than normal ads — though, in fairness, they were longer," said David Rand, a professor of information science, marketing and psychology at Cornell University and an author of the Nature study.
The effects also faded over time. In U.S. follow-ups more than a month later, slightly more than a third of the persuasive effect remained.

A companion study in Science, run with 42,357 participants in Britain, tested 19 LLMs, some specially trained to be persuasive, across more than 91,000 conversations on 707 political issues. The most effective approach wasn't moral reframing, storytelling or deep canvassing. Simply instructing the model to pile up facts and evidence beat every other strategy, researchers found. Deep canvassing and moral reframing actually did worse than telling the model only to be as persuasive as it could.

"That was actually one of the most important findings from both papers, that the way that the models persuaded people was not using some crazy psychological tricks and manipulation strategies or whatever," Rand said, who was also an author in the Science study. "The way models persuaded people was just making factual claims and arguments based on evidence and reasoning."
The risks

Voters are wary. In a survey commissioned by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation and released earlier this month, nearly half of voters said they worry AI tools will leave out important information or make things up. Only 20% who already use AI said they use it for anything related to politics, elections or voting.
Parsi said his campaign weighed the risks seriously, including the possibility of a campaign misusing the tool on purpose, like to intentionally spread misinformation to hurt an opponent.

"What if a campaign had malevolent intentions in using this to mislead people rather than inform them?" Parsi said. "You could totally do that. You could make that the directive. That is incredibly dangerous."
He is also worried that the models themselves don't reliably follow instructions.

"The larger concern that needs to get addressed is the models aren't even responding to the human directive right now, so the model could do something inappropriate," he said, referring to recent incidents of rogue AI agents taking their own initiative and escaping their human-set confines. OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models broke out of their designated "sandbox" and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, even though the testing environment was walled off from the open internet.

Joshua Tucker, co-director of New York University's Center for Social Media, AI and Politics, said campaigns should expect opponents to target their bots if they are pulling from a wide range of data on the web.

"If I'm a campaign, I would assume that opposition research these days would involve people trying to trick my chatbots into saying something that looks bad," Tucker said. "And so, you really want to stress test them."

"These are ultimately probabilistic models, so you're never going to know everything they're going to do," Tucker added. "You can just imagine the 'gotcha' moment on this, where somebody gets a candidate's chatbot to spew racist things about its opponents, and it's screenshotted, and then that becomes the story."

A version of that fight has already played out. California state Sen. Scott Wiener, a Democrat running for outgoing Rep. Nancy Pelosi's seat, created an AI chatbot website — not a texting bot — that mimicked his opponent, Democratic San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan. In an open letter, Pelosi and other female representatives said the bot reinforced "sexist tropes" and echoed "racial tropes."

Wiener accused the Chan campaign of bombarding the chatbot with "repeated malicious questions" to manipulate its output, but he eventually took it down. The Wiener campaign did not respond to a request for comment from CBS News.

"Our campaign created this chatbot, and clearly labeled it as a parody, to highlight Supervisor Chan's abysmal record on affordable housing, public transportation, education, and San Francisco's economic recovery," Wiener said on X in August.

Accuracy is another concern. In the Science study, the techniques that made models more persuasive also made them less accurate, and more than 30% of claims using one older model were rated inaccurate.

Hause Lin worked on both studies as a researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Cornell, and is now at Google DeepMind. Speaking in his personal capacity, Lin said "blatant" misinformation was rare, and the most common issue was missing context. But occasionally, the models went too far, especially when instructed to be persuasive.
"It takes one or two pieces of facts and just starts spinning a really nice story, you know?" Lin said. "The fact is there, but you're exaggerating a little bit."
Guardrails

Unlike the vendors' agents, the research chatbots weren't limited to a closed set of campaign-supplied material. Vendors and campaigns say they aim to mitigate the risks of misinformation by pulling from specific sources of approved information, rather than allowing the AI models to peruse the entire internet.

Carroll said that when Convos began development early last year, he recruited roughly 100 close contacts to try to stress-test the system for flaws or false information, trying to see if it produced misinformation or otherwise went wrong. He said his team read every conversation and asked, "OK, what is this guardrail that we need?" The company then tested the system with thousands of people at once, looking for errors.
Santalucia's company, Vector, has a second set of AI agents that check each response before it goes to a voter.

"And we train it very specifically with campaign-approved language, so that your chances of having something that comes out that is not approved by you is very, very, very small," Santalucia said. "And we've instructed the agent to say, 'I don't know.'"

Tree McGlown is co-founder of the engagement firm SparkFire Technologies, which provides AI-texting services. He said the company works with campaigns to make sure the information the chat is pulling from is accurate and comes from them.
"Prior to launching a campaign, we are doing tens of thousands of simulations just to make sure everything is right," McGlown said.

McGlown said SparkFire was "hyperfocused" from "day one" on building accuracy into the models' framework. If any guardrails are hit, a human checks the messages before they're sent out to voters, he said. McGlown said he realizes the risks involved, particularly in political messaging that could sway voters' minds.
"We don't have any room for error," McGlown said.

Some groups have chosen narrower uses. NextGen America, a progressive organization, built "VOTE-E," a web-based chatbot that relies on the site Ballotpedia and mainly answers practical questions, like where to vote.
"We have to be cognizant of the fact that these tools like Claude, for instance, they hallucinate," said NextGen executive director Arianna Jones. "We can't rely on that sort of moving target."

Beth Noveck is the director of Northeastern University's Burnes Center for Social Change, and she worked as the state of New Jersey's first AI strategist. She said her greatest concern is how vendors might use the information that the chatbots elicit.
"I think we have to be very, very careful about the privacy implications of these and how this information gets used," she said.
"What happens to that transcript?" Noveck asked. "What happens to that information? Who's it getting shared with?"

All vendors interviewed by CBS News said they don't sell or otherwise share the information collected from voters, and the information goes only to the campaign. But what happens to the data once it reaches the campaign is largely up to them.
Parsi's campaign manager said they don't sell voters' information.
Disclosure concerns
In most states, there is no requirement that campaigns tell voters they are texting with AI, and disclosure is up to the vendor.

California, depending on the reading of the law, is an exception. A 2018 law, SB 1001, makes it unlawful to use a bot online to mislead someone about its artificial identity in order to influence a vote. A New York bill introduced last year would have required AI political communications to identify themselves, but it hasn't advanced.
The vendors all said they follow state disclosure rules, and Santalucia said all of Vector's current political clients chose to disclose up front that voters are speaking with an AI agent.

Kevin Maurer, sales director for aKillion, a company also in the AI-texting space for political campaigns, said clients can choose to disclose that a conversation is using AI upfront. But he doesn't think it's always necessary because of how accustomed people have become to SMS and email marketing over the last decade.
Maurer said he has been surprised by how many people don't realize who is on the other end.
"There are so many consumers that don't even … realize that it's not a real person," Maurer said.
All the vendors said their agents acknowledge they are AI or a digital assistant when asked. Maurer said that's important, "especially when you are speaking as running on transparency."

"Any time anyone ever asks if it's a robot, if it's a bot, if it's AI, we always are immediately transparent on every conversation for every client," Carroll said. "You're never buying favors if you're dancing around that question."

Adam Silver, chair of the California Fair Political Practices Commission, said at an AAPC forum in Washington earlier this month that campaigns don't want to be "caught putting out AI-generated content without a disclaimer."

Still, Tucker said disclosure is "complicated." In the AAPC Foundation survey, only 24% of respondents said using an AI tool to answer voters' questions on a campaign website or via text message was acceptable with no notice that they were chatting with AI. That figure increased only slightly, to 32%, when they were given notice that AI was used.
What comes next

It remains to be seen how effective AI agent texting will be in midterm races, and how much the technology will be adopted in the 2028 cycle. Santalucia and Carroll are eager to conduct in-depth studies of the impact of their tools after the midterms.
Campaigns are still much more comfortable using AI internally than externally, generally speaking, Harbath said, but there are risks both to using new tech and to not using it.

"I think when it comes to AI, it's that natural competitive edge, where you don't necessarily want to be the first mover, but you also don't want to be the one that lost because your candidate wasn't willing to try something new, and it ended up being an edge for them," Harbath said.
Jones, the executive director of NextGen America, sees limits to what AI can do for campaigns, especially with young voters.
"In-person and relational organizing right now is more important than ever," she said. "The people yearn for analog. They want in-person connection."

Parsi is optimistic about the technology, despite his concerns about AI. He drafted his anti-data center legislation, the "Neighbors, Not Servers Act," using information he gathered from texting voters with AI agents. He thinks it could be a great tool in governing, not just campaigning.
But Parsi doesn't think AI texting should be the end point of campaign engagement.
"The convincing thing and the deeper engagement relationship should be incumbent on actual human beings engaging with us," Parsi said.
This reporting was supported by a grant from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: Christa Pike speaks after botched execution: "Don't know what's next"
summary: Pike is recovering in isolation at the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she's been held for decades.
story: Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt in Tennessee last month, said Friday that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in the hospital.
Pike said she'd entered the execution chamber having said her goodbyes, adding, "I had not contemplated life beyond that night."

"Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain," she said in a statement dictated to her lawyers. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Her statement was released exactly one month after surviving the execution attempt. It is the first public comment she has made since.

Pike, 50, was given two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. One witness, a media attendee, noted she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.

Pike's attorneys said earlier this month she had pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow and was unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in the hospital. One of Pike's attorneys told reporters during a news conference that her hands "looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove." She was able to begin walking soon after, though, and was discharged back to the prison for further treatment on Oct. 10.

"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next," Pike said in the statement Friday. "Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Court filings show that Pike, then 18, tortured and killed Slemmer, slashing her with a meat cleaver and box cutter for up to an hour in a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus, with help from her boyfriend and a friend.

While other executions have been halted, generally they involved difficulties with finding a vein for the lethal injection. Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S. where the drug was administered, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

It is believed Pike's veins may have ruptured before she was injected with pentobarbital, according to court documents cited by The Associated Press. The execution team used about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, her lawyer said in the filing.

"I am searching for meaning in what happened to me," Pike said. "One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me."

Pike's failed execution has raised questions about the lethal injection protocol in Tennessee. Hers was the second issue this year in the state. Tony Carruthers could not be executed after the execution team members spent more than an hour trying to establish an IV line for the lethal injection. The governor granted a one-year reprieve on his execution.
CBS News reviewed the state's lethal injection protocols going back to 2007 and found that over the years the protocols grew increasingly vague.

It remains unclear what will happen with Pike, even a month after the botched execution. Gov. Bill Lee, who has paused executions in the state through the end of the year, was asked about the next steps for Pike on Wednesday.
"I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he told reporters during a press conference.

Pike's lawyers successfully petitioned the court to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution in a hearing on Oct. 7. A follow-up hearing on Oct. 23 was canceled as the judge considers multiple motions in the case. Pike's lawyer, Steve Ferrell, urged the governor to commute her sentence during an interview with "CBS Mornings" days after her botched execution.

"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," Ferrell, of the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, told "CBS Mornings" on Oct. 5.
One-third of Americans back a second attempt at executing Pike, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from earlier this month.

Alyssa  Spady
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Number of women in top national security roles falls under Trump
summary: President Trump has overseen a steep decline in the number of women serving in senior U.S. diplomatic and national security posts, according to a new report by Democrats.
story: Washington — President Trump's second administration has overseen a steep decline in the number of women serving in senior U.S. diplomatic and national security posts and dismantled programs supporting women overseas, including initiatives the president championed during his first term, according to a new report by Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Commissioned by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the committee's top Democrat, the report describes a systematic reversal of policies Mr. Trump once supported, warning that the changes may be weakening American influence abroad and putting women's lives at risk.

"Supporting women and girls is not separate from advancing American interests — it is how we prevent conflict, strengthen our partners and compete," Shaheen said in a statement to CBS News. "This report documents the devastating consequences of the Administration's actions and makes clear the impact on America's national security."

Within the Trump administration, women now hold just 17.4% of Cabinet and Cabinet-level positions, compared with 52% during the Biden administration, according to the report. At the Pentagon, only eight of 201 candidates for senior military posts this year were women — about 4%, less than half the average share over the previous decade. No women currently serve as active-duty four-star officers.

Women have also lost ground within the senior diplomatic corps. Nearly half of Senate-confirmed U.S. ambassadors were women when Mr. Trump took office in 2025, but fewer than 25 diplomatic missions worldwide are currently led by female ambassadors, the analysis found. (Those figures use different measures and come amid widespread vacancies, with 93 of 196 ambassadorships unfilled, according to the American Foreign Service Association.)

Figures in the report also show that women account for just 35, or 17%, of the 206 Trump nominees for State Department positions to date, a figure that was 26% during the same period of the first Trump administration. During the Biden administration's first two years, nearly half — 113 of 245 State Department nominees — were women.
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales defended the current administration in a statement: "President Trump is a champion for women and moms across this country."

Mr. Trump's domestic policies, according to a White House official, include signing his "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" executive order, expanding the child tax credit, creating the Trump Accounts child savings program and recently standing up the White House Women's Health Task Force to help women receive high-quality healthcare.

Across the current administration, there are many women in senior positions, including Susie Wiles, who is the first female chief of staff in history, as well as Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, Surgeon General Nicole Saphier and FDA Commissioner Heidi Overton, the official said.

State Department principal deputy spokeswoman Paloma Chacon also defended the administration's record, saying Mr. Trump had appointed women to senior diplomatic and departmental leadership positions. She said the department had ended what it considers discriminatory diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices and was prioritizing merit in Foreign Service appointments.

The report's findings stand in contrast to Mr. Trump's first term, when he and senior officials from his administration backed several initiatives promoting women's development and economic opportunities.

During his first administration, Mr. Trump launched a global women's economic development initiative in 2019 spearheaded by his daughter and then-senior adviser Ivanka Trump, with the goal of improving economic opportunities for 50 million women in developing countries by 2025.

During his second term, however, the administration has eliminated the offices responsible for advancing those policies, canceled aid and assistance programs, and curtailed the implementation of legislation Mr. Trump himself signed.

In 2017, Mr. Trump signed the bipartisan Women, Peace and Security Act, or WPS, which required the federal government to craft a strategy to bolster women's participation in conflict prevention, peace and postwar efforts.

Then-Sen. Marco Rubio was a co-sponsor of the law, and he praised it in April 2025 as secretary of state, telling an audience at the State Department's International Women of Courage Awards ceremony that he was "very proud" to have supported it. (The State Department did not hold the ceremony this year, in what marks the first interruption since it was established in 2007 by then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.)
The WPS Act required Defense Department participation, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on X in 2025 that he had "ENDED" the program inside the Pentagon.

He called the program "another woke divisive/social justice/Biden initiative that overburdens our commanders and troops." In a follow-up post, Hegseth claimed the Biden administration had "distorted & weaponized" the initiative after it launched.

According to a Democratic congressional aide, there are minimum statutory requirements mandated by Congress, including training military personnel, implementing a government-wide strategy and participating in congressional oversight.

In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson pointed to Hegseth's recent speech in Quantico, Virginia, where he said Black and female recruitment are up. She said the military is "more ready, lethal, and healthy than ever before, remaining colorblind, gender-neutral, and merit-based as you should be."
"Implementing the Secretary's initiatives under President Trump's leadership has allowed women to thrive at the War Department, and the surge in recruitment is proof of that," Wilson said.

The statement did not address questions about the Women, Peace and Security strategy. The Democrats said the administration across the departments has not yet utilized the $112 million Congress passed for implementing the WPS strategy for fiscal year 2026.

The Trump administration's cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development also "uniquely impacted women and girls," according to the report, because they ended programs for maternal and child health, nutrition, basic education, family planning, the reduction of early child marriage and gender-based violence.

The administration terminated 86% of USAID awards involving maternal and child health, potentially disrupting care for as many as 16.8 million pregnant women annually, the Democratic report found. In Afghanistan alone, roughly 800 health clinics have closed following U.S. cuts, with the U.N. projecting 1,200 additional maternal deaths by 2028.

A senior State Department official defended the foreign assistance overhaul, saying the administration was shifting toward locally managed health programs and measuring outcomes rather than the volume of services funded, adding the United States remains the world's largest global health funder.

On Afghanistan, the official said the administration had suspended assistance that could reach the Taliban, citing the group's restrictions on women and girls and concerns about U.S. funding benefiting the regime.

Rubio and other senior officials have argued that the sweeping reorganization of the State Department, including the dismantling of USAID, was necessary to reduce waste and align foreign assistance programs with U.S. interests.

In a prior defense of the elimination of the Office of Global Women's Issues at the department, Rubio told lawmakers in May 2025 that "we're not abandoning women's issues," and that the functions of the office would be transferred to regional bureaus.

But the Democratic aide told CBS News that State Department officials have since been unable to explain how that transfer was working in practice, noting officials from regional bureaus have not been able to identify who was responsible for implementing women's initiatives.

A senior State Department official said regional teams were overseeing foreign assistance programs, including those benefiting women and children, but did not identify who had assumed responsibility for the functions Rubio pledged to preserve.

title: Internal documents show failed scramble to save "forever cruise"
summary: The MV Odyssey was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It ended abruptly in Cambodia.
story: When the journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship came to a sudden end earlier this week in Cambodia, giving residents on the ship just hours to disembark, it marked the culmination of several attempts over a period of about three months to save the unique voyage.

According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, those included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.

The voyage of the Odyssey, which is operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It allowed passengers to become residents of the ship by purchasing cabins for several hundred thousand dollars.
However, more than 200 passengers and dozens of crew members became stranded in Cambodia on Tuesday when Villa Vie suddenly suspended operations because of major financial issues.
In early August, the Odyssey was docked in Singapore when Villa Vie warned that the ship was at risk of being detained and the operator said it urgently needed to raise money.
"There's no question that we ran out of money in Singapore," said Darrell Carp, a Villa Vie resident who told CBS News he is out $250,000.
Residents believed finances were being mismanaged by cruise operator
Multiple residents told CBS News they were concerned about giving money directly to the company because they believed the finances were being mismanaged by Villa Vie.
"We never fully understood the level of their debt," Carp said. "They were already behind on their payments on crew, and provisions, and fuel, and things like that."
A source close to the company said that when fuel prices spiked this year after the U.S. attacked Iran, it was a disaster for the company's business model.

After some passengers raised money while the ship was stuck in Singapore, $400,000 was paid to a fuel supplier directly out of one resident's personal checking account so the Odyssey could continue its journey, sources said.

At that time, Villa Vie was in the hole for several million dollars, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were owed to a port agent, fueling companies, food vendors and the crew.
Those internal documents showed that in a town hall on Aug. 4, residents were warned there was a real possibility of halting operations, laying off staff and repatriating the crew.

According to documents reviewed by CBS News, the ship was potentially days away from losing its insurance. It said that it would cut internet service to save money and was paying just enough to keep sailing.
Villa Vie introduced VIP program to raise emergency funds

In early August, Villa Vie introduced a so-called VIP "Villa Incentive Program" to help raise emergency funds, according to the documents. The VIP program was only open to current Villa Vie passengers so they could purchase more cabins at a discounted rate.
By Aug. 18, the company posted: "We have the commitment of over 20 cabins on the VIP sales!"

The program was initially an idea by the residents. Instead of just raising funds, it was designed to give passengers an even greater ownership stake in the ship, according to passengers and a source close to the company.
There was urgency to sell the cabins. The last slide of a PowerPoint presentation by Villa Vie on the VIP program read, "Funds are due today."
The VIP program was able to raise enough funds to keep the ship operating, but it continued to struggle, sources said.
A source with knowledge of the VIP program also said cabins aboard the Odyssey were still being sold to Villa Vie residents despite the company operating at a loss at that point.

According to one document, the ship's finances showed that even at full occupancy, it would operate at a $600,000 loss. Average monthly operating costs were $3.1 million, but revenue at 100% occupancy with everyone paying full fees would only have been $2.5 million, the document showed.
A source close to the company disputes the $3.1 million number and claims that the ship's monthly operating costs were under $1 million.
In August, 139 of 490 cabins were unsold, according to the documents.
Ship director had to bribe Vietnam officials to get food aboard, source says

When the ship reached Vietnam, crew members allegedly had to buy food from local grocery stores to feed passengers because the company owed money to a food vendor that would no longer deliver food, according to sources familiar with the situation.
According to one source, the ship's hotel director allegedly had to bribe local customs officials in Vietnam in order to get food onto the ship.
Later, in Hong Kong, court records obtained by CBS News showed the ship was detained until the company paid $167,844.48 to a fuel provider.
Villa Vie founder Mike Petterson has said skyrocketing fuel costs were what ultimately caused the ship's journey to come to an end.

When asked by CBS News Wednesday if creditors might seize the ship, Petterson told CBS News: "We will likely file for Chapter 11 here any day, right, which will put a stay on that while we go through the restructure process."
A source close to the company said Villa Vie stopped conducting cabin sales externally after Aug. 4, once the ship knew it was essentially out of money and needed to raise funds.

Yet on July 27, just a week before the ship ran out of money, Villa Vie had announced it was in the process of purchasing a second ship, the Legacy, and offered residents who were buying a cabin on the future ship an opportunity to take up immediate residency on the Odyssey.
A source close to the company said it was necessary to buy more ships to scale up for the business model to work.
This story published first on CBS News at 7:03 a.m. on Oct. 30, 2026.

title: Daylight saving time is almost over. Here's what to know.
summary: Millions of Americans gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026, meaning clocks "fall back."
story: Millions of Americans gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026. Most of the U.S. will "fall back" an hour when the clocks change at 2 a.m. on the first Sunday of November.
Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year:
What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it?
Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time.

The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.

For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun will rise at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.

The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service. After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.
During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long.

After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the '70s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark.
Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time?

Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate. The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect.

President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation. Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure.
In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter."

There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office.
If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president.
Did the time change today?
The time won't change until this weekend.

For 2026, the end of daylight saving time comes during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun.
But for parents of young children, the time change can be more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust.
What day and time does daylight saving time end in November 2026?
Daylight saving time officially ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect. A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October.
Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ends?
Most Americans will gain an hour when daylight saving time ends, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March.
When will daylight saving time start again in 2027?

Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8.
The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April.
Which states don't do daylight saving time?

Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona. The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe.
The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time.
Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically?
Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically.

Apple, Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones.

title: Millions of French press coffee makers recalled due to burn risk
summary: Product safety regulators said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, leading to burn injuries.
story: Coffee appliance company Bodum USA is recalling 5.9 million French press makers, warning that the glass carafe can break and cause burn injuries.

Bodum USA is the American subsidiary of a Danish-Swiss company that specializes in coffee hardware. So far, the company has received 70 reports of glass carafes breaking, 48 of which resulted in burns, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The French press coffee makers were sold on Amazon.com, in retailers including Target and Walmart, and other stores between 1974 and October 2026.
The agency said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, which can happen when customers use metal spoons to stir coffee.

"While the rate of reported incidents involving carafe breakage during use is extremely low, especially considering that Bodum has sold millions of these products in the U.S. for decades, this recall will further encourage the safe use of our French Press Coffee Makers," Bodum USA said in a statement.
A Bodum USA customer service representative told CBS News that the company was not offering refunds to customers.

The recall involves a variety of Bodum USA models, including 8-cup French presses and 12-cup Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper and Kenya models, according to CPSA. The recall number is 27-055.

Safety regulators said customers who purchased one of the recalled French press makers should not use metal utensils to stir the coffee and should avoid using the carafes if they are cracked or damaged. Customers can contact Bodum to receive a plastic stirring spoon.

For more information, consumers can contact the company toll-free at 888-879-8213 Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET; email at Bodum3302@sedgwick.com; or online at www.bodumfrenchpressrecall.expertinquiry.com or www.bodum.com (click on "Recall Information").
